extraction_notes.note: The blueprint's `construction` environment is not declared by \newtheorem, so latex_facts reports no facts for its 23 instances; each was extracted as a prose node (a definition, or a claim plus a prose proof when it mainly asserts a result), and \cref's to construction labels were turned into named uses edges by hand.
definition or claim: these constructions both define an object and verify a property of it inline; typed definition because later nodes cite them for the object.
The base-change construction opens with a sentence announcing the conclusion; that sentence is the claim, the rest of the environment its proof.

\cref{cor:to-2-cocylce-wd} is a typo for cor:to-2-cocycle-wd and does not resolve; the uses edges it states were added by hand. The proof environment after lem:centralizer-inclusion-tensor is separated from it by a sentence, so its proves edge was added by hand.

All content is standard algebra re-proved for formalization with no citations; named classical theorems and standard definitions are origin external (standard, uncited), while the blueprint-specific auxiliary lemmas and constructions are origin paper.

Short prose asides ("the symmetric statement goes without saying", "this lemma can be generalized ..."), motivational section introductions, and the empty final chapter (Division Algebra over Local Fields) give no nodes.

nodes.name: Simple Ring
nodes.statement: A ring $R$ is simple if the only two-sided-ideals of $R$ are ${0}$ and $R$. An algebra is simple if it is simple as a ring.
differentia: the only two-sided-ideals of $R$ are ${0}$ and $R$

nodes.name: Division rings are simple
nodes.statement: Division rings are simple.

nodes.name: Centre of a simple ring is a field
nodes.statement: Let $A$ be a simple ring, then centre of $A$ is a field.
nodes.label: lem:center-simple-ring

nodes.name: Proof of Centre of a simple ring is a field
nodes.statement: Let $0\ne x$ be an element of centre of $A$. Then $I := \{xy | y\in A\}$ is a two-sided-ideal of $A$. Since $0\ne x\in I$, we have that $I = A$. Therefore $1 \in I$, hence $x$ is invertible.
nodes.statement_short: Multiplication by a nonzero central element generates a two-sided ideal, which must be $A$, so the element is invertible.

nodes.name: Ideal generated by x
nodes.statement: Let $0\ne x$ be an element of centre of $A$. Then $I := \{xy | y\in A\}$ is a two-sided-ideal of $A$.
nodes.statement_short: Introduce the ideal $I=xA$ for a nonzero central $x$.

nodes.name: I = A, so x invertible
nodes.statement: Since $0\ne x\in I$, we have that $I = A$. Therefore $1 \in I$, hence $x$ is invertible.
nodes.statement_short: Simplicity gives $I=A$, so $1\in I$ and $x$ is invertible.

nodes.name: Central Algebra
nodes.statement: Let $R$ be a ring and $A$ an $R$-algebra, we say $A$ is central if and only if the centre of $A$ is $R$

nodes.name: Commutative ring is central over itself
nodes.statement: Every commutative ring is a central algebra over itself.

nodes.name: Invariance of simpleness and centrality under isomorphism
nodes.statement: Simpleness is invariant under ring isomorphism and centrality is invariant under algebra isomorphism.

nodes.name: Opposite of a central algebra is central
nodes.statement: If $A$ is a central $R$-algerba, $A^{\opp}$ is also central. .
nodes.label: lem:opp-central

nodes.name: Characterization of simple rings by ring homomorphisms
nodes.statement: $R$ is a simple ring if and only if any ring homomorphism $f : R \to S$ either injective or $S$ is the trivial ring.
conclusions: $R$ is a simple ring if and only if any ring homomorphism $f : R \to S$ either injective or $S$ is the trivial ring
equivalent_conditions: any ring homomorphism $f : R \to S$ either injective or $S$ is the trivial ring
nodes.label: lem:simple-ring-iff

nodes.name: Proof of Characterization of simple rings by ring homomorphisms
nodes.statement: If $R$ is simple, then the $\ker f$ is either $\{0\}$ or $R$. The former case implies that $f$ is injective while the latter case implies that $S$ is the trivial ring. Conversely, let $I\subseteq R$ be a two-sided-ideal. Consider $\pi: R \to {}^{R}/_{I}$, either $\pi$ is injective implying that $I = \{0\}$ or that ${}^{R}/_{I}$ is the trivial ring implying that $I = R$.
nodes.statement_short: Kernel of $f$ is $0$ or $R$; conversely use the quotient map by an ideal.

nodes.name: Forward direction
nodes.statement: If $R$ is simple, then the $\ker f$ is either $\{0\}$ or $R$. The former case implies that $f$ is injective while the latter case implies that $S$ is the trivial ring.
nodes.statement_short: If $R$ is simple, $\ker f$ is $0$ or $R$.

nodes.name: Converse
nodes.statement: Conversely, let $I\subseteq R$ be a two-sided-ideal. Consider $\pi: R \to {}^{R}/_{I}$, either $\pi$ is injective implying that $I = \{0\}$ or that ${}^{R}/_{I}$ is the trivial ring implying that $I = R$.
nodes.statement_short: Apply the hypothesis to the quotient map $R\to R/I$.

nodes.name: Algebra-homomorphism version of the simple ring criterion
nodes.statement: If $A$ is a simple $R$-algebra, ``ring homomorphism'' in \cref{lem:simple-ring-iff} can be replaced with $R$-algebra homomorphism.

nodes.name: Algebra homomorphism between simple algebras of equal dimension is bijective
nodes.statement: Assume $R$ is a field. Let $A, B$ be finite dimensional $R$-algebras where $A$ is simple as well. Then any $R$-algebra homomorphism $f:A\to B$ is bijective if $\dim_{R}A=\dim_{R}B$.
assumptions: $A, B$ be finite dimensional $R$-algebras where $A$ is simple as well
nodes.label: cor:alghom-bijective-of-dim-eq

nodes.name: Proof of Algebra homomorphism between simple algebras of equal dimension is bijective
nodes.statement: By~\cref{lem:simple-ring-iff}, $f$is injective. Then $\dim_{K}\im f = \dim_{K} B - \dim_{K}\ker f = \dim_{K}B$ meaning that $f$ is surjective.
nodes.statement_short: Injectivity from the simple-ring criterion, surjectivity by dimension count.

nodes.name: Standing notation: field K and K-algebras A, B
nodes.statement: Let $K$ be a field and $A, B$ be $K$-algebras.

nodes.name: Tensor product of central algebras is central
nodes.statement: If $A$ and $B$ are central $K$-algebras, $A\otimes_{K}B$ is a central $K$-algebra as well.
nodes.label: lem:tensor-central

nodes.name: Proof of Tensor product of central algebras is central
nodes.statement: Assume $A$ and $B$ are central algebras, then by~\cref{cor:center-tensor-center} $Z\left(A\otimes_{R}B\right)=Z\left(A\right)\otimes_{R}Z\left(B\right)=R\otimes_{R}R=R$.
nodes.statement_short: Centre of tensor product is tensor of centres, which is $R$.

nodes.name: Tensor product of a simple and a central simple algebra is central simple
nodes.statement: If $A$ is a simple $K$-algebra and $B$ is a central simple $K$-algebra, $A\otimes_{K}B$ is a central simple $K$-algebra as well.
conclusions: $A\otimes_{K}B$ is a central simple $K$-algebra as well
nodes.label: thm:tensor-csa

nodes.name: Proof of Tensor product of a simple and a central simple algebra is central simple
nodes.statement: By~\cref{lem:tensor-central}, we need to prove $A\otimes_{K}B$ is a simple ring. Denote $f$ as the map $A\to A\otimes_{K}B$. It is sufficient to prove that for every two-sided-ideal $I\subseteq A\otimes_{K}B$, we have $I = \left\langle f\left(f^{-1}\left(I\right)\right)\right\rangle$. Indeed, since $A$ is simple $f^{-1}\left(I\right)$ is either $\left\{0\right\}$ or $A$, if it is $\left\{0\right\}$, then $I=\left\{0\right\}$; if it is $A$, then $I$ is $A$ as well. We will prove that $I \le \left\langle f\left(f^{-1}\left(I\right)\right)\right\rangle$, the other direction is straightforward. Without loss of generality assume $I\ne\left\{0\right\}$. Let $\McA$ be an arbitrary basis of $A$, by \cref{lem:expand-tensor-in-basis}, we see that every element $x \in A\otimes_{K}B$ can be written as $\sum_{i=0}^{n}\McA_{i}\otimes b_{i}$ for some natrual number $n$ and some choice of $b_{i}\in B$ and $\McA_{i}\in \McA$. Since $I$ is not empty, we see there exists a non-zero element $\omega\in I$ such that its expansion $\sum_{i=0}^{n}\McA_{i}\otimes b_{i}$ has the minimal $n$. In particular, all $b_{i}$ are non-zero and $n\ne0$. We have $\omega=\McA_{0}\otimes b_{0}+\sum_{i=1}^{n}\McA_{i}\otimes b_{i}$. Since $B$ is simple, $1 \in B = \left\langle\langle b_{0} \right\rangle$; hence we write $1\in\sum_{j=0}^{m}x_{i}b_{0}y_{i}$ for some $x_{i},y_{i}\in B$. Define $\Omega := \sum_{j=0}^{m}(1\otimes x_{i})\omega(1\otimes y_{i})$ which is also in $I$. We write \[ \begin{aligned} \Omega &= \McA_{0} \otimes \left(\sum_{j=0}^{m}x_{j}b_{0}y_{j}\right) + \sum_{i=1}^{n}\McA_{i}\otimes\left(\sum_{j=0}^{m}x_{j}b_{i}y_{j}\right) \\ &= \McA_{0}\otimes 1 + \sum_{i=1}^{n}\McA_{i}\otimes\left(\sum_{j=0}^{m}x_{j}b_{i}y_{j}\right) \end{aligned} \] For every $\beta\in B$, we have that $\left(1\otimes \beta\right)\Omega - \Omega\left(1\otimes \beta\right)$ is in I and is equal to \[ \sum_{i=1}^{n}\McA_{i}\otimes\left(\sum_{j=0}^{m}\beta x_{j}b_{i}y_{j}-x_{j}b_{i}y_{j}\beta\right), \] which is an expansion of $n-1$ terms, thus $\left(1\otimes\beta\right)\Omega-\Omega\left(1\otimes\beta\right)$ must be $0$. Hence we conclude that for all $i=1,\dots,n$, $\sum_{j=0}^{m}x_{j}b_{i}y_{j}\in Z\left(B\right)=K$. Hence for all $i=1,\dots,n$, we find a $\kappa_{i}\in K$ such that $\kappa_{i}=\sum_{j=0}^{m}x_{j}b_{i}y_{j}$. Hence we can calculate $\Omega$ as \[ \begin{aligned} \Omega &= \McA_{0}\otimes 1 + \sum_{i=1}^{n}\McA_{i}\otimes\left(\sum_{j=0}^{m}\right) \\ &= \McA_{0}\otimes 1 + \sum_{i=1}^{n}\McA_{i}\otimes\kappa_{i} \\ &= \left(\McA_{0}+\sum_{i=1}^{n}\kappa_{i}\cdot\McA_{i}\right) \otimes 1 \end{aligned}. \] From this, we note that $\McA_{0}+\sum_{i}^{n}\kappa_{i}\cdot\McA_{i}\in f^{-1}\left(I\right)$; since $A$ is simple, we immediately conclude that $f^{-1}\left(I\right) = A$, once we know $\McA_{0}+\sum_{i=1}^{n}\kappa_{i}\cdot \McA_{i}$ is not zero. If it is zero, by the fact that $\McA$ is a linearly independent set, we conclude that $1,\kappa_{1},\dots,\kappa_{n}$ are all zero; which is a contradiction. Since $f^{-1}\left(I\right) = A$, we know $\left\langle f\left(f^{-1}I\right)\right\rangle = A \otimes_{K} B$.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to $I=\langle f(f^{-1}(I))\rangle$; take a nonzero element of $I$ of minimal basis-expansion length. Normalise its leading coefficient to 1 and commute with $1\otimes\beta$ to force the other coefficients into $Z(B)=K$.

nodes.name: Reduction to ideals generated by A
nodes.statement: By~\cref{lem:tensor-central}, we need to prove $A\otimes_{K}B$ is a simple ring. Denote $f$ as the map $A\to A\otimes_{K}B$. It is sufficient to prove that for every two-sided-ideal $I\subseteq A\otimes_{K}B$, we have $I = \left\langle f\left(f^{-1}\left(I\right)\right)\right\rangle$. Indeed, since $A$ is simple $f^{-1}\left(I\right)$ is either $\left\{0\right\}$ or $A$, if it is $\left\{0\right\}$, then $I=\left\{0\right\}$; if it is $A$, then $I$ is $A$ as well.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce simplicity to $I=\langle f(f^{-1}(I))\rangle$.

nodes.name: One inclusion, WLOG I nonzero
nodes.statement: We will prove that $I \le \left\langle f\left(f^{-1}\left(I\right)\right)\right\rangle$, the other direction is straightforward. Without loss of generality assume $I\ne\left\{0\right\}$.
nodes.statement_short: Only one inclusion is needed; assume $I\ne0$.

nodes.name: Expansion in a basis of A
nodes.statement: Let $\McA$ be an arbitrary basis of $A$, by \cref{lem:expand-tensor-in-basis}, we see that every element $x \in A\otimes_{K}B$ can be written as $\sum_{i=0}^{n}\McA_{i}\otimes b_{i}$ for some natrual number $n$ and some choice of $b_{i}\in B$ and $\McA_{i}\in \McA$.
nodes.statement_short: Expand elements of $A\otimes B$ in a basis of $A$.

nodes.name: Minimal-length element
nodes.statement: Since $I$ is not empty, we see there exists a non-zero element $\omega\in I$ such that its expansion $\sum_{i=0}^{n}\McA_{i}\otimes b_{i}$ has the minimal $n$. In particular, all $b_{i}$ are non-zero and $n\ne0$. We have $\omega=\McA_{0}\otimes b_{0}+\sum_{i=1}^{n}\McA_{i}\otimes b_{i}$.
nodes.statement_short: Pick a nonzero $\omega\in I$ of minimal expansion length.

nodes.name: Normalise leading coefficient
nodes.statement: Since $B$ is simple, $1 \in B = \left\langle\langle b_{0} \right\rangle$; hence we write $1\in\sum_{j=0}^{m}x_{i}b_{0}y_{i}$ for some $x_{i},y_{i}\in B$. Define $\Omega := \sum_{j=0}^{m}(1\otimes x_{i})\omega(1\otimes y_{i})$ which is also in $I$. We write \[ \begin{aligned} \Omega &= \McA_{0} \otimes \left(\sum_{j=0}^{m}x_{j}b_{0}y_{j}\right) + \sum_{i=1}^{n}\McA_{i}\otimes\left(\sum_{j=0}^{m}x_{j}b_{i}y_{j}\right) \\ &= \McA_{0}\otimes 1 + \sum_{i=1}^{n}\McA_{i}\otimes\left(\sum_{j=0}^{m}x_{j}b_{i}y_{j}\right) \end{aligned} \]
nodes.statement_short: Use simplicity of $B$ to build $\Omega\in I$ with leading coefficient 1.

nodes.name: Commutator is shorter, hence zero
nodes.statement: For every $\beta\in B$, we have that $\left(1\otimes \beta\right)\Omega - \Omega\left(1\otimes \beta\right)$ is in I and is equal to \[ \sum_{i=1}^{n}\McA_{i}\otimes\left(\sum_{j=0}^{m}\beta x_{j}b_{i}y_{j}-x_{j}b_{i}y_{j}\beta\right), \] which is an expansion of $n-1$ terms, thus $\left(1\otimes\beta\right)\Omega-\Omega\left(1\otimes\beta\right)$ must be $0$.
nodes.statement_short: Commutators with $1\otimes\beta$ have shorter expansion, so vanish.

nodes.name: Coefficients are scalars
nodes.statement: Hence we conclude that for all $i=1,\dots,n$, $\sum_{j=0}^{m}x_{j}b_{i}y_{j}\in Z\left(B\right)=K$. Hence for all $i=1,\dots,n$, we find a $\kappa_{i}\in K$ such that $\kappa_{i}=\sum_{j=0}^{m}x_{j}b_{i}y_{j}$. Hence we can calculate $\Omega$ as \[ \begin{aligned} \Omega &= \McA_{0}\otimes 1 + \sum_{i=1}^{n}\McA_{i}\otimes\left(\sum_{j=0}^{m}\right) \\ &= \McA_{0}\otimes 1 + \sum_{i=1}^{n}\McA_{i}\otimes\kappa_{i} \\ &= \left(\McA_{0}+\sum_{i=1}^{n}\kappa_{i}\cdot\McA_{i}\right) \otimes 1 \end{aligned}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Coefficients lie in $Z(B)=K$, so $\Omega$ is a pure tensor with $1$.

nodes.name: Preimage is all of A
nodes.statement: From this, we note that $\McA_{0}+\sum_{i}^{n}\kappa_{i}\cdot\McA_{i}\in f^{-1}\left(I\right)$; since $A$ is simple, we immediately conclude that $f^{-1}\left(I\right) = A$, once we know $\McA_{0}+\sum_{i=1}^{n}\kappa_{i}\cdot \McA_{i}$ is not zero. If it is zero, by the fact that $\McA$ is a linearly independent set, we conclude that $1,\kappa_{1},\dots,\kappa_{n}$ are all zero; which is a contradiction.
nodes.statement_short: The resulting element of $f^{-1}(I)$ is nonzero, so $f^{-1}(I)=A$.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Since $f^{-1}\left(I\right) = A$, we know $\left\langle f\left(f^{-1}I\right)\right\rangle = A \otimes_{K} B$.
nodes.statement_short: Hence the generated ideal is everything.

nodes.name: Central simple algebras are stable under base change
nodes.statement: Central simple algebras are stable under base change. That is, if $L/K$ is a field extension and $D$ is a central simple algebra over $K$, then $L\otimes_{K} D$ is central simple over $L$.
assumptions: $D$ is a central simple algebra over $K$
nodes.label: cor:csa-basechange

nodes.name: Proof of Central simple algebras are stable under base change
nodes.statement: By~\cref{thm:tensor-csa}, $L\otimes_{K} D$ is simple. Let $x\in Z\left(L\otimes_{K}D\right)$, by~\cref{cor:center-tensor-center}, we have $x\in Z\left(L\right)\otimes Z\left(D\right)=Z\left(L\right)$. Without loss of generality, we can assume that $x = l \otimes d$ is a pure tensor, then $l \in Z\left(L\right)$ and $d \in K$. Therefore $x = d\cdot l \in L$.
nodes.statement_short: Simplicity from the tensor theorem; centrality from the centre of a tensor product.

nodes.name: Simplicity
nodes.statement: By~\cref{thm:tensor-csa}, $L\otimes_{K} D$ is simple.
nodes.statement_short: Simplicity follows from the tensor theorem.

nodes.name: Centre via centre of tensor product
nodes.statement: Let $x\in Z\left(L\otimes_{K}D\right)$, by~\cref{cor:center-tensor-center}, we have $x\in Z\left(L\right)\otimes Z\left(D\right)=Z\left(L\right)$.
nodes.statement_short: A central element lies in $Z(L)\otimes Z(D)$.

nodes.name: Conclude centrality
nodes.statement: Without loss of generality, we can assume that $x = l \otimes d$ is a pure tensor, then $l \in Z\left(L\right)$ and $d \in K$. Therefore $x = d\cdot l \in L$.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to pure tensors and conclude $x\in L$.

nodes.name: Simplicity of a tensor product implies simplicity of the factors
nodes.statement: If $A\otimes_{K} B$ is a simple ring, then $A$ and $B$ are both simple.
nodes.label: thm:tensor-simple-implies-simple

nodes.name: Proof of Simplicity of a tensor product implies simplicity of the factors
nodes.statement: By symmetry, we only prove that $A$ is simple. If $A$ or $B$ is the trivial ring then $A\otimes_{K} B$ is the trivial ring, a contradiction. Thus we assume both $A$ and $B$ are non-trivial. Suppose $A$ is not simple, by~\cref{lem:simple-ring-iff}, there exists a non-trivial $K$-algebra $A'$ and a $K$-algebra homomorphism $f : A \to A'$ such that $\ker f \not= \{0\}$. Let $F : A \otimes_{K} B\to A'\otimes_{K} B$ be the base change of $f$, then since $A\otimes_{K} B$ is simple and $A'\otimes B$ is non-trivial ($A'$ is non-trivial and $B$ is faithfully flat because $B$ is free), we conclude that $F$ is injective. Then we have that \begin{center} \begin{tikzcd} 0 \arrow{r}{0} & A \otimes_{K} B \arrow{r}{F} & A'\otimes_K B \end{tikzcd} \end{center} is exact. Since $B$ is faithfully flat as a $K$-module, tensorig with $B$ reflects exact sequences, therefore \begin{center} \begin{tikzcd} 0 \arrow{r}{0} & A \arrow{r}{f} & A' \end{tikzcd} \end{center} is exact as well. This is contradiction since $f$ is not injective.
nodes.statement_short: If $A$ is not simple, base change a non-injective map; faithful flatness of $B$ reflects exactness, a contradiction.

nodes.name: Symmetry reduction
nodes.statement: By symmetry, we only prove that $A$ is simple.
nodes.statement_short: By symmetry treat only $A$.

nodes.name: Non-triviality
nodes.statement: If $A$ or $B$ is the trivial ring then $A\otimes_{K} B$ is the trivial ring, a contradiction. Thus we assume both $A$ and $B$ are non-trivial.
nodes.statement_short: Both factors are non-trivial.

nodes.name: Non-injective map
nodes.statement: Suppose $A$ is not simple, by~\cref{lem:simple-ring-iff}, there exists a non-trivial $K$-algebra $A'$ and a $K$-algebra homomorphism $f : A \to A'$ such that $\ker f \not= \{0\}$.
nodes.statement_short: Assume $A$ not simple; get a non-injective map $f:A\to A'$.

nodes.name: Base change is injective
nodes.statement: Let $F : A \otimes_{K} B\to A'\otimes_{K} B$ be the base change of $f$, then since $A\otimes_{K} B$ is simple and $A'\otimes B$ is non-trivial ($A'$ is non-trivial and $B$ is faithfully flat because $B$ is free), we conclude that $F$ is injective. Then we have that \begin{center} \begin{tikzcd} 0 \arrow{r}{0} & A \otimes_{K} B \arrow{r}{F} & A'\otimes_K B \end{tikzcd} \end{center} is exact.
nodes.statement_short: The base change $F$ is injective by simplicity of $A\otimes B$.

nodes.name: Faithful flatness reflects exactness
nodes.statement: Since $B$ is faithfully flat as a $K$-module, tensorig with $B$ reflects exact sequences, therefore \begin{center} \begin{tikzcd} 0 \arrow{r}{0} & A \arrow{r}{f} & A' \end{tikzcd} \end{center} is exact as well. This is contradiction since $f$ is not injective.
nodes.statement_short: Faithful flatness makes $f$ injective, a contradiction.

nodes.name: Subfield
nodes.statement: For any field $K$ and $K$-algebra $A$, a subfield $B \subseteq A$ is a commutative $K$-subalgebra of $A$ that is closed under inverse for any non-zero member.
differentia: closed under inverse for any non-zero member

nodes.name: Ordering of subfields
nodes.statement: Subfields inherit a natural ordering from subalgebras.

nodes.name: Standing notation: K, D and A for subfields
nodes.statement: Let $K$ be any field and $D$ a finite dimensional central division $K$-algebra and $A$ a finite dimensional central simple algebra of $A$.

nodes.name: Dimension of a maximal subfield
nodes.statement: Let $k$ be a maximal subfield of $D$, \[ \dim_{K}D = {\left(\dim_{K}k\right)}^{2}. \]
nodes.label: lem:dim-maximal-subfield

nodes.name: Proof of Dimension of a maximal subfield
nodes.statement: By~\cref{lem:dim-centralizer}, we have that $\dim_{K} D = \dim_{K}C_{D}(k)\cdot \dim_{K}k$. Hence it is sufficient to show that $C_{D}(k) = k$. By the commutativity of $k$, we have that $k \le C_{D}(k)$. Suppose $k \ne C_{D}(k)$: let $a \in C_{D}(k)$ that is not in $k$. We see that $L := k(a)$ is another subalgebra of $D$ that is strictly larger than $k$; a contradiction. Therefore $k = C_{D}(k)$ and the theorem is proved.
nodes.statement_short: Use the centralizer dimension formula and show $C_D(k)=k$ by maximality.

nodes.name: Reduce to C_D(k) = k
nodes.statement: By~\cref{lem:dim-centralizer}, we have that $\dim_{K} D = \dim_{K}C_{D}(k)\cdot \dim_{K}k$. Hence it is sufficient to show that $C_{D}(k) = k$.
nodes.statement_short: Centralizer dimension formula reduces the claim to $C_D(k)=k$.

nodes.name: Inclusion
nodes.statement: By the commutativity of $k$, we have that $k \le C_{D}(k)$.
nodes.statement_short: $k\subseteq C_D(k)$ by commutativity.

nodes.name: Larger subfield
nodes.statement: Suppose $k \ne C_{D}(k)$: let $a \in C_{D}(k)$ that is not in $k$. We see that $L := k(a)$ is another subalgebra of $D$ that is strictly larger than $k$; a contradiction.
nodes.statement_short: An extra element would generate a larger subfield.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Therefore $k = C_{D}(k)$ and the theorem is proved.
nodes.statement_short: Hence $k=C_D(k)$.

nodes.name: Characterizations of maximal subfields
nodes.statement: Suppose $L$ is a subfield of $A$, the following are equivalent: \begin{enumerate} \item $L$ = $C_{A}(L)$ \item $\dim_{K}A = {\left(\dim_{K}L\right)}^{2}$ \item for any commutative $K$-subalgebra $L' \subseteq A$, $L \subseteq L'$ implies $L = L'$ \end{enumerate}
equivalent_conditions: for any commutative $K$-subalgebra $L' \subseteq A$, $L \subseteq L'$ implies $L = L'$
nodes.label: lem:tfae-subfield

nodes.name: Proof of Characterizations of maximal subfields
nodes.statement: We prove the following: \begin{itemize} \item ``1. implies 2.'': this is~\cref{lem:dim-centralizer}. \item ``2. implies 1.'': Since $L$ is commutative, we always have $L \subseteq C_{A}(L)$. Hence we only need to show $\dim_{K}L = \dim_{K}C_{A}(L)$. This is because by~\cref{lem:dim-centralizer}, we have that $\dim_{K}A = \dim_{K}L\cdot \dim_{K}C_{A}(L)$ and by 2. we have $\dim_{K}L\cdot \dim_{K}C_{A}(L)= \dim_{K}L\cdot \dim_{K}L$. \item ``2. implies 3.'': Since 2. implies 1., we assume $L = C_{A}(L)$, therefore all we need is to prove $L' \subseteq C_{A}(L)$. Let $x \in L'$ and $y \in L \subseteq L'$, we need to show $xy = yx$ which is commutativity of $L'$. \item ``3. implies 1.'': By commutativity of $L$, we always have $L \subseteq C_{A}(L)$. For the other direction, suppose $C_{A}(L)\not\subseteq L$, then there exists some $a \in C_{A}(L)$ but not in $L$. Consider $L' = L(a)$, by 3., we have $L' = L$ which is a contradiction. \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: Prove the cycle of implications using the centralizer dimension formula and maximality.

nodes.name: Plan
nodes.statement: We prove the following:
nodes.statement_short: Prove the implications.

nodes.name: 1 implies 2
nodes.statement: ``1. implies 2.'': this is~\cref{lem:dim-centralizer}.
nodes.statement_short: By the centralizer dimension formula.

nodes.name: 2 implies 1
nodes.statement: ``2. implies 1.'': Since $L$ is commutative, we always have $L \subseteq C_{A}(L)$. Hence we only need to show $\dim_{K}L = \dim_{K}C_{A}(L)$. This is because by~\cref{lem:dim-centralizer}, we have that $\dim_{K}A = \dim_{K}L\cdot \dim_{K}C_{A}(L)$ and by 2. we have $\dim_{K}L\cdot \dim_{K}C_{A}(L)= \dim_{K}L\cdot \dim_{K}L$.
nodes.statement_short: Compare dimensions of $L$ and $C_A(L)$.

nodes.name: 2 implies 3
nodes.statement: ``2. implies 3.'': Since 2. implies 1., we assume $L = C_{A}(L)$, therefore all we need is to prove $L' \subseteq C_{A}(L)$. Let $x \in L'$ and $y \in L \subseteq L'$, we need to show $xy = yx$ which is commutativity of $L'$.
nodes.statement_short: A larger commutative subalgebra centralizes $L$.

nodes.name: 3 implies 1
nodes.statement: ``3. implies 1.'': By commutativity of $L$, we always have $L \subseteq C_{A}(L)$. For the other direction, suppose $C_{A}(L)\not\subseteq L$, then there exists some $a \in C_{A}(L)$ but not in $L$. Consider $L' = L(a)$, by 3., we have $L' = L$ which is a contradiction.
nodes.statement_short: An element of $C_A(L)$ outside $L$ contradicts maximality.

nodes.name: Standing notation: ring R and n
nodes.statement: Let $R$ be a ring and $0 \ne n\in \mathbb{N}$.

nodes.name: Functor from R-modules to Mat_n(R)-modules
nodes.statement: If $M$ is an $R$-module, we have a natural $\Mat_{n}(R)$-module structure on $\widehat{M}:=M^{n}$ given by $(m_{ij})\cdot (v_{k})=\sum_{j}m_{ij}\cdot v_{j}$. If $f : M \to N$ is an $R$-linear map, then $\widehat{f} : M^{n}\to N^{n}$ given by $(v_{i}) \mapsto (f(v_{i}))$ is a $\Mat_{n}(R)$-linear map. Thus we have a well-defined functor $\MOD_{R} \Longrightarrow \MOD_{\Mat_{n}(R)}$.
nodes.statement_short: $M\mapsto M^n$ with matrix action defines a functor $\MOD_R\to\MOD_{\Mat_n(R)}$.

nodes.name: Left modules and matrix units
nodes.statement: Note that all modules are assumed to be left modules; when we need to consider right $R$-modules, we will consider left $R^{\opp}$-modules instead. We use $\delta_{ij}$ to denote the matrix whose $(i,j)$-th entry is $1$ and $0$ elsewhere. $\delta_{ij}$ forms a basis for matrices.

nodes.name: Functor from Mat_n(R)-modules to R-modules
nodes.statement: If $M$ is a $\Mat_{n}(R)$-module, then $\widetilde{M} := \{\delta_{ij}\cdot m | m \in M\} \subseteq M$ is an $R$-module whose $R$-action is given by $r \cdot (\delta_{ij}\cdot m) := (r\cdot \delta_{ij})\cdot m$. More over if $f : M \to N$ is a $\Mat_{n}(R)$-linear map, $\widetilde{f} : \widetilde{M} \to \widetilde{N}$ given by the restriction of $f$ is $R$-linear. Hence, we have a functor $\MOD_{\Mat_{n}(R)}\Longrightarrow \MOD_{R}$.
nodes.statement_short: $M\mapsto \{\delta_{ij}m\}$ defines a functor $\MOD_{\Mat_n(R)}\to\MOD_R$.

nodes.name: Morita Equivalence
nodes.statement: The functors constructed in \cref{con:morita-eqv-functor0} and \cref{con:morita-eqv-functor1} form an equivalence of category.
conclusions: The functors constructed in \cref{con:morita-eqv-functor0} and \cref{con:morita-eqv-functor1} form an equivalence of category
nodes.label: thm:morita

nodes.name: Proof of Morita Equivalence
nodes.statement: Let $M$ be an $R$-module, then the unit $\widetilde{\widehat{M}} \cong M$ is given by \[ \begin{aligned} x \mapsto \sum_{j} x_{j} \\ (x,0,\dots,0) \mapsfrom x \end{aligned} \] Let $M$ be an $\Mat_{n}(R)$-module, then the counit $\widehat{\widetilde{M}}\cong M$ is given by $m \mapsto (\delta_{i0}\cdot m)$. This map is both injective and surjective.
nodes.statement_short: Write down the unit and counit of the adjunction explicitly.

nodes.name: Unit
nodes.statement: Let $M$ be an $R$-module, then the unit $\widetilde{\widehat{M}} \cong M$ is given by \[ \begin{aligned} x \mapsto \sum_{j} x_{j} \\ (x,0,\dots,0) \mapsfrom x \end{aligned} \]
nodes.statement_short: Explicit unit isomorphism.

nodes.name: Counit
nodes.statement: Let $M$ be an $\Mat_{n}(R)$-module, then the counit $\widehat{\widetilde{M}}\cong M$ is given by $m \mapsto (\delta_{i0}\cdot m)$. This map is both injective and surjective.
nodes.statement_short: Explicit counit isomorphism.

nodes.name: Standing notation: finite dimensional simple k-algebra A
nodes.statement: Let $A$ be a finite dimensional simple $k$-algebra.

nodes.name: Simple modules over a simple algebra are isomorphic
nodes.statement: Let $M$ and $N$ be simple $A$-modules, then $M$ and $N$ are isomorphic as $A$-modules.
nodes.label: lem:isomorphic-simple-mod

nodes.name: Proof of Simple modules over a simple algebra are isomorphic
nodes.statement: By~\cref{thm:wed-artin-algebra}, there exists non-zero $n\in\mathbb N$, $k$-division algebra $D$ such that $A\cong \Mat_{n}(D)$ as $k$-algebras. Then by~\cref{thm:morita}, we have equivalence of category $e : \MOD_{A}\cong\MOD_{D}$. Since simple module is a categorical notion (it can be defined in terms monomorphisms), $e(M)$ and $e(N)$ are simple $D$-modules. Since $D$ is a division ring, $e(M)$ and $e(N)$ are isomorphic as $D$-modules, therefore $M$ and $N$ are isomorphic as $A$-modules.
nodes.statement_short: Transport along Wedderburn-Artin and Morita to modules over a division ring.

nodes.name: Transport to D-modules
nodes.statement: By~\cref{thm:wed-artin-algebra}, there exists non-zero $n\in\mathbb N$, $k$-division algebra $D$ such that $A\cong \Mat_{n}(D)$ as $k$-algebras. Then by~\cref{thm:morita}, we have equivalence of category $e : \MOD_{A}\cong\MOD_{D}$.
nodes.statement_short: Wedderburn-Artin plus Morita give $\MOD_A\cong\MOD_D$.

nodes.name: Simplicity is preserved
nodes.statement: Since simple module is a categorical notion (it can be defined in terms monomorphisms), $e(M)$ and $e(N)$ are simple $D$-modules.
nodes.statement_short: Images of simple modules are simple.

nodes.name: Conclude over a division ring
nodes.statement: Since $D$ is a division ring, $e(M)$ and $e(N)$ are isomorphic as $D$-modules, therefore $M$ and $N$ are isomorphic as $A$-modules.
nodes.statement_short: Simple $D$-modules are isomorphic; transport back.

nodes.name: Modules over a simple algebra are direct sums of a simple module
nodes.statement: Let $M$ be an $A$-module, there exists a simple $A$-module $S$ such that $M$ is a direct sum of copies of $S$, i.e. $M \cong \bigoplus_{i \in \iota} S$ for some indexing set $\iota$.
conclusions: there exists a simple $A$-module $S$ such that $M$ is a direct sum of copies of $S$
nodes.label: lem:direct-sum-simple-mod

nodes.name: Proof of Modules over a simple algebra are direct sums of a simple module
nodes.statement: By~\cref{thm:wed-artin-algebra}, there exists non-zero $n\in\mathbb N$, $k$-division algebra $D$ such that $A\cong \Mat_{n}(D)$ as $k$-algebras. Then by~\cref{thm:morita}, we have equivalence of category $e : \MOD_{A}\cong\MOD_{D}$. Since simple module is a categorical notion (it can be defined in terms monomorphisms), $e^{-1}(D)$ is a simple module over $A$. Since $e(M)$ is a free module over $D$, we can write $e(M)$ as $\bigoplus_{i\in \iota} D$ for some indexing set $\iota$. By precomposing the unit of $e$, we get an isomorphism $M \cong e^{-1}\left(\bigoplus_{i\in\iota} D\right)$. We only need to prove $e^{-1}\left(\bigoplus_{i\in\iota} D\right)\cong\bigoplus_{i\in\iota}e^{-1}\left(D\right)$. This is because direct sum is the categorical coproduct.
nodes.statement_short: Via Morita, modules over $D$ are free, hence direct sums of $D$; pull back the decomposition.

nodes.name: Transport to D-modules
nodes.statement: By~\cref{thm:wed-artin-algebra}, there exists non-zero $n\in\mathbb N$, $k$-division algebra $D$ such that $A\cong \Mat_{n}(D)$ as $k$-algebras. Then by~\cref{thm:morita}, we have equivalence of category $e : \MOD_{A}\cong\MOD_{D}$.
nodes.statement_short: Wedderburn-Artin plus Morita give $\MOD_A\cong\MOD_D$.

nodes.name: The simple module
nodes.statement: Since simple module is a categorical notion (it can be defined in terms monomorphisms), $e^{-1}(D)$ is a simple module over $A$.
nodes.statement_short: $e^{-1}(D)$ is simple.

nodes.name: Free module decomposition
nodes.statement: Since $e(M)$ is a free module over $D$, we can write $e(M)$ as $\bigoplus_{i\in \iota} D$ for some indexing set $\iota$. By precomposing the unit of $e$, we get an isomorphism $M \cong e^{-1}\left(\bigoplus_{i\in\iota} D\right)$.
nodes.statement_short: $e(M)$ is free, giving $M\cong e^{-1}(\bigoplus D)$.

nodes.name: Equivalences preserve coproducts
nodes.statement: We only need to prove $e^{-1}\left(\bigoplus_{i\in\iota} D\right)\cong\bigoplus_{i\in\iota}e^{-1}\left(D\right)$. This is because direct sum is the categorical coproduct.
nodes.statement_short: Direct sums are coproducts, preserved by the equivalence.

nodes.name: Any simple module can be used in the direct sum decomposition
nodes.statement: Note that by~\cref{lem:isomorphic-simple-mod}, any two simple $A$-module are isomorphic, hence for any $A$-module $M$ and {\em any} simple $A$-module $S$, we can write $M$ as a direct sum of copies of $S$.

nodes.name: Modules isomorphic iff equal dimension
nodes.statement: Let $M$ and $N$ be two finite $A$-module with compatible $k$-action. Then $M$ and $N$ are isomorphic as $A$-module if and only if $\dim_{k} M$ and $\dim_{k} N$ are equal.
assumptions: $M$ and $N$ be two finite $A$-module with compatible $k$-action
conclusions: $M$ and $N$ are isomorphic as $A$-module if and only if $\dim_{k} M$ and $\dim_{k} N$ are equal
nodes.label: lem:iso-of-dim-eq

nodes.name: Proof of Modules isomorphic iff equal dimension
nodes.statement: The forward direction is trivial as an $A$-linear isomorphism is a $k$-linear isomorphism as well. Conversely, suppose $\dim_{k}M = \dim_{k}N$. By~\cref{lem:direct-sum-simple-mod}, there exists a simple $A$-module $S$ such that $M \cong \bigoplus_{i\in\iota} S$ and $N \cong \bigoplus_{i\in\iota'} S$ as $A$-modules. Without loss of generality $S \ne 0$, for otherwise we have $M \cong N$ anyway. If either of $\iota$ or $\iota'$ is empty, then $\dim_{k}M = \dim_{k} N = 0$ implying that $M = N = 0$, we again have $M \cong N$. Thus, we assume both $\iota$ and $\iota'$ are non-empty. By pulling back the $A$-module structure on $S$ to a $k$-module structure along $k \hookrightarrow A$, $M, N, S, \bigoplus_{i\in\iota} S, \bigoplus_{i\in\iota'} S$ are all finite dimensional $k$-vector spaces. Hence $\iota$ and $\iota'$ are finite. The equality $\dim_{k}M=\dim_{k}N$ tells us that $\iota \cong \iota'$ as set, hence $M \cong \bigoplus_{i\in\iota}S\cong\bigoplus_{i\in\iota'}S\cong N$ as required.
nodes.statement_short: Decompose both modules as sums of one simple module; equal dimension forces equal index sets.

nodes.name: Forward and setup of converse
nodes.statement: The forward direction is trivial as an $A$-linear isomorphism is a $k$-linear isomorphism as well. Conversely, suppose $\dim_{k}M = \dim_{k}N$. By~\cref{lem:direct-sum-simple-mod}, there exists a simple $A$-module $S$ such that $M \cong \bigoplus_{i\in\iota} S$ and $N \cong \bigoplus_{i\in\iota'} S$ as $A$-modules.
nodes.statement_short: Forward is clear; for the converse decompose into copies of one simple $S$.

nodes.name: Degenerate cases
nodes.statement: Without loss of generality $S \ne 0$, for otherwise we have $M \cong N$ anyway. If either of $\iota$ or $\iota'$ is empty, then $\dim_{k}M = \dim_{k} N = 0$ implying that $M = N = 0$, we again have $M \cong N$.
nodes.statement_short: Dispose of $S=0$ and empty index sets.

nodes.name: Index sets are finite
nodes.statement: Thus, we assume both $\iota$ and $\iota'$ are non-empty. By pulling back the $A$-module structure on $S$ to a $k$-module structure along $k \hookrightarrow A$, $M, N, S, \bigoplus_{i\in\iota} S, \bigoplus_{i\in\iota'} S$ are all finite dimensional $k$-vector spaces. Hence $\iota$ and $\iota'$ are finite.
nodes.statement_short: Finite dimensionality makes the index sets finite.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: The equality $\dim_{k}M=\dim_{k}N$ tells us that $\iota \cong \iota'$ as set, hence $M \cong \bigoplus_{i\in\iota}S\cong\bigoplus_{i\in\iota'}S\cong N$ as required.
nodes.statement_short: Equal dimensions give equal index set sizes, hence $M\cong N$.

nodes.name: Standing notation: A isomorphic to Mat_n(D)
nodes.statement: Let $A \cong \Mat_{n}(D)$ as $k$-algebras for some $k$-division algebra and $n\ne0$.

nodes.name: D^n is a simple A-module
nodes.statement: $D^{n}$ is a simple $A$-module where the module structure is given by pulling back the $\Mat_{n}(D)$-module structure of $D^{n}$.
nodes.label: lem:exists-simple-mod

nodes.name: Proof of D^n is a simple A-module
nodes.statement: By~\cref{thm:morita}, we have $\MOD_{A}\cong\MOD_{D}\cong\MOD_{\Mat_{n}(D)}$. Since $D$ is a simple $D$-module, $D^{n}$ is a simple $\Mat_{n}(D)$ module and consequently, a simple $A$-module.
nodes.statement_short: Morita equivalence transports simplicity of $D$ to $D^n$.

nodes.name: A-linear and Mat_n(D)-linear endomorphisms agree
nodes.statement: Note that any $A$-linear endomorphism of $D^{n}$ is $\Mat_{n}(D)$-linear, and vice versa. Thus we have $\End_{A}\left(D^{n}\right)\cong \End_{\Mat_{n}(D)}\left(D^{n}\right)$ as $k$-algebras.

nodes.name: Endomorphisms of D^n are D^op
nodes.statement: $\End_{A}\left(D^{n}\right)$ is isomorphic to $D^{\opp}$ as $k$-algebras.
nodes.label: lem:end-vec-iso

nodes.name: Proof of Endomorphisms of D^n are D^op
nodes.statement: Indeed, we calculate: \[ \begin{aligned} \End_{A}\left(D^{n}\right) &\cong \End_{\Mat_{n}(D)}\left(D^{n}\right) & \\ &\cong \End_{D}D & \text{by~\cref{thm:morita},}~\MOD_{D}\cong\MOD_{\Mat_{n}D}\\ &\cong D^{\opp} \end{aligned} \]
nodes.statement_short: Chain of isomorphisms through Morita equivalence.

nodes.name: Endomorphism algebra of a simple module is D^op
nodes.statement: Let $M$ be a simple $A$-module, then $\End_{A} M\cong D^{\opp}$ as $k$-algebras.
nodes.label: lem:end-simple-iso

nodes.name: Proof of Endomorphism algebra of a simple module is D^op
nodes.statement: By~\cref{thm:morita}, $D^{n}$ is simple as $A$-module; hence by~\cref{lem:isomorphic-simple-mod}, $D^{n}$ and $M$ are isomorphic as $A$-module. \Cref{lem:end-vec-iso} gives the desired result.
nodes.statement_short: Simple modules are isomorphic to $D^n$, whose endomorphisms are $D^{op}$.

nodes.name: Endomorphism algebra of a simple module is simple
nodes.statement: In particular, if $M$ is a simple $A$-module, then $\End_{A}M$ is a simple $k$-algbera.

nodes.name: Endomorphism algebra of a simple module is finite dimensional
nodes.statement: Let $M$ be a simple $A$-module, then $\End_{A}M$ has finite $k$-dimension.

nodes.name: Proof of Endomorphism algebra of a simple module is finite dimensional
nodes.statement: By~\cref{thm:wed}, such $D$ and $n$ always exists. Hence we only need to show $D^{\opp}$ has finite $k$-dimension. Since $\dim_{k}A=\dim_{k}\Mat_{n}(D)$ are both finite, we conclude $D^{\opp}$ is finite as a $k$-vector space by pulling back the finiteness along $D \hookrightarrow \Mat_{n}(D)$.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to finiteness of $D^{op}$, pulled back from $\Mat_n(D)$.

nodes.name: Reduce to D^op
nodes.statement: By~\cref{thm:wed}, such $D$ and $n$ always exists. Hence we only need to show $D^{\opp}$ has finite $k$-dimension.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to finite dimensionality of $D^{op}$.

nodes.name: Finiteness pulled back
nodes.statement: Since $\dim_{k}A=\dim_{k}\Mat_{n}(D)$ are both finite, we conclude $D^{\opp}$ is finite as a $k$-vector space by pulling back the finiteness along $D \hookrightarrow \Mat_{n}(D)$.
nodes.statement_short: Pull back finiteness along $D\hookrightarrow\Mat_n(D)$.

nodes.name: Canonical map A to End_{End_A M} M
nodes.statement: Note that for all $A$-module $M$, $\End_{\End_{A}M}M$ is a $k$-algebra as well, with $k \hookrightarrow \End_{\End_{A}M}M$ given by $a \mapsto (x \mapsto a\cdot x)$. Thus, we always have a $k$-algebra homomorphism $A \to \End_{\End_{A}M}M$ given by the $A$-action on $M$. When $A$ is a simple ring, this map is injective.

nodes.name: Balanced Module
nodes.statement: For any ring $A$ and $A$-module $M$, we say $M$ is a balanced $A$-module, if the $A$-linear map $A \to \End_{\End_{A}M}M$ is surjective.
nodes.label: def:balanced-mod

nodes.name: Balancedness is invariant under isomorphism
nodes.statement: Balancedness is invariant under linear isomorphism.

nodes.name: A ring is balanced over itself
nodes.statement: For any ring $A$, $A$ is balanced as $A$-module.
nodes.label: lem:balanced-self

nodes.name: Proof of A ring is balanced over itself
nodes.statement: If $f \in \End_{\End_{A}M}A$, then the image of $f(1)$ under $A \to\End_{\End_{A}}A$ is $f$ again.
nodes.statement_short: An endomorphism is determined by the image of 1.

nodes.name: Simple modules are balanced
nodes.statement: Any simple $A$-module is balanced.

nodes.name: Proof of Simple modules are balanced
nodes.statement: Indeed, if $M$ is a simple $A$-module, then $A \cong \bigoplus_{i\in\iota} M$ for some indexing set $\iota$ by~\cref{lem:direct-sum-simple-mod}. Since $A$ is balanced, $\bigoplus_{i\in\iota}M$ is balanced. Let $g \in \End_{\End_{A}M}M$, we can define a corresponding $G \in \End_{\End_{\bigoplus_{i}M}}\left(\bigoplus_{i}M\right)$ by sending $(v_{i})$ to $(g(v_{i}))$. Since $\bigoplus_{i}M$ is balanced, we know that for some $a\in A$, $G$ is the image of $a$ under $A \to \End_{\End_{\bigoplus_{i}M}}\left(\bigoplus_{i}M\right)$. Then the image of $a$ under $A \to \End_{\End_{A}M}M$ is $g$.
nodes.statement_short: Write $A$ as a sum of copies of $M$ and lift endomorphisms diagonally.

nodes.name: A is a sum of copies of M
nodes.statement: Indeed, if $M$ is a simple $A$-module, then $A \cong \bigoplus_{i\in\iota} M$ for some indexing set $\iota$ by~\cref{lem:direct-sum-simple-mod}. Since $A$ is balanced, $\bigoplus_{i\in\iota}M$ is balanced.
nodes.statement_short: $A\cong\bigoplus M$ is balanced.

nodes.name: Lift g diagonally
nodes.statement: Let $g \in \End_{\End_{A}M}M$, we can define a corresponding $G \in \End_{\End_{\bigoplus_{i}M}}\left(\bigoplus_{i}M\right)$ by sending $(v_{i})$ to $(g(v_{i}))$. Since $\bigoplus_{i}M$ is balanced, we know that for some $a\in A$, $G$ is the image of $a$ under $A \to \End_{\End_{\bigoplus_{i}M}}\left(\bigoplus_{i}M\right)$.
nodes.statement_short: Lift $g$ to $G$ on $\bigoplus M$, realised by some $a\in A$.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Then the image of $a$ under $A \to \End_{\End_{A}M}M$ is $g$.
nodes.statement_short: $a$ realises $g$.

nodes.name: A is the double endomorphism algebra of a simple module
nodes.statement: For any simple $A$-module $M$, we have $A \cong \End_{\End_{A}M}M$ as $k$-algebras.
nodes.label: lem:iso-end-end

nodes.name: Proof of A is the double endomorphism algebra of a simple module
nodes.statement: The canonical map $A \to \End_{\End_{A}M}M$ is both injective and surjective, as $M$ is a balanced $A$-module and $A$ is a simple ring.
nodes.statement_short: Canonical map is injective (simplicity) and surjective (balanced).

nodes.name: Expansion of tensors in a basis
nodes.statement: Let $M$ and $N$ be $R$-modules such that $\mathcal{C}_{i\in\iota}$ is a basis for $N$, then every elements of $x \in M \otimes_{R} N$ can be uniquely written as $\sum_{i\in\iota}m_{i}\otimes \mathcal{C}_{i}$ where only finitely many $m_{i}$'s are non-zero
assumptions: $M$ and $N$ be $R$-modules such that $\mathcal{C}_{i\in\iota}$ is a basis for $N$
conclusions: every elements of $x \in M \otimes_{R} N$ can be uniquely written as
nodes.label: lem:expand-tensor-in-basis

nodes.name: Proof of Expansion of tensors in a basis
nodes.statement: Given the basis $\mathcal{C}$, we have $R$-linear isomorphism $N \cong\bigoplus_{i\in\iota}R$, hence $M\otimes_{R}N \cong \bigoplus_{i\in\iota}(M\otimes_{R}R)\cong\bigoplus_{i\in\iota}M$ as $R$-modules.
nodes.statement_short: A basis gives $N\cong\bigoplus R$ and hence $M\otimes N\cong\bigoplus M$.

nodes.name: Intersection of tensor submodules
nodes.statement: Let $K$ be a field, $M$ and $N$ be flat $K$-modules. Suppose $p \subseteq M$ and $q \subseteq N$ are $K$-submodules, then $(p \otimes_{K} N) \sqcap (M \otimes_{K} q) = p \otimes_{K} q$ as $K$-submodules.
assumptions: $K$ be a field, $M$ and $N$ be flat $K$-modules
nodes.label: lem:submodule-tensor-submodule

nodes.name: Proof of Intersection of tensor submodules
nodes.statement: The hard direction is to show $(p \otimes_{R} N) \sqcap (M \otimes_{R} q) \le p \otimes_{R} q$. Consider the following diagram: \begin{center} \begin{tikzcd} p \otimes_{K} q \ar[r, "u"] \ar[d, "\alpha"] & M \otimes_{K} q \ar[r, "v"] \ar[d, "\beta"] & {}^{M}/_{p} \otimes_{K} q \ar[d, "\gamma"] \\ p \otimes_{K} N \ar[r, "u'"] & M \otimes_{K} N \ar[r, "v'"] & ^{M}/_{p} \otimes_{K} N \end{tikzcd} \end{center} Since $^{M}/_{p}$ is flat, $\gamma$ is injective. Let $z \in (p \otimes_{R} N) \sqcap (M \otimes_{R} q) = \im \beta \sqcap \im u'$. By abusing notation, replace $z$ with some elements of $M \otimes_{K} q$ and continue with $\beta(z)\in\im \beta \sqcap \im u'$. Since $v'(\beta(z))=\gamma(v(z))$ and that $\beta(z)\in \im u'$, we conclude that $\gamma(v(z))=0$, that is $z\in\ker v=\im u$. We abuse notation again, let $z \in p \otimes_{K} q$, we need to show $\beta(u(z))\in\im \beta \sqcap \im u'$, but $\beta\circ u=u'\circ\alpha$, we finish the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Diagram chase in the tensored exact sequences using flatness of the quotient.

nodes.name: Reduction and diagram
nodes.statement: The hard direction is to show $(p \otimes_{R} N) \sqcap (M \otimes_{R} q) \le p \otimes_{R} q$. Consider the following diagram: \begin{center} \begin{tikzcd} p \otimes_{K} q \ar[r, "u"] \ar[d, "\alpha"] & M \otimes_{K} q \ar[r, "v"] \ar[d, "\beta"] & {}^{M}/_{p} \otimes_{K} q \ar[d, "\gamma"] \\ p \otimes_{K} N \ar[r, "u'"] & M \otimes_{K} N \ar[r, "v'"] & ^{M}/_{p} \otimes_{K} N \end{tikzcd} \end{center}
nodes.statement_short: Only one inclusion is hard; set up the commutative diagram.

nodes.name: Take z in the intersection
nodes.statement: Since $^{M}/_{p}$ is flat, $\gamma$ is injective. Let $z \in (p \otimes_{R} N) \sqcap (M \otimes_{R} q) = \im \beta \sqcap \im u'$. By abusing notation, replace $z$ with some elements of $M \otimes_{K} q$ and continue with $\beta(z)\in\im \beta \sqcap \im u'$.
nodes.statement_short: Flatness makes $\gamma$ injective; take $z$ in the intersection.

nodes.name: Diagram chase
nodes.statement: Since $v'(\beta(z))=\gamma(v(z))$ and that $\beta(z)\in \im u'$, we conclude that $\gamma(v(z))=0$, that is $z\in\ker v=\im u$.
nodes.statement_short: Chase: $z\in\ker v=\im u$.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: We abuse notation again, let $z \in p \otimes_{K} q$, we need to show $\beta(u(z))\in\im \beta \sqcap \im u'$, but $\beta\circ u=u'\circ\alpha$, we finish the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Commutativity of the square finishes.

nodes.name: Standing notation: commutative ring R and R-algebras A, B
nodes.statement: Let $R$ be a commutative ring and $A$, $B$ be two $R$-algebras.

nodes.name: Centralizer and centre notation
nodes.statement: We denote centralizer of $S\subseteq A$ by $C_{A}S$ and centre of $A$ by $Z(A)$.

nodes.name: Centralizer of a supremum of subalgebras
nodes.statement: Let $S, T$ be two subalgebras of $A$, then $C_{A}(S\sqcup T)=C_{A}(S)\sqcap C_{A}(T)$.
nodes.label: lem:sup-centralizer

nodes.name: Centralizer of the image of a subalgebra in a tensor product
nodes.statement: If we assume $B$ is free as $R$-module, then for any $R$-subalgebra $S$, we have that $C_{A\otimes_{R}B}\left(\im\left(S\to A\otimes_{R}B\right)\right)$ is $C_{A}(S) \otimes_{R} B$
nodes.label: lem:centralizer-inclusion-tensor

nodes.name: Proof of Centralizer of the image of a subalgebra in a tensor product
nodes.statement: Let $w\in C_{A\otimes_{R}B}\left(\im\left(S\to A\otimes_{R}B\right)\right)$. Since $B$ is free, we choose an arbitrary basis $\mathcal{B}$; by~\cref{lem:expand-tensor-in-basis}, we write $w = \sum_{i}m_{i}\otimes_{K}\mathcal{B}_{i}$. It is sufficient to show that $m_{i}\in C_{A}(S)$ for all $i$. Let $a \in S$, we need to show that $m_{i}\cdot a = a \cdot m_{i}$. Since $w$ is in the centralizer, $w \cdot (a\otimes 1) = (a\otimes 1)\cdot w$. Hence we have $\sum_{i}(a\cdot m_{i})\otimes\mathcal{B}_{i}=\sum_{i}(m_{i}\cdot a)\otimes\mathcal{B}_{i}$. By the uniqueness of~\cref{lem:expand-tensor-in-basis}, we conclude $a\cdot m_{i}=m_{i}\cdot a$.
nodes.statement_short: Expand an element in a basis of $B$ and compare coefficients by uniqueness of the expansion.

nodes.name: Expand w in a basis of B
nodes.statement: Let $w\in C_{A\otimes_{R}B}\left(\im\left(S\to A\otimes_{R}B\right)\right)$. Since $B$ is free, we choose an arbitrary basis $\mathcal{B}$; by~\cref{lem:expand-tensor-in-basis}, we write $w = \sum_{i}m_{i}\otimes_{K}\mathcal{B}_{i}$.
nodes.statement_short: Expand $w$ in a basis of $B$.

nodes.name: Reduce to coefficients
nodes.statement: It is sufficient to show that $m_{i}\in C_{A}(S)$ for all $i$. Let $a \in S$, we need to show that $m_{i}\cdot a = a \cdot m_{i}$.
nodes.statement_short: Suffices that each coefficient commutes with $S$.

nodes.name: Commute with a tensor 1
nodes.statement: Since $w$ is in the centralizer, $w \cdot (a\otimes 1) = (a\otimes 1)\cdot w$. Hence we have $\sum_{i}(a\cdot m_{i})\otimes\mathcal{B}_{i}=\sum_{i}(m_{i}\cdot a)\otimes\mathcal{B}_{i}$.
nodes.statement_short: Compare $w(a\otimes1)$ and $(a\otimes1)w$.

nodes.name: Uniqueness of expansion
nodes.statement: By the uniqueness of~\cref{lem:expand-tensor-in-basis}, we conclude $a\cdot m_{i}=m_{i}\cdot a$.
nodes.statement_short: Uniqueness of the expansion gives the claim.

nodes.name: Centralizer of the image of A in A tensor B
nodes.statement: A useful special case is when $S=A$, then since $C_{A}(A)=Z(A)$, we have $C_{A\otimes_{R}B}\left(\im\left(A\to A\otimes_{R} B\right)\right)$ is equal to $Z(A)\otimes_{R} B$. Since $\im\left(R\otimes_{R}B\to A\otimes_{R}B\right)=\im\left(A\to A\otimes_{R}B\right)$, we conclude its centralizer in $A\otimes_{R}B$ is $Z(A)\otimes_{R}B$.

nodes.name: Centralizer of a tensor product of subalgebras
nodes.statement: Assume $R$ is a field. Let $S$ and $T$ be $R$-subalgebras of $A$ and $B$ respectively. Then $C_{A\otimes_{R}B}\left(S\otimes_{R}T\right)$ is equal to $C_{A}(S)\otimes_{R}C_{B}(T)$
nodes.label: cor:centralizer-tensor-centralizer

nodes.name: Proof of Centralizer of a tensor product of subalgebras
nodes.statement: From~\cref{lem:submodule-tensor-submodule}, $C_{A}(S)\otimes_{R}C_{B}(T)$ is equal to $\left(C_{A}(S)\otimes_{R} B\right)\sqcap \left(A\otimes_{R}C_{B}(T)\right)$. The left hand side $C_{A}(S)\otimes_{R} B$ is equal to $C_{A\otimes_{R}B}\left(\im\left(S\to A\otimes_{R}B\right)\right)$ and the right hand side is equal to $C_{A\otimes_{R}B}\left(\im\left(T\to A\otimes_{R}B\right)\right)$. Hence by~\cref{lem:sup-centralizer}, their intersection is equal to \[C_{A\otimes_{R}B}\left(\im\left(S\to A\otimes_{R} B\right)\sqcup \im\left(T\to A\otimes_{R}B\right)\right)\] This is precisely $C_{A\otimes_{R}B}\left(S\otimes_{R}T\right)$.
nodes.statement_short: Intersect the two centralizers using the submodule intersection lemma and the supremum lemma.

nodes.name: Intersection of tensor submodules
nodes.statement: From~\cref{lem:submodule-tensor-submodule}, $C_{A}(S)\otimes_{R}C_{B}(T)$ is equal to $\left(C_{A}(S)\otimes_{R} B\right)\sqcap \left(A\otimes_{R}C_{B}(T)\right)$.
nodes.statement_short: Write the tensor of centralizers as an intersection.

nodes.name: Identify each side as a centralizer
nodes.statement: The left hand side $C_{A}(S)\otimes_{R} B$ is equal to $C_{A\otimes_{R}B}\left(\im\left(S\to A\otimes_{R}B\right)\right)$ and the right hand side is equal to $C_{A\otimes_{R}B}\left(\im\left(T\to A\otimes_{R}B\right)\right)$.
nodes.statement_short: Each side is the centralizer of an image.

nodes.name: Centralizer of a supremum
nodes.statement: Hence by~\cref{lem:sup-centralizer}, their intersection is equal to \[C_{A\otimes_{R}B}\left(\im\left(S\to A\otimes_{R} B\right)\sqcup \im\left(T\to A\otimes_{R}B\right)\right)\]
nodes.statement_short: The intersection is the centralizer of the supremum.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: This is precisely $C_{A\otimes_{R}B}\left(S\otimes_{R}T\right)$.
nodes.statement_short: Which is the centralizer of $S\otimes T$.

nodes.name: Centre of a tensor product
nodes.statement: Assume $R$ is a field. The centre of $A\otimes_{R} B$ is $Z\left(A\right)\otimes_{R}Z\left(B\right)$.
nodes.label: cor:center-tensor-center

nodes.name: Proof of Centre of a tensor product
nodes.statement: Special case of~\cref{cor:centralizer-tensor-centralizer}.
nodes.statement_short: Special case $S=A$, $T=B$.

nodes.name: Canonical map from A tensor A^op to End_R A
nodes.statement: Let $R$ be a commutative ring and $A$ an $R$-algebra. Then we have an $R$-algebra homomorphism $A\otimes_{R}A^{\opp} \cong \End_{R}A$ given by $a\otimes 1 \mapsto (a\cdot\bullet)$ and $1\otimes a \mapsto (\bullet\cdot a)$. When $R$ is a field and $A$ is a finite dimensional central simple algebra, this morphism is an isomorphism by~\cref{cor:alghom-bijective-of-dim-eq}.
nodes.statement_short: $a\otimes b\mapsto(x\mapsto axb)$ gives $A\otimes A^{op}\to\End_R A$, an isomorphism for finite dimensional central simple $A$.

nodes.name: Isomorphism End_A(M^n) with Mat_n(End_A M)
nodes.statement: Let $A$ be an $R$-algebra and $M$ an $A$-module. We have isomorphism $\End_{A}\left(M^{n}\right)\cong \Mat_{n}\left(\End_{A}M\right)$ as $R$-algebras. For any $f \in \End_{A}\left(M^{n}\right)$, we define a matrix $M$ whose $(i,j)$-th entry is \[ x \mapsto f\left(0,\dots,x,\dots,0\right)_{i}, \] where $x$ is at the $j$-th position. On the other hand, if $M \in \Mat_{n}\left(\End_{A}M\right)$, we define an $A$-linear map $f : M^{n}\to M^{n}$ by \[ v \mapsto \left(\sum_{j}M_{ij}v_{j}\right)_{i}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Endomorphisms of $M^n$ correspond to $n\times n$ matrices of endomorphisms of $M$.

nodes.name: Mat_m(Mat_n(A)) is Mat_mn(A)
nodes.statement: Let $A$ be an $R$-algebra. Then $\Mat_{m}\left(\Mat_{n}(A)\right) \cong \Mat_{mn}(A)$.

nodes.name: Proof of the matrix-of-matrices isomorphism
nodes.statement: The trick is to think $\Mat_{m}A$ as $\{0,\dots,m-1\} \times \{0,\dots,m-1\} \to A$. Since the indexing set $\{0,\dots,mn-1\}$ bijects with $\left(\{0,\dots,m-1\}\times\{0,\dots,n-1\}\right)$, the isomorphism is just function currying, function uncurrying, precomposing and postcomposing bijections.
nodes.statement_short: Reindex via the bijection $\{0..mn-1\}\cong\{0..m-1\}\times\{0..n-1\}$ (currying).

nodes.name: Mat_mn(A tensor B) is Mat_m(A) tensor Mat_n(B)
nodes.statement: Let $A, B$ be $R$-algebras. Then $\Mat_{mn}\left(A\otimes_{R}B\right)\cong\Mat_{m}(A)\otimes_{R}\Mat_{n}B$ as $K$-algebras.

nodes.name: Proof of the Kronecker product isomorphism
nodes.statement: We first construct $R$-algebra isomorphism $A \otimes_{R}\Mat_{n}(R) \cong \Mat_{n}(A)$: \[ \begin{aligned} & a \otimes 1 \mapsto \diag{a}~\text{and}~ 1\otimes (m_{ij}) \mapsto (m_{ij})\\ & \sum_{i,j} m_{ij}\otimes \delta_{ij}\mapsfrom (m_{ij}), \end{aligned} \] where $\diag$ is the diagonal matrix and $\delta_{ij}$ the matrix whose only non-zero entry is at $(i,j)$-th and is equal to $1$. Thus $\Mat_{m}(A)\otimes_{R}\Mat_{n}(B)\cong \left(A\otimes_{R}B\right)\otimes_{R} \left(\Mat_{m}(R)\otimes_{R} \Mat_{n}(R)\right)$ as $R$-algebra. The Kronecker product gives us an $R$-algebra map $\Mat_{m}(R)\otimes_{R}\Mat_{n}(R) \to \Mat_{mn}(R)$. We want this map to be an isomorphism. By~\cref{lem:simple-ring-iff}, we only need to prove it to be surjective: for all $\delta_{ij} \in \Mat_{mn}(R)$, we interpret $\Mat_{mn}(R)$ as a function $\{0,\dots,m-1\}\times\{0,\dots,n-1\}\to R$, then $\delta_{ij}$ is the image of $\delta_{ab}\otimes \delta_{cd} \in \Mat_{m}(R)\otimes_{R}\Mat_{n}(R)$ where $i = (a, c)$ and $j = (b,d)$. Combine everything together, we see $\Mat_{mn}\left(A\otimes_{R}B\right)$ is isomorphic to $\Mat_{mn}\left(A\otimes_{R} B\right)$ as $R$-algebras.
nodes.statement_short: Identify $A\otimes\Mat_n(R)\cong\Mat_n(A)$, then show the Kronecker map $\Mat_m(R)\otimes\Mat_n(R)\to\Mat_{mn}(R)$ is an isomorphism.

nodes.name: Isomorphism A tensor Mat_n(R) with Mat_n(A)
nodes.statement: We first construct $R$-algebra isomorphism $A \otimes_{R}\Mat_{n}(R) \cong \Mat_{n}(A)$: \[ \begin{aligned} & a \otimes 1 \mapsto \diag{a}~\text{and}~ 1\otimes (m_{ij}) \mapsto (m_{ij})\\ & \sum_{i,j} m_{ij}\otimes \delta_{ij}\mapsfrom (m_{ij}), \end{aligned} \] where $\diag$ is the diagonal matrix and $\delta_{ij}$ the matrix whose only non-zero entry is at $(i,j)$-th and is equal to $1$.
nodes.statement_short: Construct $A\otimes\Mat_n(R)\cong\Mat_n(A)$ explicitly.

nodes.name: Kronecker map is an isomorphism
nodes.statement: Thus $\Mat_{m}(A)\otimes_{R}\Mat_{n}(B)\cong \left(A\otimes_{R}B\right)\otimes_{R} \left(\Mat_{m}(R)\otimes_{R} \Mat_{n}(R)\right)$ as $R$-algebra. The Kronecker product gives us an $R$-algebra map $\Mat_{m}(R)\otimes_{R}\Mat_{n}(R) \to \Mat_{mn}(R)$. We want this map to be an isomorphism. By~\cref{lem:simple-ring-iff}, we only need to prove it to be surjective: for all $\delta_{ij} \in \Mat_{mn}(R)$, we interpret $\Mat_{mn}(R)$ as a function $\{0,\dots,m-1\}\times\{0,\dots,n-1\}\to R$, then $\delta_{ij}$ is the image of $\delta_{ab}\otimes \delta_{cd} \in \Mat_{m}(R)\otimes_{R}\Mat_{n}(R)$ where $i = (a, c)$ and $j = (b,d)$.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to the Kronecker map and show it is surjective, hence bijective.

nodes.name: Combine
nodes.statement: Combine everything together, we see $\Mat_{mn}\left(A\otimes_{R}B\right)$ is isomorphic to $\Mat_{mn}\left(A\otimes_{R} B\right)$ as $R$-algebras.
nodes.statement_short: Combine the isomorphisms.

nodes.name: Minimal ideal of simple rings
nodes.statement: Let $A$ be a ring and $I$ a non-trivial minimal left ideal of $A$, then $I$ is a simple $A$-module.
assumptions: $A$ be a ring and $I$ a non-trivial minimal left ideal of $A$
nodes.label: lemma:min-ideal-simple-ring

nodes.name: Proof of Minimal ideal of simple rings
nodes.statement: Let $J\le I$ be an $A$-submodule of $I$, suppose $J$ is non-trivial, we prove that $J=I$. Then the image $J'$ of $J$ under $I \hookrightarrow A$ is a non-trivial left ideal of $A$. Since $I \hookrightarrow A$ is injective, it is sufficient to prove that $J' = I$. This is because $J'\le I$ and $J' \not< J$.
nodes.statement_short: A nonzero submodule of a minimal left ideal is a left ideal inside it, hence equal.

nodes.name: Nonzero submodule
nodes.statement: Let $J\le I$ be an $A$-submodule of $I$, suppose $J$ is non-trivial, we prove that $J=I$. Then the image $J'$ of $J$ under $I \hookrightarrow A$ is a non-trivial left ideal of $A$.
nodes.statement_short: A nonzero submodule $J$ gives a nonzero left ideal $J'$.

nodes.name: Minimality
nodes.statement: Since $I \hookrightarrow A$ is injective, it is sufficient to prove that $J' = I$. This is because $J'\le I$ and $J' \not< J$.
nodes.statement_short: Minimality of $I$ forces $J'=I$.

nodes.name: Unit decomposition via a left ideal
nodes.statement: Let $A$ be a simple ring and $I$ a non-trivial left ideal. One can write $1 \in A$ as $\sum_{i=0}^{n}x_{i}y_{i}$ for some $x_{i}\in I$ and $y_{i} \in A$.
assumptions: $A$ be a simple ring and $I$ a non-trivial left ideal
conclusions: One can write $1 \in A$ as $\sum_{i=0}^{n}x_{i}y_{i}$ for some $x_{i}\in I$ and $y_{i} \in A$

nodes.name: Proof of Unit decomposition via a left ideal
nodes.statement: Let $I'$ be the two-sided ideal spanned by $I$. Then since $A$ is a simple ring, $I' = A$. Thus $1 \in I'$. One can write $1 \in A$ as $\sum_{i}a_{i}x_{i}b_{i}$ for some $x_{i}\in I$ and $a_{i},b_{i}\in A$, since $I$ is a left ideal $a_{i}x_{i}\in I$ as well.
nodes.statement_short: The two-sided ideal generated by $I$ is $A$, so 1 is a sum of products.

nodes.name: Generated two-sided ideal
nodes.statement: Let $I'$ be the two-sided ideal spanned by $I$. Then since $A$ is a simple ring, $I' = A$.
nodes.statement_short: The two-sided ideal generated by $I$ is $A$.

nodes.name: Write 1
nodes.statement: Thus $1 \in I'$. One can write $1 \in A$ as $\sum_{i}a_{i}x_{i}b_{i}$ for some $x_{i}\in I$ and $a_{i},b_{i}\in A$, since $I$ is a left ideal $a_{i}x_{i}\in I$ as well.
nodes.statement_short: Write $1$ as $\sum a_i x_i b_i$ and absorb $a_i$ into $I$.

nodes.name: Minimal decomposition of 1
nodes.statement: Now, we can find the smallest $n$ such that $1\in A$ can be written as $\sum_{i=0}^{n}x_{i}y_{i}$ for some $x_{i}\in I$ and $y_{i}\in A$. Let us fix the notations $n$, $x_{i}$ and $y_{i}$

nodes.name: Minimal decomposition has non-zero terms
nodes.statement: The $n$, $x_{i}$ and $y_{i}$ are all non-zero.

nodes.name: Proof of Minimal decomposition has non-zero terms
nodes.statement: If $n$ is $0$, then $1 = 0$ in $A$, but all simple rings are non-trivial. We argue by contradiction to prove that all $x_{i}$ and $y_{i}$ are non-zero. Assume there exists a $j$ such that $y_{j}\ne0$ implies $x_{j} = 0$. Without loss of generality, we assume $j = 0$. Then $1 = \sum_{i=0}^{n}x_{i}y_{i}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_{i}y_{i}$. This contradicts the minimality of $n$.
nodes.statement_short: A zero term could be dropped, contradicting minimality of $n$.

nodes.name: n nonzero
nodes.statement: If $n$ is $0$, then $1 = 0$ in $A$, but all simple rings are non-trivial.
nodes.statement_short: $n=0$ would make $A$ trivial.

nodes.name: Terms nonzero
nodes.statement: We argue by contradiction to prove that all $x_{i}$ and $y_{i}$ are non-zero. Assume there exists a $j$ such that $y_{j}\ne0$ implies $x_{j} = 0$. Without loss of generality, we assume $j = 0$. Then $1 = \sum_{i=0}^{n}x_{i}y_{i}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_{i}y_{i}$. This contradicts the minimality of $n$.
nodes.statement_short: A zero term could be removed, contradicting minimality.

nodes.name: Wedderburn
nodes.statement: Let $A$ be a simple ring and $I$ a non-trivial minimal left ideal. Then there exists a non-zero $n \in \mathbb{N}$ such that $A \cong I^{n}$ as $A$-modules.
assumptions: $A$ be a simple ring and $I$ a non-trivial minimal left ideal
conclusions: there exists a non-zero $n \in \mathbb{N}$ such that $A \cong I^{n}$ as $A$-modules
nodes.label: thm:wed

nodes.name: Proof of Wedderburn
nodes.statement: We continue to write $1 = \sum_{i=0}^{n}x_{i}y_{i}$ in the shortest possible manner. Then we can define an $A$-linear map $g : I^{n}\to A$ by $(v_{i})\mapsto \sum v_{i}y_{i}$. Then $g$ is surjective: if $a \in A$, then $(ax_{i})$ is mapped to $a$ under $g$. $g$ is injective as well: support $g(v_{i})=0=\sum_{i}v_{i}y_{i}$ with $(v_{i})$ not all zero. Without loss of generality, we assume $v_{0} \ne 0$, then the ideal $\langle v_{0}\rangle$ is equal to $I$ (since $I$ is simple\cref{lemma:min-ideal-simple-ring}). Thus $x_{0}\in I = \langle v_{0}\rangle$; implying that $x_{0}=r\cdot v_{0}$ for some $r\in A$. Thus $1=1 - r\cdot 0 = \sum_{i=0}^{n}x_{i}y_{i}-\sum_{i=0}^{n}r\cdot v_{i}y_{i}$. In this way, we cancelled the term at $i=0$, contradicting the minimality of $n$. Hence $g$ is an isomorphism.
nodes.statement_short: Map $I^n\to A$ by $(v_i)\mapsto\sum v_i y_i$; surjective directly, injective by minimality of the decomposition of 1.

nodes.name: Define g
nodes.statement: We continue to write $1 = \sum_{i=0}^{n}x_{i}y_{i}$ in the shortest possible manner. Then we can define an $A$-linear map $g : I^{n}\to A$ by $(v_{i})\mapsto \sum v_{i}y_{i}$.
nodes.statement_short: Define $g:I^n\to A$, $(v_i)\mapsto\sum v_iy_i$.

nodes.name: Surjectivity
nodes.statement: Then $g$ is surjective: if $a \in A$, then $(ax_{i})$ is mapped to $a$ under $g$.
nodes.statement_short: $(ax_i)\mapsto a$.

nodes.name: Injectivity
nodes.statement: $g$ is injective as well: support $g(v_{i})=0=\sum_{i}v_{i}y_{i}$ with $(v_{i})$ not all zero. Without loss of generality, we assume $v_{0} \ne 0$, then the ideal $\langle v_{0}\rangle$ is equal to $I$ (since $I$ is simple\cref{lemma:min-ideal-simple-ring}). Thus $x_{0}\in I = \langle v_{0}\rangle$; implying that $x_{0}=r\cdot v_{0}$ for some $r\in A$. Thus $1=1 - r\cdot 0 = \sum_{i=0}^{n}x_{i}y_{i}-\sum_{i=0}^{n}r\cdot v_{i}y_{i}$. In this way, we cancelled the term at $i=0$, contradicting the minimality of $n$.
nodes.statement_short: A nonzero kernel element would shorten the decomposition of 1.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Hence $g$ is an isomorphism.
nodes.statement_short: $g$ is an isomorphism.

nodes.name: Wedderburn-Artin (Ideal)
nodes.statement: Let $A$ be an Artinian simple ring. There exists a non-zero $n$ and an ideal $I \subseteq A$ such that $I$ is simple as an $A$-module and $A \cong I^{n}$ as $A$-module.
conclusions: There exists a non-zero $n$ and an ideal $I \subseteq A$ such that $I$ is simple as an $A$-module and $A \cong I^{n}$ as $A$-module
nodes.label: thm:wed-artin-ideal

nodes.name: Proof of Wedderburn-Artin (Ideal)
nodes.statement: By~\cref{thm:wed}, we only need a minimal left ideal. Since $A$ is Artinian, such ideal exists.
nodes.statement_short: Artinian rings have minimal left ideals; apply Wedderburn.

nodes.name: Wedderburn-Artin (Algebra)
nodes.statement: Let $K$ be a field and $B$ an finite dimensional simple algebra over $K$. There exists a non-zero $n\in\mathbb{N}$ and a division $K$-algebra $S$ such that $B \cong \Mat_{n}(S)$.
assumptions: $K$ be a field and $B$ an finite dimensional simple algebra over $K$
conclusions: There exists a non-zero $n\in\mathbb{N}$ and a division $K$-algebra $S$ such that $B \cong \Mat_{n}(S)$
nodes.label: thm:wed-artin-algebra

nodes.name: Proof of Wedderburn-Artin (Algebra)
nodes.statement: By~\cref{thm:wed-artin-ideal}, we can find a $n$ and a minimal left ideal $I$ such $A \cong I^{n}$ as $A$-modules. Note that ${\left(\End_{B}I\right)}^{\opp}$ is a division ring. Then since $B^{\opp}\cong\End_{B}B\cong{\End_{B}(I^{n})}\cong\Mat_{n}\left(\End_{B}I\right)$ as rings where the final isomorphism is from~\cref{con:end-vec-iso-matrix}, we have $e : B\cong \Mat_{n}\left(\End_{B}I\right)^{\opp}$ as rings. We also have a $K$-algebra structure on ${\left(\End_{B} I\right)}^{\opp}$ given by $(a \cdot f)(x)=f(a\cdot x)$, and this algebra structure promotes the ring isomorphism $e$ to a $k$-algebra isomorphism.
nodes.statement_short: From $B\cong I^n$ take endomorphisms: $B^{op}\cong\Mat_n(\End_B I)$.

nodes.name: Minimal ideal decomposition
nodes.statement: By~\cref{thm:wed-artin-ideal}, we can find a $n$ and a minimal left ideal $I$ such $A \cong I^{n}$ as $A$-modules.
nodes.statement_short: Get $B\cong I^n$.

nodes.name: Endomorphism algebra
nodes.statement: Note that ${\left(\End_{B}I\right)}^{\opp}$ is a division ring. Then since $B^{\opp}\cong\End_{B}B\cong{\End_{B}(I^{n})}\cong\Mat_{n}\left(\End_{B}I\right)$ as rings where the final isomorphism is from~\cref{con:end-vec-iso-matrix}, we have $e : B\cong \Mat_{n}\left(\End_{B}I\right)^{\opp}$ as rings.
nodes.statement_short: $B^{op}\cong\Mat_n(\End_B I)$, so $B\cong\Mat_n(\End_B I)^{op}$.

nodes.name: Algebra structure
nodes.statement: We also have a $K$-algebra structure on ${\left(\End_{B} I\right)}^{\opp}$ given by $(a \cdot f)(x)=f(a\cdot x)$, and this algebra structure promotes the ring isomorphism $e$ to a $k$-algebra isomorphism.
nodes.statement_short: Promote the ring isomorphism to a $K$-algebra isomorphism.

nodes.name: Uniqueness of Wedderburn-Artin theorem
nodes.statement: Let $B$ be a finite-dimensional simple $K$-algebra. Suppose $B$ is isomorphic as $k$-algebras to both $\Mat_{n}(D)$ and $\Mat_{n'}(D')$ where $n, n'$ are non-zero natural numbers and $D, D'$ are $k$-division algebra, then $n = n'$ and $D \cong D'$ as $k$-algebras.
assumptions: $B$ is isomorphic as $k$-algebras to both $\Mat_{n}(D)$ and $\Mat_{n'}(D')$ where $n, n'$ are non-zero natural numbers and $D, D'$ are $k$-division algebra
nodes.label: thm:wed-artin-uniq

nodes.name: Proof of Uniqueness of Wedderburn-Artin theorem
nodes.statement: Since $D^{n}$ is a simple $B$-module, by~\cref{lem:end-simple-iso}, we see that $\End_{A}D^{n}\cong D^{\opp}$ and $\End_{A}D^{n}\cong D'^{\opp}$ as $k$-algebras. Thus $D^{\opp}\cong D'^{\opp}$ as $k$-algebras, consequently $D\cong D'$ as $k$-algebras as well. Since $A \cong \Mat_{n}(D)\cong \Mat_{n'}(D')\cong \Mat_{n'}(D)$ as $k$-algebras and $A$ is finite $k$-dimensional, a dimension argument shows that $n=n'$.
nodes.statement_short: Endomorphisms of the simple module recover $D^{op}$; dimension count gives $n=n'$.

nodes.name: D is recovered
nodes.statement: Since $D^{n}$ is a simple $B$-module, by~\cref{lem:end-simple-iso}, we see that $\End_{A}D^{n}\cong D^{\opp}$ and $\End_{A}D^{n}\cong D'^{\opp}$ as $k$-algebras. Thus $D^{\opp}\cong D'^{\opp}$ as $k$-algebras, consequently $D\cong D'$ as $k$-algebras as well.
nodes.statement_short: Endomorphisms of the simple module give $D\cong D'$.

nodes.name: Dimension count
nodes.statement: Since $A \cong \Mat_{n}(D)\cong \Mat_{n'}(D')\cong \Mat_{n'}(D)$ as $k$-algebras and $A$ is finite $k$-dimensional, a dimension argument shows that $n=n'$.
nodes.statement_short: Dimension count gives $n=n'$.

nodes.name: Standing notation for Skolem-Noether: K, A, B
nodes.statement: Let $K$ be a field, $A$, $B$ be $K$-algebras where $A$ is central simple and finite $K$-dimensional and $B$ is simple.

nodes.name: Standing notation: simple A-module M
nodes.statement: Let $M$ be a simple $A$-module.

nodes.name: Module M^f
nodes.statement: For any $K$-algebra homomorphism $f : B \to A$, we give $M$ a $B \otimes_{K}\End_{A}M$-module structure by defining $(b\otimes l)\cdot m$ to be $f(b)\cdot l(m)$. To emphasis $f$, we denote $M$ with the $B\otimes_{K}\End_{A}M$-module structure by $M^{f}$.
nodes.statement_short: For $f:B\to A$, $M$ becomes a $B\otimes_K\End_A M$-module via $(b\otimes l)m=f(b)l(m)$.

nodes.name: M^f is finitely generated
nodes.statement: Let $f : B \to A$ be a $K$-algebra homomorphism, $M^{f}$ is finitely generated as a $B\otimes_{K}\End_{A}M$-module.

nodes.name: Proof of M^f is finitely generated
nodes.statement: Since $M$ is a finite $A$-module and $A$ a finite dimensional $K$-vector space, $M$ is a finite dimensional $K$-vector space as well. Suppose $S \subseteq M$ generates $M$ as $K$-module, the claim is that $S$ generates $M^{f}$ as well. Let $x \in M^{f}$, we write $x = \sum_{i}\lambda_{i}\cdot s_{i}$ with $\lambda_{i}\in K$ and $s_{i}\in S$. Note that $\lambda_{i}\cdot s_{i} = (\rho(\lambda_{i})\otimes\mathbf{1}_{M})$ in $M^{f}$ where $\rho : K \to B$ is the map giving $B$ its $K$-algebra structure. Hence $x$ is in the span of $S$ in $M^{f}$ as well.
nodes.statement_short: A $K$-spanning set of $M$ also generates $M^f$.

nodes.name: M finite dimensional
nodes.statement: Since $M$ is a finite $A$-module and $A$ a finite dimensional $K$-vector space, $M$ is a finite dimensional $K$-vector space as well.
nodes.statement_short: $M$ is finite dimensional over $K$.

nodes.name: Claim on generators
nodes.statement: Suppose $S \subseteq M$ generates $M$ as $K$-module, the claim is that $S$ generates $M^{f}$ as well.
nodes.statement_short: A $K$-spanning set generates $M^f$.

nodes.name: Verify
nodes.statement: Let $x \in M^{f}$, we write $x = \sum_{i}\lambda_{i}\cdot s_{i}$ with $\lambda_{i}\in K$ and $s_{i}\in S$. Note that $\lambda_{i}\cdot s_{i} = (\rho(\lambda_{i})\otimes\mathbf{1}_{M})$ in $M^{f}$ where $\rho : K \to B$ is the map giving $B$ its $K$-algebra structure. Hence $x$ is in the span of $S$ in $M^{f}$ as well.
nodes.statement_short: Scalars act through $\rho(\lambda)\otimes1$.

nodes.name: B is finite dimensional
nodes.statement: Given that $B$ is simple, any $k$-algebra homomorphism $f : B\to A$ injective; therefore by finite $K$-dimensionality of $A$, $B$ is finite $K$-dimensional as well.

nodes.name: M^f and M^g are isomorphic
nodes.statement: Let $f,g : B \to A$ be two $K$-algebra homomorphisms. Then $M^{f}$ and $M^{g}$ are isomorphic as $B\otimes_{K}\End_{A}M$-module.
nodes.label: lem:iso-fg

nodes.name: Proof of M^f and M^g are isomorphic
nodes.statement: By~\cref{lem:iso-of-dim-eq}, it is sufficient to prove $\dim_{K}M^{f}=\dim_{K}M^{g}$. But as $K$-vector space, $M^{f}$ and $M^{g}$ are {\em literally\/} $M$.
nodes.statement_short: Both are $M$ as $K$-spaces, so dimensions agree.

nodes.name: Skolem-Noether
nodes.statement: Let $f, g : B \to A$ be two $K$-algebra homomorphism. Then $f$ and $g$ differ only by a conjugation. That is there exists a unit $x \in A^{\times}$ such that $g = x f x^{-1}$.
assumptions: $f, g : B \to A$ be two $K$-algebra homomorphism
conclusions: $f$ and $g$ differ only by a conjugation
there exists a unit $x \in A^{\times}$ such that $g = x f x^{-1}$
nodes.label: thm:skolem-noether

nodes.name: Proof of Skolem-Noether
nodes.statement: Let $M$ be any simple $A$-module (which exists by~\cref{lem:exists-simple-mod}). By~\cref{lem:iso-fg}, we have some isomorphism $\phi : M^{f}\cong M^{g}$ as $B\otimes_{K}\End_{A}M$-module. Since $M$ is simple, we have that $M$ is a balanced $A$-module by~\cref{lem:iso-end-end}. Let $e$ denote the $k$-algerba isomorphism $A \cong \End_{\End_{A}M}M$ given by the $A$-action on $M$. Since both $\phi$ and $\phi^{-1}$ defines an element of $\End_{\End_{A}M}M$, we define $a := e^{-1}(\phi)$ and $b := e^{-1}(\phi^{-1})$. Then $ab = 1$ since $e(ab)=e(a)\cdot e(b)=\phi\phi^{-1}=1$. We prove that the image of $f$ and $afb$ under $e$ are the same; that is for all $x\in B$ and $m\in M$, $e(g(x))(m) = e(a f(x) b)(m)$. The right hand side is equal to \[ \begin{aligned} e(af(x)b)(m) &=\left(e(a)\circ e(f(x))\circ e(b)\right)(m) \\ &=\left(\phi\circ e(f(x))\circ \phi^{-1}\right)(m)\\ &=\phi\left(f(x)\cdot\phi^{-1}(m)\right) \\ \end{aligned}. \] Similarly, the left hand side is equal to $g(x)\cdot m$. Note that $\phi$ is $B\otimes \End_{A}M$-linear. Therefore $\phi\left(\left(x\otimes\mathbf{1}\right)\cdot \phi^{-1}(m)\right) = \left(x\otimes\mathbf{1}\right)\cdot m$. Unfolding the definition of $M^{f}$ and $M^{g}$, we see this is saying precisely $\phi\left(f(x)\cdot\phi^{-1}(m)\right)=g(x)\cdot m$.
nodes.statement_short: An isomorphism $M^f\cong M^g$ lies in $\End_{\End_A M}M\cong A$, giving the conjugating unit. Key step: the isomorphism is $B\otimes\End_A M$-linear, which unfolds to $g=afb$.

nodes.name: Isomorphism phi
nodes.statement: Let $M$ be any simple $A$-module (which exists by~\cref{lem:exists-simple-mod}). By~\cref{lem:iso-fg}, we have some isomorphism $\phi : M^{f}\cong M^{g}$ as $B\otimes_{K}\End_{A}M$-module.
nodes.statement_short: Take a simple $M$ and an isomorphism $\phi:M^f\cong M^g$.

nodes.name: A is a double endomorphism algebra
nodes.statement: Since $M$ is simple, we have that $M$ is a balanced $A$-module by~\cref{lem:iso-end-end}. Let $e$ denote the $k$-algerba isomorphism $A \cong \End_{\End_{A}M}M$ given by the $A$-action on $M$.
nodes.statement_short: $e:A\cong\End_{\End_A M}M$.

nodes.name: Units a and b
nodes.statement: Since both $\phi$ and $\phi^{-1}$ defines an element of $\End_{\End_{A}M}M$, we define $a := e^{-1}(\phi)$ and $b := e^{-1}(\phi^{-1})$. Then $ab = 1$ since $e(ab)=e(a)\cdot e(b)=\phi\phi^{-1}=1$.

nodes.name: g = a f b
nodes.statement: We prove that the image of $f$ and $afb$ under $e$ are the same; that is for all $x\in B$ and $m\in M$, $e(g(x))(m) = e(a f(x) b)(m)$. The right hand side is equal to \[ \begin{aligned} e(af(x)b)(m) &=\left(e(a)\circ e(f(x))\circ e(b)\right)(m) \\ &=\left(\phi\circ e(f(x))\circ \phi^{-1}\right)(m)\\ &=\phi\left(f(x)\cdot\phi^{-1}(m)\right) \\ \end{aligned}. \] Similarly, the left hand side is equal to $g(x)\cdot m$. Note that $\phi$ is $B\otimes \End_{A}M$-linear. Therefore $\phi\left(\left(x\otimes\mathbf{1}\right)\cdot \phi^{-1}(m)\right) = \left(x\otimes\mathbf{1}\right)\cdot m$. Unfolding the definition of $M^{f}$ and $M^{g}$, we see this is saying precisely $\phi\left(f(x)\cdot\phi^{-1}(m)\right)=g(x)\cdot m$.
nodes.statement_short: Show $e(g(x))=e(af(x)b)$.

nodes.name: Expand both sides
nodes.statement: The right hand side is equal to \[ \begin{aligned} e(af(x)b)(m) &=\left(e(a)\circ e(f(x))\circ e(b)\right)(m) \\ &=\left(\phi\circ e(f(x))\circ \phi^{-1}\right)(m)\\ &=\phi\left(f(x)\cdot\phi^{-1}(m)\right) \\ \end{aligned}. \] Similarly, the left hand side is equal to $g(x)\cdot m$.
nodes.statement_short: Compute both sides.

nodes.name: Linearity of phi
nodes.statement: Note that $\phi$ is $B\otimes \End_{A}M$-linear. Therefore $\phi\left(\left(x\otimes\mathbf{1}\right)\cdot \phi^{-1}(m)\right) = \left(x\otimes\mathbf{1}\right)\cdot m$.
nodes.statement_short: Use $B\otimes\End_A M$-linearity of $\phi$.

nodes.name: Unfold
nodes.statement: Unfolding the definition of $M^{f}$ and $M^{g}$, we see this is saying precisely $\phi\left(f(x)\cdot\phi^{-1}(m)\right)=g(x)\cdot m$.
nodes.statement_short: Unfolding the module structures gives the equality.

nodes.name: Standing notation: field F and F-algebra A
nodes.statement: In this section let $F$ be a field and $A$ an $F$-algebra.

nodes.name: Left and right multiplication algebras
nodes.statement: Define $\McL_{A} \subseteq \End_{F}A$ to be \[\left\{f : A \to A|f(x)=ax~\text{for some}~a\in A\right\},\] i.e. $F$-linear maps defined by left multiplication; similarly define $\McR_{A}$.
nodes.statement_short: $\McL_A$ ($\McR_A$): the $F$-linear maps of $A$ given by left (right) multiplication.

nodes.name: Notation with the base field
nodes.statement: When we need to stree the underlying field is $F$, we also write $\McL_{A}^{F}$ and $\McR_{A}^{F}$.

nodes.name: A is finite dimensional central simple
nodes.statement: We assume $A$ to be a finite dimensional central simple $F$-algebra.

nodes.name: Centralizer of left multiplications is contained in right multiplications
nodes.statement: The centralizer of $\McL_{A}$ in $\End_{F}A$ is smaller than or equal to $\McR_{A}$: \[ C_{\End_{F}A}\left(\McL_{A}\right) \le \McR_{A}. \]
nodes.label: lem:centralizer-mul-left-le

nodes.name: Proof of Centralizer of left multiplications is contained in right multiplications
nodes.statement: Indeed, let $x \in C_{\End_{F}A}\left(\McL_{A}\right)$. Recall from~\cref{con:self-tensor-opp-iso-end} that $e : A\otimes_{F}A^{\opp}\cong \End_{F}A$ as $F$-algebras. Then $e^{-1}(x)$ is in $C_{A\otimes_{F}A^{\opp}}\left(\im\left(A\to A\otimes_{F}A^{\opp}\right)\right)$ (for $e$ sends $a\otimes 1$ to the $F$-linear map $(a\cdot\bullet)$). Since $C_{A\otimes_{F}A^{\opp}}\left(\im\left(A\to A\otimes_{F}A^{\opp}\right)\right) = Z(A)\otimes_{F}A^{\opp}=F\otimes_{F}A^{\opp}=\im\left(A^{\opp}\to A\otimes_{F}A^{\opp}\right)$, we find some $y\in A^{\opp}$ such that $1 \otimes y = e^{-1}(x)$. Therefore $e\left(1\otimes y\right) = x$; but $e\left(1\otimes y\right)$ is in $\McR_{A}$ for it is the linear map $(\bullet\cdot y)$.
nodes.statement_short: Transport to $A\otimes A^{op}$ and use the centralizer of $A\otimes1$, which is $1\otimes A^{op}$.

nodes.name: Recall the isomorphism
nodes.statement: Indeed, let $x \in C_{\End_{F}A}\left(\McL_{A}\right)$. Recall from~\cref{con:self-tensor-opp-iso-end} that $e : A\otimes_{F}A^{\opp}\cong \End_{F}A$ as $F$-algebras.
nodes.statement_short: Take $x$ and recall $A\otimes A^{op}\cong\End_F A$.

nodes.name: Transport
nodes.statement: Then $e^{-1}(x)$ is in $C_{A\otimes_{F}A^{\opp}}\left(\im\left(A\to A\otimes_{F}A^{\opp}\right)\right)$ (for $e$ sends $a\otimes 1$ to the $F$-linear map $(a\cdot\bullet)$).
nodes.statement_short: $e^{-1}(x)$ centralizes $A\otimes1$.

nodes.name: Centralizer computation
nodes.statement: Since $C_{A\otimes_{F}A^{\opp}}\left(\im\left(A\to A\otimes_{F}A^{\opp}\right)\right) = Z(A)\otimes_{F}A^{\opp}=F\otimes_{F}A^{\opp}=\im\left(A^{\opp}\to A\otimes_{F}A^{\opp}\right)$, we find some $y\in A^{\opp}$ such that $1 \otimes y = e^{-1}(x)$.
nodes.statement_short: That centralizer is $1\otimes A^{op}$.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Therefore $e\left(1\otimes y\right) = x$; but $e\left(1\otimes y\right)$ is in $\McR_{A}$ for it is the linear map $(\bullet\cdot y)$.
nodes.statement_short: Hence $x$ is right multiplication.

nodes.name: Elements centralizing left multiplications are Z(B)-linear
