nodes.statement: For any $F$-algebra $B$, every element in $C_{\End_{F}B}\left(\McL_{B}\right)$ is in fact $Z(B)$-linear. Let $x\in C_{\End_{F}B}\left(\McL_{B}\right)$, $z\in Z(B)$ and $b \in B$, we have $x(z\cdot b) = z\cdot x(b)$ because $x$ commutes with the linear map $\left(z\cdot\bullet\right)$.
nodes.label: rem:mul-left-center-linear

nodes.name: A as a Z(A)-algebra
nodes.statement: $A$ is a $Z(A)$-algebra whose algebra structure is given by $Z(A)\hookrightarrow A$. By~\cref{lem:center-simple-ring}, $Z(A)$ is a field. $A$ is finite dimensional as a $Z(A)$-module because of the tower $A/Z(A)/F$.

nodes.name: Right multiplication algebra is the opposite algebra
nodes.statement: As $F$-algebras, we have $\McR_{A}\cong A^{\opp}$.
nodes.label: lem:mul-right-iso-opp

nodes.name: Proof of Right multiplication algebra is the opposite algebra
nodes.statement: We prove the map $A^{\opp} \to \McR_{A}$ is bijective. It is injective because if $\left(\bullet \cdot a\right) = \left(\bullet\cdot b\right)$, then $a = 1 \cdot a = 1 \cdot b = b$. The map is surjective by the definition of $\McR_{A}$.
nodes.statement_short: The map $A^{op}\to\McR_A$ is injective (evaluate at 1) and surjective by definition.

nodes.name: Injectivity
nodes.statement: We prove the map $A^{\opp} \to \McR_{A}$ is bijective. It is injective because if $\left(\bullet \cdot a\right) = \left(\bullet\cdot b\right)$, then $a = 1 \cdot a = 1 \cdot b = b$.
nodes.statement_short: Injective by evaluating at 1.

nodes.name: Surjectivity
nodes.statement: The map is surjective by the definition of $\McR_{A}$.
nodes.statement_short: Surjective by definition.

nodes.name: Centralizer of left multiplications equals right multiplications
nodes.statement: Let $B$ be any simple $F$-algebra ({\em not\/} necessarily central). The centralizer of $\McL_{B}$ in $\End_{F}B$ is equal to $\McR_{B}$.
conclusions: The centralizer of $\McL_{B}$ in $\End_{F}B$ is equal to $\McR_{B}$
nodes.label: lem:centralizer-mul-left-eq-mul-right

nodes.name: Proof of Centralizer of left multiplications equals right multiplications
nodes.statement: It is straightforward to show $\McR_{B}^{F}\le C_{\End_{F}A}\left(\McL_{B}^{F}\right)$. So we only need to prove $C_{\End_{F}A}\left(\McL_{B}^{F}\right)\le \McR_{B}^{F}$. By~\cref{lem:centralizer-mul-left-le}, since $B$ is a central simple finite dimensional $Z(B)$-algebra, we have that \[ C_{\End_{Z(B)}B}\left(\McL_{B}^{Z(B)}\right) \le \McR_{B}^{Z(B)}. \] Suppose $f\in\End_{F}B$ is in $C_{\End_{F}B}B$, by~\cref{rem:mul-left-center-linear}, $f$ is $Z(B)$-linear as well. Then $f$ is in $\McR_{B}^{Z(B)}$; that is $f$ is equal to $\left(\bullet\cdot b\right)$ for some $b \in B$ as $Z(B)$-linear maps. Then $f$ is also equal to $\left(\bullet\cdot b\right)$ as $F$-linear maps.
nodes.statement_short: Apply the central simple case over $Z(B)$, using that such maps are $Z(B)$-linear.

nodes.name: Reduce to one inclusion
nodes.statement: It is straightforward to show $\McR_{B}^{F}\le C_{\End_{F}A}\left(\McL_{B}^{F}\right)$. So we only need to prove $C_{\End_{F}A}\left(\McL_{B}^{F}\right)\le \McR_{B}^{F}$.
nodes.statement_short: Only $C(\McL_B)\le\McR_B$ is needed.

nodes.name: Central simple case over Z(B)
nodes.statement: By~\cref{lem:centralizer-mul-left-le}, since $B$ is a central simple finite dimensional $Z(B)$-algebra, we have that \[ C_{\End_{Z(B)}B}\left(\McL_{B}^{Z(B)}\right) \le \McR_{B}^{Z(B)}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Apply the lemma over $Z(B)$.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Suppose $f\in\End_{F}B$ is in $C_{\End_{F}B}B$, by~\cref{rem:mul-left-center-linear}, $f$ is $Z(B)$-linear as well. Then $f$ is in $\McR_{B}^{Z(B)}$; that is $f$ is equal to $\left(\bullet\cdot b\right)$ for some $b \in B$ as $Z(B)$-linear maps. Then $f$ is also equal to $\left(\bullet\cdot b\right)$ as $F$-linear maps.
nodes.statement_short: Such $f$ is $Z(B)$-linear, hence a right multiplication.

nodes.name: Conjugate subalgebra xSx^{-1}
nodes.statement: Let $B$ be any $F$-algebra and $S\subseteq B$ an $F$-subalgebra. For any $x\in B^{\times}$, we have that $x S x^{-1}:=\{xsx^{-1}|s\in S\}$ is an $F$-subalgebra of $B$ as well. We have the obvious $F$-algebra isomorphism $S \cong xSx^{-1}$ given by $s\mapsto xsx^{-1}$ and $x^{-1}tx\mapsfrom t$. Therefore $\dim_{F}S=\dim_{F}xSx^{-1}$ and $S$ is a simple ring if and only if $xSx^{-1}$ is a simple ring.

nodes.name: Centralizer of a conjugate
nodes.statement: Let $B$ be any $F$-algebra, $x \in B^{\times}$ and $S\subseteq B$ be an $F$-subalgebra of $B$, then $C_{B}(xSx^{-1})=x\left(C_{B}(S)\right)x^{-1}$.
assumptions: $B$ be any $F$-algebra, $x \in B^{\times}$ and $S\subseteq B$ be an $F$-subalgebra of $B$
nodes.label: lem:centralizer-conj

nodes.name: Proof of Centralizer of a conjugate
nodes.statement: If $a \in C_{B}\left(xSx^{-1}\right)$, then $x^{-1}ax$ is in $C_{B}(S)$. Conversely if $a$ is equal to $xbx^{-1}$ with $b\in C_{B}(S)$, then it is in $C_{B}\left(xSx^{-1}\right)$ as well.
nodes.statement_short: Conjugate elements back and forth.

nodes.name: End_F B is central simple
nodes.statement: For any finite dimensional $F$-module $B$, we have isomorphism $\End_{F}B \cong \Mat_{\dim_{F}B}F$ as $F$-algebras. Hence $\End_{F} B$ is a finite-dimensional central simple algebra over $F$.

nodes.name: A tensor R_S is simple
nodes.statement: Let $S\subseteq A$ be a simple $F$-subalgebra, then $A \otimes_{F} \McR_{S}$ is a simple ring.
nodes.label: lem:tensor-mul-right-simple

nodes.name: Proof of A tensor R_S is simple
nodes.statement: By~\cref{lem:mul-right-iso-opp}, we have $A\otimes \McR_{S}\cong A\otimes S^{\opp}$ as $F$-algebras. The claim follows from~\cref{thm:tensor-csa}.
nodes.statement_short: Identify $\McR_S\cong S^{op}$ and apply the tensor theorem.

nodes.name: Centralizer tensor End_F S is a conjugate of A tensor R_S
nodes.statement: Let $S\subseteq A$ be a simple $F$-subalgebra, then there exists an $x\in \left(A\otimes_{F}\End_{F}S\right)^{\times}$ such that $C_{A}(S)\otimes_{F}\End_{F}S$ is isomorphic to $x\left(A\otimes_{F}\McR_{S}\right)x^{-1}$ as $F$-algebras.
nodes.label: lem:centralizer-tensor-end-eq-conj-tensor-mul-right

nodes.name: Proof of Centralizer tensor End_F S is a conjugate of A tensor R_S
nodes.statement: By~\cref{lem:tensor-central} and~\cref{thm:tensor-csa}, $A \otimes_{F}C_{A}(S)$ is a central simple $F$-algebra. Let $f : S \to A\otimes_{F}\End_{F}S$ be an $F$-algebra homomorphism defined by $s \mapsto s \otimes \mathbf{1}_{S}$ and $g : S \to A \otimes_{F}\End_{F}S$ be an $F$-algebra homomorphism defined by $\mathbf{1}_{A} \otimes \left(s\cdot\bullet\right)$. Then by~\cref{thm:skolem-noether}, we that there exists some $x\in \left(A\otimes_{F}\End_{F}S\right)^{\times}$ such that $f = xgx^{-1}$. Then we have $S\otimes_{F}\End_{F}S$ is equal to $x\left(A\otimes_{F}\McL_{S}\right)x^{-1}$: indeed the left hand side is $\im f$ while the right handside is $x\left(\im g\right)x^{-1}$. Therefore $C_{A\otimes_{F}\End_{F}S}\left(S\otimes_{F}\End_{F}S\right) = C_{A\otimes_{F}\End_{F}S}\left(x\left(A\otimes_{F}\McR_{S}\right)x^{-1}\right)$. By~\cref{lem:centralizer-conj}, the right hand side is equal to $xC_{A\otimes_{F}\End_{F}S}\left(A\otimes_{F}\McL_{S}\right)x^{-1}$ which is $x\left(A\otimes_{F}C_{\End_{F}S}\left(\McL_{S}\right)\right)x^{-1}$ by~\cref{lem:centralizer-inclusion-tensor} which is $x\left(A\otimes_{F}\McR_{S}\right)x^{-1}$ by~\cref{lem:centralizer-mul-left-eq-mul-right}.
nodes.statement_short: Skolem-Noether conjugates the two embeddings of $S$; compute centralizers of both sides.

nodes.name: Central simple tensor
nodes.statement: By~\cref{lem:tensor-central} and~\cref{thm:tensor-csa}, $A \otimes_{F}C_{A}(S)$ is a central simple $F$-algebra.
nodes.statement_short: The tensor algebra is central simple.

nodes.name: Skolem-Noether
nodes.statement: Let $f : S \to A\otimes_{F}\End_{F}S$ be an $F$-algebra homomorphism defined by $s \mapsto s \otimes \mathbf{1}_{S}$ and $g : S \to A \otimes_{F}\End_{F}S$ be an $F$-algebra homomorphism defined by $\mathbf{1}_{A} \otimes \left(s\cdot\bullet\right)$. Then by~\cref{thm:skolem-noether}, we that there exists some $x\in \left(A\otimes_{F}\End_{F}S\right)^{\times}$ such that $f = xgx^{-1}$.
nodes.statement_short: Two embeddings of $S$ are conjugate by some $x$.

nodes.name: Images conjugate
nodes.statement: Then we have $S\otimes_{F}\End_{F}S$ is equal to $x\left(A\otimes_{F}\McL_{S}\right)x^{-1}$: indeed the left hand side is $\im f$ while the right handside is $x\left(\im g\right)x^{-1}$.
nodes.statement_short: Compare the images.

nodes.name: Centralizers agree
nodes.statement: Therefore $C_{A\otimes_{F}\End_{F}S}\left(S\otimes_{F}\End_{F}S\right) = C_{A\otimes_{F}\End_{F}S}\left(x\left(A\otimes_{F}\McR_{S}\right)x^{-1}\right)$.
nodes.statement_short: Take centralizers.

nodes.name: Compute centralizer
nodes.statement: By~\cref{lem:centralizer-conj}, the right hand side is equal to $xC_{A\otimes_{F}\End_{F}S}\left(A\otimes_{F}\McL_{S}\right)x^{-1}$ which is $x\left(A\otimes_{F}C_{\End_{F}S}\left(\McL_{S}\right)\right)x^{-1}$ by~\cref{lem:centralizer-inclusion-tensor} which is $x\left(A\otimes_{F}\McR_{S}\right)x^{-1}$ by~\cref{lem:centralizer-mul-left-eq-mul-right}.
nodes.statement_short: Compute via conjugation and tensor centralizer lemmas.

nodes.name: Centralizer of a simple subalgebra is simple
nodes.statement: Let $S\subseteq A$ be a simple $F$-subalgebra, then $C_{A}(S)$ is simple as well.
nodes.label: lem:simple-centralizer

nodes.name: Proof of Centralizer of a simple subalgebra is simple
nodes.statement: By~\cref{lem:centralizer-tensor-end-eq-conj-tensor-mul-right}, $C_{A}(S) \otimes_{F}\End_{F}S$ is isomorphic to $x\left(A\otimes_{F}\McR_{S}\right)x^{-1}$ as $F$-algebras. Then $C(S)\otimes_{F}\End_{F}S$ is simple since $A\otimes_{F}\McR_{S}$ is simple by~\cref{lem:tensor-mul-right-simple}. By~\cref{thm:tensor-simple-implies-simple}, $C_{A}(S)$ is simple.
nodes.statement_short: The tensor with $\End_F S$ is a conjugate of a simple ring, so the factor is simple.

nodes.name: Conjugate isomorphism
nodes.statement: By~\cref{lem:centralizer-tensor-end-eq-conj-tensor-mul-right}, $C_{A}(S) \otimes_{F}\End_{F}S$ is isomorphic to $x\left(A\otimes_{F}\McR_{S}\right)x^{-1}$ as $F$-algebras.
nodes.statement_short: Get the isomorphism with a conjugate.

nodes.name: Simplicity of the tensor
nodes.statement: Then $C(S)\otimes_{F}\End_{F}S$ is simple since $A\otimes_{F}\McR_{S}$ is simple by~\cref{lem:tensor-mul-right-simple}.
nodes.statement_short: The tensor product is simple.

nodes.name: Factor is simple
nodes.statement: By~\cref{thm:tensor-simple-implies-simple}, $C_{A}(S)$ is simple.
nodes.statement_short: Hence $C_A(S)$ is simple.

nodes.name: Dimension of the centralizer
nodes.statement: Let $S\subseteq A$ be a simple $F$-subalgebra. Then \[ \dim_{F}C_{A}(S)\cdot\dim_{F}S=\dim_{F}A. \]
nodes.label: lem:dim-centralizer

nodes.name: Proof of Dimension of the centralizer
nodes.statement: By~\cref{lem:centralizer-tensor-end-eq-conj-tensor-mul-right}, $C_{A}(S) \otimes_{F}\End_{F}S$ is isomorphic to $x\left(A\otimes_{F}\McR_{S}\right)x^{-1}$ as $F$-algebras. Hence $\dim_{F}\left(C_{A}(S)\otimes_{F}\End_{F}S\right)=\dim_{F}\left(A\otimes_{F}\McR_{S}\right)$ where the left hand side is $\dim_{F}C_{A}(S)\cdot \dim_{F}\End_{F}S$ and the right hand side is $\dim_{F}A\cdot\dim_{F}\McR_{S}$. Since $\dim_{F}\End_{F}S=\dim_{F}S^{2}$ and $\dim_{F}\McR_{S}=\dim S$ (by~\cref{lem:mul-right-iso-opp}), we proved this lemma.
nodes.statement_short: Compare dimensions of the two isomorphic algebras.

nodes.name: Conjugate isomorphism
nodes.statement: By~\cref{lem:centralizer-tensor-end-eq-conj-tensor-mul-right}, $C_{A}(S) \otimes_{F}\End_{F}S$ is isomorphic to $x\left(A\otimes_{F}\McR_{S}\right)x^{-1}$ as $F$-algebras.
nodes.statement_short: Get the isomorphism with a conjugate.

nodes.name: Compare dimensions
nodes.statement: Hence $\dim_{F}\left(C_{A}(S)\otimes_{F}\End_{F}S\right)=\dim_{F}\left(A\otimes_{F}\McR_{S}\right)$ where the left hand side is $\dim_{F}C_{A}(S)\cdot \dim_{F}\End_{F}S$ and the right hand side is $\dim_{F}A\cdot\dim_{F}\McR_{S}$.
nodes.statement_short: Equate dimensions of both sides.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Since $\dim_{F}\End_{F}S=\dim_{F}S^{2}$ and $\dim_{F}\McR_{S}=\dim S$ (by~\cref{lem:mul-right-iso-opp}), we proved this lemma.
nodes.statement_short: Substitute $\dim\End_F S$ and $\dim\McR_S$.

nodes.name: A is a central simple subalgebra tensor its centralizer
nodes.statement: Let $S \subseteq A$ be a central simple $F$-subalgebra, \[ A \cong B \ox_{F} C_{A}(B). \]
nodes.label: cor:self-tensor-centralizer

nodes.name: Proof of A is a central simple subalgebra tensor its centralizer
nodes.statement: By~\cref{lem:simple-centralizer}, $C_{A}(B)$ is simple and by~\cref{thm:tensor-csa}, $B \ox_{F} C_{A}(B)$ is simple. Hence the map $B \ox_{F} C_{A}(B) \to A$ induced by $B \hookrightarrow A$ and $C_{A}(B) \hookrightarrow A$ is injective. By~\cref{cor:alghom-bijective-of-dim-eq}, we only need to show $\dim_{F}B\ox_{F}C_{A}(B) =\dim_{F}A$ which is precisely~\cref{lem:dim-centralizer}.
nodes.statement_short: The multiplication map is injective by simplicity and bijective by dimension.

nodes.name: Tensor is simple
nodes.statement: By~\cref{lem:simple-centralizer}, $C_{A}(B)$ is simple and by~\cref{thm:tensor-csa}, $B \ox_{F} C_{A}(B)$ is simple.
nodes.statement_short: $B\otimes C_A(B)$ is simple.

nodes.name: Injectivity
nodes.statement: Hence the map $B \ox_{F} C_{A}(B) \to A$ induced by $B \hookrightarrow A$ and $C_{A}(B) \hookrightarrow A$ is injective.
nodes.statement_short: The multiplication map is injective.

nodes.name: Dimension
nodes.statement: By~\cref{cor:alghom-bijective-of-dim-eq}, we only need to show $\dim_{F}B\ox_{F}C_{A}(B) =\dim_{F}A$ which is precisely~\cref{lem:dim-centralizer}.
nodes.statement_short: Bijective by the dimension formula.

nodes.name: Double Centralizer
nodes.statement: Let $S\subseteq A$ be a simple $F$-subalgebra, we have \[ C_{A}\left(C_{A}(S)\right) = S. \]
nodes.label: thm:double-centralizer

nodes.name: Proof of Double Centralizer
nodes.statement: It is straightforward that $S \le C_{A}\left(C_{A}(S)\right)$. By~\cref{lem:simple-centralizer}, $C_{A}(S)$ is simple, hence $\dim_{F}C_{A}\left(C_{A}(S)\right)\cdot \dim_{F}C_{A}(S)=\dim_{F}A=\dim_{F}C_{A}(S)\cdot \dim_{F}S$ (by applying~\cref{lem:dim-centralizer} twice), i.e. $\dim_{F}C_{A}\left(C_{A}(S)\right) = \dim_{F}S$. This equality of dimension gives us the desired result.
nodes.statement_short: Inclusion plus equality of dimensions from the centralizer dimension formula.

nodes.name: Equal dimensions
nodes.statement: It is straightforward that $S \le C_{A}\left(C_{A}(S)\right)$. By~\cref{lem:simple-centralizer}, $C_{A}(S)$ is simple, hence $\dim_{F}C_{A}\left(C_{A}(S)\right)\cdot \dim_{F}C_{A}(S)=\dim_{F}A=\dim_{F}C_{A}(S)\cdot \dim_{F}S$ (by applying~\cref{lem:dim-centralizer} twice), i.e. $\dim_{F}C_{A}\left(C_{A}(S)\right) = \dim_{F}S$.
nodes.statement_short: Inclusion and the dimension formula applied twice.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: This equality of dimension gives us the desired result.
nodes.statement_short: Equal dimension gives equality.

nodes.name: Standing notation: field K
nodes.statement: Let $K$ be a field.

nodes.name: Class CSA_K of central simple algebras
nodes.statement: We denote the class of finite dimensional central simple $K$-algebras as $\CSA_{K}$. When $K$ is clear, we drop the subscript.

nodes.name: CSA is closed under tensor product
nodes.statement: By~\cref{lem:tensor-central} and~\cref{thm:tensor-csa}, $\CSA$ is closed under tensor product, that is if $A, B\in\CSA$, we have $A\otimes_{K} B\in\CSA$ as well.

nodes.name: Brauer Equivalence
nodes.statement: For any two $A, B\in\CSA$, we say $A$ and $B$ are Brauer equivalent, when there exists $m, n \in \mathbb{N}_{\ge0}$ such that $\Mat_{m}(A)\cong \Mat_{n}B$ as $K$-algebras. We denote this relation as $A\sim_{\Br_{K}} B$, when $K$ is clear, we drop the subscript.
nodes.label: def:br-eqv

nodes.name: Isomorphic algebras are Brauer equivalent
nodes.statement: Isomorphic $K$-algebras are Brauer equivalent.

nodes.name: Brauer equivalence is reflexive
nodes.statement: $\sim_{\Br}$ is reflexive.

nodes.name: Proof of Brauer equivalence is reflexive
nodes.statement: Indeed, $A \cong \Mat_{1}(A)$ as $K$-algerbas.
nodes.statement_short: $A\cong\Mat_1(A)$.

nodes.name: Brauer equivalence is symmetric
nodes.statement: $\sim_{\Br}$ is symmetric.

nodes.name: Proof of Brauer equivalence is symmetric
nodes.statement: Indeed, just exchange $m$ and $n$.
nodes.statement_short: Swap $m$ and $n$.

nodes.name: Brauer equivalence is transitive
nodes.statement: $\sim_{\Br}$ is transitive.

nodes.name: Proof of Brauer equivalence is transitive
nodes.statement: Let $A\sim_{\Br}B$ and $B\sim_{\Br}C$; that is for some $m,n,p, q\in\mathbb{N}_{\ge0}$ we have $\Mat_{n}(A)\cong\Mat_{m}(B)$ and $\Mat_{p}(B)\cong \Mat_{q}(C)$ as $K$-algebras. Hence, from~\cref{con:matrix-matrix}, we have the following: \[ \begin{aligned} \Mat_{np}(A)&\cong \Mat_{p}\left(\Mat_{n}(A)\right)\cong\Mat_{p}\left(\Mat_{m}(B)\right)\\ &\cong\Mat_{mp}(B)\cong\Mat_{m}\left(\Mat_{p}(B)\right)\\ &\cong\Mat_{m}\left(\Mat_{q}(C)\right)\cong\Mat_{mq}(C). \end{aligned} \] In another word, $A\sim_{\Br}C$.
nodes.statement_short: Compose the matrix isomorphisms using $\Mat_p(\Mat_n)\cong\Mat_{np}$.

nodes.name: Compose isomorphisms
nodes.statement: Let $A\sim_{\Br}B$ and $B\sim_{\Br}C$; that is for some $m,n,p, q\in\mathbb{N}_{\ge0}$ we have $\Mat_{n}(A)\cong\Mat_{m}(B)$ and $\Mat_{p}(B)\cong \Mat_{q}(C)$ as $K$-algebras. Hence, from~\cref{con:matrix-matrix}, we have the following: \[ \begin{aligned} \Mat_{np}(A)&\cong \Mat_{p}\left(\Mat_{n}(A)\right)\cong\Mat_{p}\left(\Mat_{m}(B)\right)\\ &\cong\Mat_{mp}(B)\cong\Mat_{m}\left(\Mat_{p}(B)\right)\\ &\cong\Mat_{m}\left(\Mat_{q}(C)\right)\cong\Mat_{mq}(C). \end{aligned} \]
nodes.statement_short: Chain matrix isomorphisms.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: In another word, $A\sim_{\Br}C$.
nodes.statement_short: Hence $A\sim C$.

nodes.name: Brauer group Br(K) as a set
nodes.statement: Hence $\sim_{\Br}$ is really an equivalence relation, we denote the quotient ${}^{\CSA}/_{\sim_{\Br}}$ as $\Br(K)$.

nodes.name: Tensor product descends to Br(K)
nodes.statement: $(\bullet\otimes_{K}\bullet):\CSA\times\CSA \to \CSA$ descends to a function on $\Br(K)$.
nodes.label: lem:br-mul-wd

nodes.name: Proof of Tensor product descends to Br(K)
nodes.statement: We need to prove that for all $A, B, C, D \in \CSA$ such that $A\sim_{\Br} B$ and $C\sim_{\Br}D$, $A\otimes_{R}C \sim_{\Br} B\otimes_{R}D$ as well. Suppose $\Mat_{m}(A)\cong \Mat_{n}(B)$ as $K$-algebras and $\Mat_{p}(C)\cong\Mat_{q}(D)$, by~\cref{con:matrix-tensor-matrix}, we have \[ \begin{aligned} \Mat_{mp}\left(A\otimes_{R} C\right)&\cong \Mat_{m}(A)\otimes_{R}\Mat_{p}(C) \\ &\cong \Mat_{n}(B)\otimes_{R}\Mat_{q}(D)\\ &\cong \Mat_{nq}\left(B\otimes_{R}D\right). \end{aligned} \]
nodes.statement_short: Tensor the matrix isomorphisms using the Kronecker isomorphism.

nodes.name: Brauer Group
nodes.statement: $\Br(K)$ forms a group under $[A]_{\sim_{\Br}}\cdot[B]_{\sim_{\Br}}=[A\otimes_{K}B]_{\sim_{\Br}}$ with neutral element $[K]_{\sim_{\Br}}$ where $A, B\in\CSA$ and $[A]_{\sim_{Br}}^{-1}=[A^{\opp}]_{\sim_{\Br}}$. We need to prove the following properties: \begin{enumerate} \item associativity: for all $A, B, C\in\CSA$, $[A]_{\sim_{\Br}}\cdot\left([B]_{\sim_{\Br}}\cdot[C]_{\sim_{\Br}}\right)=\left([A]_{\sim_{\Br}}\cdot[B]_{\sim_{\Br}}\right)\cdot [C]_{\sim_{\Br}}$ because $A\ox_{R}\left(B\ox_{R}C\right)\cong \left(A\ox_{R}B\right)\ox_{R}C$ as $K$-algebras. \item neutral element: for all $A\in \CSA$, $[K]_{\sim_{\Br}}\cdot[A]_{\sim_{\Br}}=[A]_{\sim_{\Br}}=[A]_{\sim_{\Br}}\cdot [K]_{\sim_{\Br}}$. Since $[K]_{\sim_{\Br}}\cdot[A]_{\sim_{\Br}}=[K\ox_{K} A]_{\sim_{\Br}}$, in~\cref{con:matrix-tensor-matrix}, we see that $\Mat_{n}(A)\cong A\ox_{K}\Mat_{n}(K)$, by~\cref{lem:br-mul-wd}, $A\ox_{K}\Mat_{n}(K)$ is Brauer equivalent to $A\ox_{K} K$ since $K\sim_{\Br}\Mat_{n}(K)$. \item cancellation: for all $A \in \CSA$, we need $[A]_{\sim_{\Br}}\cdot[A^{\opp}]_{\sim_{\Br}}$, that is we want $A\ox_{K}A^{\opp}\sim_{\Br} K$. By~\cref{con:self-tensor-opp-iso-end}, we have $A\ox_{K}A^{\opp}\cong \End_{K}A$ which is isomorphic to $\Mat_{\dim_{K}A}(K)$ as $K$-algebras.
nodes.statement_short: $\Br(K)$ is a group under tensor product with identity $[K]$ and inverse $[A^{op}]$; associativity, unit and inverses are checked.

nodes.name: Brauer group of an algebraically closed field is trivial
nodes.statement: If $K$ is algebraically closed, $\Br(K)$ is trivial; in particular $\br_{n}(\mathbb{C})$ is trivial.
nodes.label: thm:br-triv-alg-closed

nodes.name: Proof of Brauer group of an algebraically closed field is trivial
nodes.statement: We need to show that every $A\in\CSA$ is isomorphic to $\Mat_{n}(K)$ for some $K$ when $K$ is algebraically closed. Indeed, by~\cref{thm:wed-artin-algebra}, $A \cong \Mat_{n}(D)$ for some division algebra $D$ and $n\in\nat_{\ge0}$. Since $K$ is algebraically closed and $D$ is an integral domain and finite dimensional, the structure morphism $\rho: K\to D$ is a isomorphism; therefore $A\cong \Mat_{n}(K)$.
nodes.statement_short: Every central simple algebra is $\Mat_n(D)$ and $D=K$ when $K$ is algebraically closed.

nodes.name: Goal
nodes.statement: We need to show that every $A\in\CSA$ is isomorphic to $\Mat_{n}(K)$ for some $K$ when $K$ is algebraically closed.
nodes.statement_short: Every central simple algebra is a matrix algebra over $K$.

nodes.name: Wedderburn-Artin
nodes.statement: Indeed, by~\cref{thm:wed-artin-algebra}, $A \cong \Mat_{n}(D)$ for some division algebra $D$ and $n\in\nat_{\ge0}$.
nodes.statement_short: $A\cong\Mat_n(D)$.

nodes.name: D = K
nodes.statement: Since $K$ is algebraically closed and $D$ is an integral domain and finite dimensional, the structure morphism $\rho: K\to D$ is a isomorphism; therefore $A\cong \Mat_{n}(K)$.
nodes.statement_short: A finite dimensional division algebra over algebraically closed $K$ is $K$.

nodes.name: Common division algebra of two central simple algebras
nodes.statement: Let $A, B \in \csa_{K}$. There exists a division $K$-algebra $D$ and non-zero $m,n\in\mathbb{N}$ such that $A\cong\mat_{m}(D)$ and $B\cong\mat_{n}(D)$ as $K$-algebras.
conclusions: There exists a division $K$-algebra $D$ and non-zero $m,n\in\mathbb{N}$ such that $A\cong\mat_{m}(D)$ and $B\cong\mat_{n}(D)$ as $K$-algebras
nodes.label: lem:common-div-alg

nodes.name: Proof of Common division algebra of two central simple algebras
nodes.statement: By~\cref{thm:wed-artin-algebra}, we can find division algebras $S_{A}, S_{B}$ and non-zero $m, n\in\mathbb{N}$ such that $A\cong\mat_{n}\left(S_{A}\right)$ and $B\cong\mat_{m}\left(S_{B}\right)$ as $K$-algebras. Hence $B\sim_{\br}A\sim_{\br}\mat_{n}\left(S_{A}\right)\sim_{\br}S_{A}$, in another word, for some non-zero $a, a'\in\mathbb{N}$, we have $\mat_{a}(B)\cong\mat_{a'}\left(S_{A}\right)$ as $K$-algebras. Hence, by~\cref{thm:wed-artin-uniq}, we have that $S_{A}\cong S_{B}$ as $K$-algebras and the lemma is proved.
nodes.statement_short: Wedderburn-Artin for each algebra, then uniqueness identifies the division algebras.

nodes.name: Wedderburn-Artin for both
nodes.statement: By~\cref{thm:wed-artin-algebra}, we can find division algebras $S_{A}, S_{B}$ and non-zero $m, n\in\mathbb{N}$ such that $A\cong\mat_{n}\left(S_{A}\right)$ and $B\cong\mat_{m}\left(S_{B}\right)$ as $K$-algebras.
nodes.statement_short: Write both as matrix algebras.

nodes.name: Brauer equivalent matrix algebras
nodes.statement: Hence $B\sim_{\br}A\sim_{\br}\mat_{n}\left(S_{A}\right)\sim_{\br}S_{A}$, in another word, for some non-zero $a, a'\in\mathbb{N}$, we have $\mat_{a}(B)\cong\mat_{a'}\left(S_{A}\right)$ as $K$-algebras.
nodes.statement_short: Chain Brauer equivalences.

nodes.name: Uniqueness
nodes.statement: Hence, by~\cref{thm:wed-artin-uniq}, we have that $S_{A}\cong S_{B}$ as $K$-algebras and the lemma is proved.
nodes.statement_short: Uniqueness identifies the division algebras.

nodes.name: Standing notation: field extension E/K
nodes.statement: In this section let $E/K$ be a field extension.

nodes.name: Base change notation A_E
nodes.statement: For brevity, if $A\in \CSA_{K}$, we denote $E\ox_{K}A$ as $A_{E}$ when this causes no confusion.

nodes.name: Base change preserves Brauer equivalence
nodes.statement: We will construct a series of isomorphisms (either over $K$ or $E$) to arrive at the conclusion that $A\sim_{\Br_{K}}B$ implies $A_{E}\sim_{\Br_{E}}B_{E}$.
nodes.statement_short: Brauer equivalence over $K$ is preserved by base change to $E$, giving a homomorphism $\Br(K)\to\Br(E)$.

nodes.name: Proof that base change descends to Brauer groups
nodes.statement:
Assume $m,n\in
at_{\ge0}$ are such that $\Mat_{m}(A)\cong\Mat_{n}(B)$ are $K$-algebras. Then we do the following calculation: as $E$-algebras \[  egin{aligned} \Mat_{m}\left(A_{E}ight) &\cong A_{E}\otimes_{E}\Mat_{m}(E) &	ext{see~\cref{con:matrix-tensor-matrix}}\ &\cong A_{E}\otimes_{E}\left(E\ox_{K} \Mat_{m}(K)ight) & 	ext{see}~\dagger\ &\cong E \ox_{K}\left(A\ox_{K}\Mat_{m}(K)ight) &	ext{see}~\ddagger\ &\cong E\ox_{K}\Mat_{m}(A) &	ext{see~\cref{con:matrix-tensor-matrix} and}~\dagger\!\!\dagger \ \Mat_{n}\left(B_{E}ight) &\cong E\ox_{K}\Mat_{n}(B) &	ext{same as the case of}~A\ Mat_{m}\left(A_{E}ight)&\cong \Mat_{n}\left(B_{E}ight) &	ext{see}~\dagger\!\!\dagger \end{aligned}. \] 
oindent$\dagger$: Wee need to check $\Mat_{m}(E)\cong E\otimes_{K}\Mat_{m}K$ as $E$-algebras since~\cref{con:matrix-tensor-matrix} only gives a $K$-algebra isomorphism. If $e \in E$, then its image in $E\ox_{K}\Mat_{m}(K)$ is $e\otimes 1$ and its image in $\Mat_{m}(E)$ is $\diag(e)$ which under the $K$-algebra isomorphism is mapped to $\sum_{ij}\diag(e)_{ij}\cdot \delta_{ij}=e\ox1$. 
oindent$\ddagger$: This is defined by combining two $E$-algebra homomorphisms \[ A_{E}	o A_{E}\ox_{K}\Mat_{m}(K)	o E\ox_{K}\left(A\ox_{K}\Mat_{m}(K)ight)\] and \[ E\ox_{K}\Mat_{m}(K)	o \left(E\ox_{K}\Mat_{m}(K)ight)\ox_{K}A 	o E\ox_{K}(A\ox_{K}\Mat_{m}(K)). \] Since $\left(E\ox_{K}Aight)\ox_{E}\left(E\ox_{K}\Mat_{m}(K)ight)$ is a simple ring, this morphism is automatically injective. It is surjective as well: let $x\in E\ox_{K}\left(A\ox_{K}\Mat_{m}(K)ight)$, without loss of generality, assume $x=e\ox (a\ox\delta_{ij})$ for some $e\in E$, $a\in A$. Then precisely $\left(e\ox aight)\ox\left(1\ox\delta_{ij}ight)$ is mapped to $x$. 
oindent$\dagger\!\dagger$: a $K$-algebra isomorphism $A\cong B$ gives an $E$-algebra isomorphism $E\ox_{K}A \cong E\ox_{K} B$. Thus we have a well defined function $\Br(K)	o\Br(E)$. We now check that this is a group homomorphism. $[K]_{\sim_{\Br_{K}}}$ is mapped to $[E\ox_{K}K]_{\sim_{\Br_{E}}}$ but $E\ox_{K}K\cong E$ as $E$-algebra. For $A, B\in\CSA_{K}$, we have that $[AB]_{\sim_{\Br_{K}}}$ is mapped to $\left(A\ox_{K}Bight)_{E}\cong A_{E}\ox_{E} B_{E}$ as $E$-algebras; hence $[AB]_{\sim_{\Br_{K}}}$ and $[A]_{\sim_{\Br_{K}}}\cdot[B]_{\sim_{\Br_{K}}}$ have the same image under base change.
nodes.statement_short: Chain explicit $E$-algebra isomorphisms $\Mat_m(A_E)\cong E\otimes_K\Mat_m(A)$, then check identity and products are preserved.

nodes.name: Chain of isomorphisms
nodes.statement: Assume $m,n\in\nat_{\ge0}$ are such that $\Mat_{m}(A)\cong\Mat_{n}(B)$ are $K$-algebras. Then we do the following calculation: as $E$-algebras \[ \begin{aligned} \Mat_{m}\left(A_{E}\right) &\cong A_{E}\otimes_{E}\Mat_{m}(E) &\text{see~\cref{con:matrix-tensor-matrix}}\\ &\cong A_{E}\otimes_{E}\left(E\ox_{K} \Mat_{m}(K)\right) & \text{see}~\dagger\\ &\cong E \ox_{K}\left(A\ox_{K}\Mat_{m}(K)\right) &\text{see}~\ddagger\\ &\cong E\ox_{K}\Mat_{m}(A) &\text{see~\cref{con:matrix-tensor-matrix} and}~\dagger\!\!\dagger \\ \Mat_{n}\left(B_{E}\right) &\cong E\ox_{K}\Mat_{n}(B) &\text{same as the case of}~A\\ Mat_{m}\left(A_{E}\right)&\cong \Mat_{n}\left(B_{E}\right) &\text{see}~\dagger\!\!\dagger \end{aligned}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Chain $E$-algebra isomorphisms.

nodes.name: Dagger
nodes.statement: \noindent$\dagger$: Wee need to check $\Mat_{m}(E)\cong E\otimes_{K}\Mat_{m}K$ as $E$-algebras since~\cref{con:matrix-tensor-matrix} only gives a $K$-algebra isomorphism. If $e \in E$, then its image in $E\ox_{K}\Mat_{m}(K)$ is $e\otimes 1$ and its image in $\Mat_{m}(E)$ is $\diag(e)$ which under the $K$-algebra isomorphism is mapped to $\sum_{ij}\diag(e)_{ij}\cdot \delta_{ij}=e\ox1$.
nodes.statement_short: Check the isomorphism is $E$-linear.

nodes.name: Double dagger
nodes.statement: \noindent$\ddagger$: This is defined by combining two $E$-algebra homomorphisms \[ A_{E}\to A_{E}\ox_{K}\Mat_{m}(K)\to E\ox_{K}\left(A\ox_{K}\Mat_{m}(K)\right)\] and \[ E\ox_{K}\Mat_{m}(K)\to \left(E\ox_{K}\Mat_{m}(K)\right)\ox_{K}A \to E\ox_{K}(A\ox_{K}\Mat_{m}(K)). \] Since $\left(E\ox_{K}A\right)\ox_{E}\left(E\ox_{K}\Mat_{m}(K)\right)$ is a simple ring, this morphism is automatically injective. It is surjective as well: let $x\in E\ox_{K}\left(A\ox_{K}\Mat_{m}(K)\right)$, without loss of generality, assume $x=e\ox (a\ox\delta_{ij})$ for some $e\in E$, $a\in A$. Then precisely $\left(e\ox a\right)\ox\left(1\ox\delta_{ij}\right)$ is mapped to $x$.
nodes.statement_short: Construct the isomorphism; injective by simplicity, surjective directly.

nodes.name: Double dagger 2
nodes.statement: \noindent$\dagger\!\dagger$: a $K$-algebra isomorphism $A\cong B$ gives an $E$-algebra isomorphism $E\ox_{K}A \cong E\ox_{K} B$.
nodes.statement_short: Base change of isomorphisms.

nodes.name: Homomorphism
nodes.statement: Thus we have a well defined function $\Br(K)\to\Br(E)$. We now check that this is a group homomorphism. $[K]_{\sim_{\Br_{K}}}$ is mapped to $[E\ox_{K}K]_{\sim_{\Br_{E}}}$ but $E\ox_{K}K\cong E$ as $E$-algebra. For $A, B\in\CSA_{K}$, we have that $[AB]_{\sim_{\Br_{K}}}$ is mapped to $\left(A\ox_{K}B\right)_{E}\cong A_{E}\ox_{E} B_{E}$ as $E$-algebras; hence $[AB]_{\sim_{\Br_{K}}}$ and $[A]_{\sim_{\Br_{K}}}\cdot[B]_{\sim_{\Br_{K}}}$ have the same image under base change.
nodes.statement_short: Check unit and products.

nodes.name: Base change morphism Br_K^E
nodes.statement: Denote the base change morphism in~\cref{con:br-base-change} as $\Br_{K}^{E}$.

nodes.name: Base change along identity is identity
nodes.statement: $\Br_{K}^{K}$ is identity.
nodes.label: lem:br-base-change-self

nodes.name: Proof of Base change along identity is identity
nodes.statement: If $A\in\CSA$, then $A\sim_{\Br}K\ox_{K}A$.
nodes.statement_short: $A\sim K\otimes_K A$.

nodes.name: Base change along a tower
nodes.statement: Consider the tower of field extension $E/F/K$, \[ \Br_{K}^{E} = \Br_{E}^{F}\circ\Br_{K}^{E}. \]
nodes.label: lem:br-base-change-tower

nodes.name: Proof of Base change along a tower
nodes.statement: If $A\in\CSA_{K}$, then $E\ox_{F}\left(F\ox_{K}A\right)$ is isomorphic to $E \ox_{F} A$ as $E$-algebras.
nodes.statement_short: Associativity of base change.

nodes.name: Br is a functor
nodes.statement: $\Br$ forms a functor from category of field to category of abelian groups.
conclusions: $\Br$ forms a functor from category of field to category of abelian groups

nodes.name: Proof of Br is a functor
nodes.statement: This is the categorical version of~\cref{lem:br-base-change-self} and~\cref{lem:br-base-change-tower}.
nodes.statement_short: Categorical restatement of the two base change lemmas.

nodes.name: Relative Brauer Group
nodes.statement: Let $E/K$ be a field extension, we define the relative Brauer group $\Br(E/K)$ to be the kernel of the base change morphism $\Br_{K}^{E}$.
nodes.genus: the kernel of the base change morphism $\Br_{K}^{E}$

nodes.name: Unpacking the relative Brauer group
nodes.statement: Unpacking the definition of the relative Brauer group, we see that for any $A \in \CSA_{K}$, if $E\ox_{K}A\cong\mat_{n}(E)$ as $E$-algebras, then $\br^{E}_{K}\left([A]_{\sim_{\br}}\right)=1$.

nodes.name: Splitting Field
nodes.statement: For any field extension $E/K$ and any $K$-algebra $A$, we say $E$ is a splitting field of $A$ if and only if $E\ox_{K}A \cong \mat_{n}(E)$ as $E$-algebras for some non-zero $n$. We also say $E$ splits $A$ or $A$ is splited by $E$

nodes.name: Splitting iff membership in the relative Brauer group
nodes.statement: Let $E/K$ be a field extension and $A\in\csa_{K}$, $E$ splits $A$ if and only if $[A]_{\sim_{\br}}\in\br(E/K)$.
nodes.label: thm:split-iff-mem-relative

nodes.name: Proof of Splitting iff membership in the relative Brauer group
nodes.statement: The ``only if'' part is by definition. For the other direction, we know by definition that $\mat_{n}(E\ox_{K}A)\cong\mat_{m}(E)$ as $E$-algebras for some non-zero $m, n$. By~\cref{thm:wed-artin-algebra}, we find some division algebra $D$ and non-zero natural number $p$ such that $E\ox_{K}A\cong \mat_{p}(D)$ as $E$-algebras. Thus $\mat_{pm}(E)\cong\mat_{pn}\left(E\ox_{K}A\right)\cong\mat_{p^{2}n}(D)$ as $E$-algebras. By~\cref{thm:wed-artin-uniq}, we conclude that $E\cong D$ as $E$-algebras. Hence $E\ox_{K}A\cong \mat_{p}(E)$, in another word, $E$ splits $A$.
nodes.statement_short: One direction by definition; for the other compare Wedderburn-Artin decompositions via uniqueness.

nodes.name: Only if
nodes.statement: The ``only if'' part is by definition.
nodes.statement_short: By definition.

nodes.name: If
nodes.statement: For the other direction, we know by definition that $\mat_{n}(E\ox_{K}A)\cong\mat_{m}(E)$ as $E$-algebras for some non-zero $m, n$.
nodes.statement_short: Get $\Mat_n(E\otimes A)\cong\Mat_m(E)$.

nodes.name: Wedderburn-Artin
nodes.statement: By~\cref{thm:wed-artin-algebra}, we find some division algebra $D$ and non-zero natural number $p$ such that $E\ox_{K}A\cong \mat_{p}(D)$ as $E$-algebras. Thus $\mat_{pm}(E)\cong\mat_{pn}\left(E\ox_{K}A\right)\cong\mat_{p^{2}n}(D)$ as $E$-algebras.
nodes.statement_short: Write $E\otimes A\cong\Mat_p(D)$.

nodes.name: Uniqueness
nodes.statement: By~\cref{thm:wed-artin-uniq}, we conclude that $E\cong D$ as $E$-algebras. Hence $E\ox_{K}A\cong \mat_{p}(E)$, in another word, $E$ splits $A$.
nodes.statement_short: Uniqueness gives $D\cong E$.

nodes.name: Algebraically closed fields split everything
nodes.statement: In light of~\cref{lem:br-base-change-tower}, if $K$ is algebraic closed then $K$ splits any $K$-algebra $A$. Indeed, $K$ splits $A$ if and only if $[A]_{\sim\br}$ but $[A]_{\sim\br}$ is equal to $1$.

nodes.name: Splitting is invariant under Brauer equivalence
nodes.statement: If two $\csa_{K}$ are Brauer equivalent, in another word, $A \sim_{\br_{K}} B$, then $E$ splits $A$ if and only if $E$ splits $B$. Indeed, if $A$ and $B$ are equivalent, then $[A]_{\sim\br} \in \br(E/K)$ if and only if $[B]_{\sim\br}\in\br(E/K)$.

nodes.name: Standing notation: finite extension K/F
nodes.statement: In this section, let $K/F$ be a finite dimensional field extension.

nodes.name: Good representative of the inverse class
nodes.statement: Let $A\in\csa_{F}$ splitted by $K$. There exists a $B\in\csa_{F}$ such that \begin{itemize} \item $[A]_{\sim_{\br}}[B]_{\sim_{\br}}=1$ \item there exists $F$-algebra map $K\hookrightarrow B$ \item ${\left(\dim_{F}K\right)}^{2}=\dim_{F}B$. \end{itemize}
nodes.label: lem:good-rep-inv

nodes.name: Proof of Good representative of the inverse class
nodes.statement: Since $K$ splits $A$, we find a non-zero natural number $n$ such that $K\ox_{F}A\cong\mat_{n}K\cong\End_{K}\left(K^{n}\right)$ as $K$-algebras. We define an $F$-algebra map $\iota: A\to\End_{F}\left(K^{n}\right)$ by \begin{center} \begin{tikzcd} A \arrow{r} & K \ox_{F} A \arrow{r}{\cong} & \End_K\left(K^n\right) \arrow{r}{|_{F}} & \End_F\left(K^n\right) \end{tikzcd}, \end{center} where $|_{F}$ is restriction of scalars. Since $A$ is simple, $\iota$ is injective, therefore $A \cong \iota(A)$ as $F$-algebras. Define $B$ as $C_{\End_{F}\left(K^{n}\right)}(\iota(A))$, the centralizer of the range of $\iota$ in $\End_{F}\left(K^{n}\right)$. We construct an embedding $K \hookrightarrow B$ by $r \mapsto (r \cdot \bullet)$ $B$ is a central $F$-algebra: if $x \in Z(B)$, then $x \in \iota(A)$ because by~\cref{thm:double-centralizer}, it is sufficient to prove that $x$ is in $C_{\End_{F}\left(K^{n}\right)}\left(B\right)$ which follows from the fact that $x \in Z(B)$. In fact, $x \in Z(\iota(A))$: suppose $a \in A$, we need to check $x \cdot \iota(a) = \iota(a)\cdot x$, this is the case because $B$ is defined as the centralizer of $\iota(A)$. Since $\iota(A) \cong A$ as $F$-algebras, $\iota(A)$ is $F$-central, hence $x \in F$. $B$ is a simple ring: by~\cref{lem:simple-centralizer}, it is sufficient to prove that $\iota(A)$ is a simple ring which comes from $A \cong \iota(A)$ as $F$-algebras. By~\cref{cor:self-tensor-centralizer}, we have $F$-algebra isomorphism $\End_{F}\left(K^{n}\right)\cong \iota(A)\ox_{F}B \cong A \ox_{F}B$. Since $\End_{F}\left(K^{n}\right)\cong\mat_{\dim_{F}\left(K^{n}\right)}\left(F\right)$ as $F$-algebras, we see that $[A]_{\sim_{\br}}$ and $[B]_{\sim_{\br}}$ are inverses. By~\cref{lem:dim-centralizer}, $\dim_{F}B\cdot \dim_{F}\iota(A) = \dim_{F}B\cdot\dim_{F}A = \dim_{F}\End_{F}\left(K^{n}\right) = {\left(\dim_{F}\left(K^{n}\right)\right)}^{2}={\left(\dim_{F}K\cdot \dim_{K}\left(K^{n}\right)\right)}^{2}=n^{2}\cdot{\left(\dim_{F}K\right)}^{2}$. On the other hand, since $K\ox_{F}A\cong\mat_{n}K$, we have $\dim_{F}K\ox_{F}A=\dim_{F}K\cdot\dim_{F}A=\dim_{F}\mat_{n}K=\dim_{F}K\dim_{K}\mat_{n}K=n^{2}\dim_{F}K$. Since $\dim_{F}K\ne 0$ , we conclude $\dim_{F}A=n^{2}$. Since $n\ne 0$ and $\dim_{F}(B)\cdot \dim_{F}(A)=n^{2}\dim_{F}(B)=n^{2}{\left(\dim_{F}K\right)}^{2}$, we get the desired result.
nodes.statement_short: Embed $A$ into $\End_F(K^n)$ and take $B$ its centralizer. Key step: double centralizer and dimension formula show $B$ is central simple, inverse to $A$, of dimension $(\dim_F K)^2$.

nodes.name: Construct B
nodes.statement: Since $K$ splits $A$, we find a non-zero natural number $n$ such that $K\ox_{F}A\cong\mat_{n}K\cong\End_{K}\left(K^{n}\right)$ as $K$-algebras. We define an $F$-algebra map $\iota: A\to\End_{F}\left(K^{n}\right)$ by \begin{center} \begin{tikzcd} A \arrow{r} & K \ox_{F} A \arrow{r}{\cong} & \End_K\left(K^n\right) \arrow{r}{|_{F}} & \End_F\left(K^n\right) \end{tikzcd}, \end{center} where $|_{F}$ is restriction of scalars. Since $A$ is simple, $\iota$ is injective, therefore $A \cong \iota(A)$ as $F$-algebras. Define $B$ as $C_{\End_{F}\left(K^{n}\right)}(\iota(A))$, the centralizer of the range of $\iota$ in $\End_{F}\left(K^{n}\right)$. We construct an embedding $K \hookrightarrow B$ by $r \mapsto (r \cdot \bullet)$
nodes.statement_short: Embed $A$ in $\End_F(K^n)$ and let $B$ be its centralizer.

nodes.name: B is central
nodes.statement: $B$ is a central $F$-algebra: if $x \in Z(B)$, then $x \in \iota(A)$ because by~\cref{thm:double-centralizer}, it is sufficient to prove that $x$ is in $C_{\End_{F}\left(K^{n}\right)}\left(B\right)$ which follows from the fact that $x \in Z(B)$. In fact, $x \in Z(\iota(A))$: suppose $a \in A$, we need to check $x \cdot \iota(a) = \iota(a)\cdot x$, this is the case because $B$ is defined as the centralizer of $\iota(A)$. Since $\iota(A) \cong A$ as $F$-algebras, $\iota(A)$ is $F$-central, hence $x \in F$.
nodes.statement_short: Double centralizer shows $Z(B)\subseteq Z(\iota(A))=F$.

nodes.name: B is simple
nodes.statement: $B$ is a simple ring: by~\cref{lem:simple-centralizer}, it is sufficient to prove that $\iota(A)$ is a simple ring which comes from $A \cong \iota(A)$ as $F$-algebras.
nodes.statement_short: Centralizer of a simple subalgebra is simple.

nodes.name: Inverse classes
nodes.statement: By~\cref{cor:self-tensor-centralizer}, we have $F$-algebra isomorphism $\End_{F}\left(K^{n}\right)\cong \iota(A)\ox_{F}B \cong A \ox_{F}B$. Since $\End_{F}\left(K^{n}\right)\cong\mat_{\dim_{F}\left(K^{n}\right)}\left(F\right)$ as $F$-algebras, we see that $[A]_{\sim_{\br}}$ and $[B]_{\sim_{\br}}$ are inverses.
nodes.statement_short: $A\otimes B$ is a matrix algebra.

nodes.name: Dimension
nodes.statement: By~\cref{lem:dim-centralizer}, $\dim_{F}B\cdot \dim_{F}\iota(A) = \dim_{F}B\cdot\dim_{F}A = \dim_{F}\End_{F}\left(K^{n}\right) = {\left(\dim_{F}\left(K^{n}\right)\right)}^{2}={\left(\dim_{F}K\cdot \dim_{K}\left(K^{n}\right)\right)}^{2}=n^{2}\cdot{\left(\dim_{F}K\right)}^{2}$. On the other hand, since $K\ox_{F}A\cong\mat_{n}K$, we have $\dim_{F}K\ox_{F}A=\dim_{F}K\cdot\dim_{F}A=\dim_{F}\mat_{n}K=\dim_{F}K\dim_{K}\mat_{n}K=n^{2}\dim_{F}K$. Since $\dim_{F}K\ne 0$ , we conclude $\dim_{F}A=n^{2}$. Since $n\ne 0$ and $\dim_{F}(B)\cdot \dim_{F}(A)=n^{2}\dim_{F}(B)=n^{2}{\left(\dim_{F}K\right)}^{2}$, we get the desired result.
nodes.statement_short: Dimension count gives $\dim_F B=(\dim_F K)^2$.

nodes.name: Good representative lemma
nodes.statement: Let $A\in\csa_{F}$ splitted by $K$. There exists a $B \in \csa_{F}$ such that \begin{itemize} \item $[B]_{\sim_{\br}}=[A]_{\sim_{\br}}$ \item there exists an $F$-algebra map $K\hookrightarrow B$ \item ${\left(\dim_{F}K\right)}^{2}=\dim_{F}B$. \end{itemize}
nodes.label: cor:good-rep

nodes.name: Proof of Good representative lemma
nodes.statement: Let $B$ and $\iota : K \hookrightarrow B$ be as in~\cref{lem:good-rep-inv}. Consider $B^{\opp}$ and $K \hookrightarrow B \to B^{\opp}$. This works.
nodes.statement_short: Take the opposite of the inverse representative.

nodes.name: Splitting iff good representative exists
nodes.statement: Let $A\in\csa_{F}$. $K$ splits $A$ if and only if there exists a $B\in\csa_{F}$ such that \begin{itemize} \item $[B]_{\sim_{\br}}=[A]_{\sim_{\br}}$ \item there exists an $F$-algebra map $K \hookrightarrow B$ \item ${\left(\dim_{F}K\right)}^{2}=\dim_{F}B$. \end{itemize}
conclusions: $K$ splits $A$ if and only if there exists a $B\in\csa_{F}$ such that
nodes.label: thm:good-rep-iff-split

nodes.name: Proof of Splitting iff good representative exists
nodes.statement: The ``if'' direction is~\cref{cor:good-rep}. For the ``only if'' direction, let $B \in\csa_{F}$ and $\iota : K \hookrightarrow B$ be given. We give $B$ a $K$-module structure by right multiplication, that is for any $a \in K$ and $b \in B$, we define $a \cdot b := b \cdot \iota(a)$. Since $B$ is a finite dimensional $F$-vector space and $K/F$ is a finite dimensional field extension, $B$ is a finite dimensional $K$-vector space as well. Since $[B]_{\sim_{\br}}=[A]_{\sim_{\br}}$, it is sufficient to show that $K$ splits $B$. We define an $F$-bilinear map $\mu : K \to B \to \End_{K}B$ by $(c, a) \mapsto (c \cdot a \cdot \bullet)$ which induce an $F$-linear map $\mu' : K \ox_{F} B \to \End_{K}B$. Since for any $r, c\in K$ and $a \in B$, we have $\mu'\left(r \cdot c\ox a\right)(a') = a a' \iota(rc)=aa'\iota(c)\iota(r)=r\cdot \mu'(c\ox a)$, that is $\mu'$ is $K$-linear as well. Note that \[\mu'(1)=\mu'(1\ox 1) = (1\cdot 1\cdot \bullet) = 1\] and that \[ \begin{aligned} \mu'(c\ox a \cdot c'\ox a')(a'') &= \mu'(cc'\ox aa')(a'') \\ &= cc' \cdot aa' \cdot a'' \\ &= aa' a'' \iota(c c') \\ &= a(a' a'' \iota(c'))\iota(c) \\ &=\mu'(c \ox a)(a' a'' \iota(c'))\\ &=\mu'(c\ox a)\left(\mu'(c'\ox a')(a'')\right) \\ &= \left(\mu'(c\ox a)\circ\mu'(c'\ox a')\right)(a'') \end{aligned}, \] that is, $\mu'$ is an $K$-algebra map. If we can show that $\mu'$ is a bijection, we will prove the result for $K\ox_{F} B \cong \End_{K} B \cong \mat_{\dim_{K} B}K$ as $K$-algebras. By~\cref{cor:alghom-bijective-of-dim-eq}, it is sufficient to show $\dim_{K}K\ox_{F}B = \dim_{K}\End_{K}B$. Let $n$ denote $\dim_{F}K$. Since, $\dim_{F}K\dim_{K}K\ox_{F}B =\dim_{F}K\ox_{F}B=\dim_{F}K \dim_{F}B$. we have $\dim_{K}K\ox_{F}B = \dim_{F}B = {\left(\dim_{F}K\right)}^{2}$. On the other hand, since ${\left(\dim_{F}K\right)}^{2}=\dim_{F} B = \dim_{F}K\dim_{K}B$, we have $\dim_{K} B = \dim_{F}K$; thus $\dim_{K}\End_{K} B = {\left(\dim_{K}B\right)}^{2}={\left(\dim_{F}K\right)}^{2}$ and the result is proved.
nodes.statement_short: One direction is the corollary; for the other build a $K$-algebra map $K\otimes_F B\to\End_K B$ and show it is bijective by dimension count.

nodes.name: If
nodes.statement: The ``if'' direction is~\cref{cor:good-rep}.
nodes.statement_short: This is the good representative corollary.

nodes.name: Only if
nodes.statement: For the ``only if'' direction, let $B \in\csa_{F}$ and $\iota : K \hookrightarrow B$ be given. We give $B$ a $K$-module structure by right multiplication, that is for any $a \in K$ and $b \in B$, we define $a \cdot b := b \cdot \iota(a)$. Since $B$ is a finite dimensional $F$-vector space and $K/F$ is a finite dimensional field extension, $B$ is a finite dimensional $K$-vector space as well. Since $[B]_{\sim_{\br}}=[A]_{\sim_{\br}}$, it is sufficient to show that $K$ splits $B$. We define an $F$-bilinear map $\mu : K \to B \to \End_{K}B$ by $(c, a) \mapsto (c \cdot a \cdot \bullet)$ which induce an $F$-linear map $\mu' : K \ox_{F} B \to \End_{K}B$. Since for any $r, c\in K$ and $a \in B$, we have $\mu'\left(r \cdot c\ox a\right)(a') = a a' \iota(rc)=aa'\iota(c)\iota(r)=r\cdot \mu'(c\ox a)$, that is $\mu'$ is $K$-linear as well. Note that \[\mu'(1)=\mu'(1\ox 1) = (1\cdot 1\cdot \bullet) = 1\] and that \[ \begin{aligned} \mu'(c\ox a \cdot c'\ox a')(a'') &= \mu'(cc'\ox aa')(a'') \\ &= cc' \cdot aa' \cdot a'' \\ &= aa' a'' \iota(c c') \\ &= a(a' a'' \iota(c'))\iota(c) \\ &=\mu'(c \ox a)(a' a'' \iota(c'))\\ &=\mu'(c\ox a)\left(\mu'(c'\ox a')(a'')\right) \\ &= \left(\mu'(c\ox a)\circ\mu'(c'\ox a')\right)(a'') \end{aligned}, \] that is, $\mu'$ is an $K$-algebra map. If we can show that $\mu'$ is a bijection, we will prove the result for $K\ox_{F} B \cong \End_{K} B \cong \mat_{\dim_{K} B}K$ as $K$-algebras. By~\cref{cor:alghom-bijective-of-dim-eq}, it is sufficient to show $\dim_{K}K\ox_{F}B = \dim_{K}\End_{K}B$. Let $n$ denote $\dim_{F}K$. Since, $\dim_{F}K\dim_{K}K\ox_{F}B =\dim_{F}K\ox_{F}B=\dim_{F}K \dim_{F}B$. we have $\dim_{K}K\ox_{F}B = \dim_{F}B = {\left(\dim_{F}K\right)}^{2}$. On the other hand, since ${\left(\dim_{F}K\right)}^{2}=\dim_{F} B = \dim_{F}K\dim_{K}B$, we have $\dim_{K} B = \dim_{F}K$; thus $\dim_{K}\End_{K} B = {\left(\dim_{K}B\right)}^{2}={\left(\dim_{F}K\right)}^{2}$ and the result is proved.
nodes.statement_short: Show $K$ splits $B$.

nodes.name: K-module structure and reduction
nodes.statement: We give $B$ a $K$-module structure by right multiplication, that is for any $a \in K$ and $b \in B$, we define $a \cdot b := b \cdot \iota(a)$. Since $B$ is a finite dimensional $F$-vector space and $K/F$ is a finite dimensional field extension, $B$ is a finite dimensional $K$-vector space as well. Since $[B]_{\sim_{\br}}=[A]_{\sim_{\br}}$, it is sufficient to show that $K$ splits $B$.
nodes.statement_short: Make $B$ a $K$-space by right multiplication; suffices that $K$ splits $B$.

nodes.name: Algebra map mu
nodes.statement: We define an $F$-bilinear map $\mu : K \to B \to \End_{K}B$ by $(c, a) \mapsto (c \cdot a \cdot \bullet)$ which induce an $F$-linear map $\mu' : K \ox_{F} B \to \End_{K}B$. Since for any $r, c\in K$ and $a \in B$, we have $\mu'\left(r \cdot c\ox a\right)(a') = a a' \iota(rc)=aa'\iota(c)\iota(r)=r\cdot \mu'(c\ox a)$, that is $\mu'$ is $K$-linear as well. Note that \[\mu'(1)=\mu'(1\ox 1) = (1\cdot 1\cdot \bullet) = 1\] and that \[ \begin{aligned} \mu'(c\ox a \cdot c'\ox a')(a'') &= \mu'(cc'\ox aa')(a'') \\ &= cc' \cdot aa' \cdot a'' \\ &= aa' a'' \iota(c c') \\ &= a(a' a'' \iota(c'))\iota(c) \\ &=\mu'(c \ox a)(a' a'' \iota(c'))\\ &=\mu'(c\ox a)\left(\mu'(c'\ox a')(a'')\right) \\ &= \left(\mu'(c\ox a)\circ\mu'(c'\ox a')\right)(a'') \end{aligned}, \] that is, $\mu'$ is an $K$-algebra map.
nodes.statement_short: Build the $K$-algebra map $\mu':K\otimes_F B\to\End_K B$.

nodes.name: Bijectivity by dimension
nodes.statement: If we can show that $\mu'$ is a bijection, we will prove the result for $K\ox_{F} B \cong \End_{K} B \cong \mat_{\dim_{K} B}K$ as $K$-algebras. By~\cref{cor:alghom-bijective-of-dim-eq}, it is sufficient to show $\dim_{K}K\ox_{F}B = \dim_{K}\End_{K}B$. Let $n$ denote $\dim_{F}K$. Since, $\dim_{F}K\dim_{K}K\ox_{F}B =\dim_{F}K\ox_{F}B=\dim_{F}K \dim_{F}B$. we have $\dim_{K}K\ox_{F}B = \dim_{F}B = {\left(\dim_{F}K\right)}^{2}$. On the other hand, since ${\left(\dim_{F}K\right)}^{2}=\dim_{F} B = \dim_{F}K\dim_{K}B$, we have $\dim_{K} B = \dim_{F}K$; thus $\dim_{K}\End_{K} B = {\left(\dim_{K}B\right)}^{2}={\left(\dim_{F}K\right)}^{2}$ and the result is proved.
nodes.statement_short: Show $\mu'$ bijective by dimension count.

nodes.name: Good Representation
nodes.statement: For any $X \in \br(F)$, a $K$-good representation of $X$ is an $A \in \csa_{F}$ and an $F$-algebra map $K \hookrightarrow A$ such that $[A]_{\sim_{\br}} = X$ and $\dim_{F}A={\left(\dim_{F}K\right)}^{2}$. We often denote the $F$-algebra map $K \hookrightarrow A$ as $\iota$ or $\iota_{A}$.
nodes.label: def:good-rep

nodes.name: Relative Brauer group membership iff good representation
nodes.statement: For any $X\in\br(F)$, $X\in\br(K/F)$ if and only if $X$ admits a good representation.
conclusions: $X\in\br(K/F)$ if and only if $X$ admits a good representation
nodes.label: cor:mem-relative-br-iff-good-rep

nodes.name: Proof of Relative Brauer group membership iff good representation
nodes.statement: Rephrase of~\cref{thm:good-rep-iff-split} and~\cref{thm:split-iff-mem-relative}.
nodes.statement_short: Combine the splitting criteria.

nodes.name: Standing notation: good representation A of X
nodes.statement: Let $X \in \br(F)$ and $A$ be a good representation of $X$.

nodes.name: Range of iota is a simple ring
nodes.statement: The range $\iota_{A}(A)$ is a simple ring.
conclusions: The range $\iota_{A}(A)$ is a simple ring

nodes.name: Proof of Range of iota is a simple ring
nodes.statement: Because $K$ is a simple ring, $\iota_{A}$ is injective therefore $\iota_{A}(A)\cong K$.
nodes.statement_short: $\iota_A$ is injective, so its range is isomorphic to $K$.

nodes.name: Range of iota is self-centralizing
nodes.statement: $C_{A}\left(\iota_{A}(A)\right) = \iota_{A}(A)$.
nodes.label: lem:centralizer-range-good-rep

nodes.name: Proof of Range of iota is self-centralizing
nodes.statement: In the language of~\cref{sec:subfield}, $\iota_{A}(A)$ is a subfield of $A$, hence by~\cref{lem:tfae-subfield}, we only need to show $\dim_{F}A = {\left(\dim_{F}\iota_{A}(A)\right)}^{2}$. But $\dim_{F}A={\left(\dim_{F}K\right)}^{2}$ and $\iota(A)\cong K$.
nodes.statement_short: Apply the TFAE lemma for subfields with the dimension condition.

nodes.name: K-module structure on a good representation
nodes.statement: We give $A$ a $K$-module structure by {\em left\/} multiplication, that is for any $c \in K$ and $a \in A$, we define $c\cdot a$ to be $\iota_{A}(c)a$. Note that if $c \in F$ then $\iota_{A}(c)a = c \cdot a$, in another word, the $K$-action and the $F$-action on $A$ are compatible. Then $A$ is a finite dimensional $K$-vector space and $\dim_{K}A=\dim_{F}K$: indeed $\dim_{F}K\cdot\dim_{K}A = \dim_{F}K\cdot \dim_{F}K = \dim_{F}A$.
nodes.statement_short: $K$ acts on $A$ by left multiplication through $\iota_A$; then $\dim_K A=\dim_F K$.

nodes.name: Good representations are isomorphic
nodes.statement: If $A$ and $B$ are two good representations of $X$, then $A \cong B$ as $F$-algebras.
assumptions: $A$ and $B$ are two good representations of $X$
nodes.label: lem:good-rep-iso

nodes.name: Proof of Good representations are isomorphic
nodes.statement: By~\cref{lem:common-div-alg}, we find a division $F$-algebra $D$ and non-zero natural numbers $m, n$ such that $A \cong \mat_{m}(D)$ and $B \cong \mat_{n}(D)$ as $F$-algebras. Therefore \[ \begin{aligned} {\left(\dim_{F}K\right)}^{2} &= \dim_{F}A &= m^{2}\dim_{F}D \\ &= \dim_{F}B &= n^{2}\dim_{F}D. \end{aligned} \] Therefore $m = n$ and $A \cong \mat_{m}D =\mat_{n}D\cong B$.
nodes.statement_short: Both are matrix algebras over a common division algebra of the same dimension.

nodes.name: Common division algebra
nodes.statement: By~\cref{lem:common-div-alg}, we find a division $F$-algebra $D$ and non-zero natural numbers $m, n$ such that $A \cong \mat_{m}(D)$ and $B \cong \mat_{n}(D)$ as $F$-algebras.
nodes.statement_short: Write both as matrix algebras over $D$.

nodes.name: Dimensions
nodes.statement: Therefore \[ \begin{aligned} {\left(\dim_{F}K\right)}^{2} &= \dim_{F}A &= m^{2}\dim_{F}D \\ &= \dim_{F}B &= n^{2}\dim_{F}D. \end{aligned} \]
nodes.statement_short: Compare dimensions.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Therefore $m = n$ and $A \cong \mat_{m}D =\mat_{n}D\cong B$.
nodes.statement_short: $m=n$, so $A\cong B$.

nodes.name: Standing notation for conjugation factors
nodes.statement: In this section, let $K/F$ be a field extension, $X \in \br(F)$ and $A$ be a $K$-good representation of $X$.

nodes.name: Galois action notation
nodes.statement: Since $\gal(K/F)$ acts on $K^{\star}$, for $x\in K^{\star}$,we feel free to write $\sigma\cdot x$ when it feels more readable than $\sigma(x)$, for example when there are nested brackets.

nodes.name: Conjugation Factor
nodes.statement: With respect to $A$, a conjugation factor of $\sigma$ is a unit $x_{\sigma} \in A^{\star}$ such that for all $c \in K$, \[ x_{\sigma} \iota_{A}(c)x_{\sigma}^{-1} = \iota_{A}(\sigma \cdot c). \] A conjugation sequence is a sequence $x:\gal(K/F) \to A^{\star}$ such that for all $\sigma\in\gal(K/F)$, $x_{\sigma}$ is a conjugation factor of $\sigma$. When we want to stress $A$, we say $A$-conjugation factor and $A$-conjugation sequence.
nodes.statement_short: A unit $x_\sigma$ with $x_\sigma\iota_A(c)x_\sigma^{-1}=\iota_A(\sigma c)$; a conjugation sequence picks one for each $\sigma$.
nodes.label: def:conj-factor

nodes.name: Alternative equalities for conjugation factors
nodes.statement: When $x_{\sigma}$ is a conjugation factor of $\sigma$, the equalities $x_{\sigma}\iota_{A}(c) = x_{\sigma}\iota_{A}(\sigma(c))$ and $\iota_{A}(c)x_{\sigma}^{-1}=x_{\sigma}^{-1}\iota_{A}(\sigma(c))$ are also useful.
nodes.label: rem:conj-factor-alternative-eq

nodes.name: Existence of a conjugation sequence
nodes.statement: $A$ has a conjugation sequence:

nodes.name: Proof of existence of conjugation sequences
nodes.statement: let $\sigma \in \gal(K/F)$, we have two $F$-algebra homomorphisms $K \to A$ given by $\iota_{A}$ and $\iota_{A}\circ \sigma$. Applying~\cref{thm:skolem-noether} to $\iota_{A}$ and $\iota_{A}\circ \sigma$ gives us the desired conjugation factor.
nodes.statement_short: Apply Skolem-Noether to $\iota_A$ and $\iota_A\circ\sigma$.

nodes.name: Product of conjugation factors
nodes.statement: If $x$ is a conjugation factor of $\sigma$ and $y$ of $\tau$, then $xy$ is a conjugation factor of $\sigma\tau$.
assumptions: $x$ is a conjugation factor of $\sigma$ and $y$ of $\tau$

nodes.name: Proof that products of conjugation factors are conjugation factors
nodes.statement: For any $c \in K$ \[ \iota_{A}(\sigma \cdot\tau(c)) = x\iota_{A}(\tau\cdot c)x^{-1} = xy\iota_{A}(c)y^{-1}x^{-1}=\left(xy\right)\iota_{A}{\left(xy\right)}^{-1}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Direct computation of $\iota_A(\sigma\tau c)$.

nodes.name: Conjugation sequence is a basis
nodes.statement: If $x$ is an $A$-conjugation sequence, then $\{x_{\sigma}|\sigma\in \gal(K/F)\}$ is an $K$-linearly independent set. When $K/F$ is finite dimensional and Galois, $\{x_{\sigma}|\sigma\in \gal(K/F)\}$ is a $K$-basis for $A$.
nodes.label: thm:conj-seq-basis

nodes.name: Proof of Conjugation sequence is a basis
nodes.statement: Suppose $\{x_{\sigma}\}$ is linearly dependent. Let $J \subseteq \gal(K/F)$ be such that $\{x_{\sigma}|\sigma\in J\}$ is a maximally linearly independent subset. Then $J \ne \gal(K/F)$, let $\sigma \in\gal(K/F)$ be an arbitrary automorphism that is not in $J$. Since $\{x_{\tau}|\tau\in J\}$ is maximally linearly independent, $x_\sigma \in \left\langle x_{\tau}|\tau\in J\right\rangle$. Hence, by~\cref{con:good-rep-mod} we have \[ x_\sigma = \sum_{\tau\in J'}\lambda_{\tau}\cdot x_{\tau} = \sum_{\tau\in J'}\iota_{A}\left(\lambda_{\tau}\right)x_{\tau}, \] for some non-zero $\lambda_{\tau}\in K$ and $J' \subseteq J$. For each $c \in K$, we have the following equality \[ \begin{aligned} \iota_{A}\left(\sigma \cdot c\right) x_{\sigma} &= x_{\sigma} \iota_{A}(c) &\text{by~\cref{def:conj-factor}}\\ &= \sum_{\tau\in J'}\lambda_{\tau}\cdot x_{\tau}\iota_{A}(c) & \\ &= \sum_{\tau\in J'}\lambda_{\tau}\cdot \iota_{A}\left(\tau\cdot c\right)x_{\tau} &\text{by~\cref{def:conj-factor} again}\\ &=\sum_{\tau\in J'}\iota_{A}\left(\lambda_{\tau}\tau(c)\right)x_{\tau};\\ \iota_{A}\left(\sigma\cdot c\right)x_{\sigma} &= \sum_{\tau\in J'}\iota_{A}\left(\lambda_{\tau}\right) x_{\tau}\iota_{A}(c)\\ &= \sum_{\tau\in J'}\iota_{A}\left(\sigma(c)\lambda_{\tau}\right)x_{\tau}. \end{aligned} \] Since $\{x_{\tau}|\tau\in J'\}$ is linearly independent, we have that for each $\tau \in J'$, $\lambda_{\tau}\tau(c) = \sigma(c)\lambda_{\tau} = \lambda_{\tau}\sigma(c)$. Note that $J'$ is not empty, for otherwise $x_{\sigma}=\sum_{\tau\in\emptyset}\lambda_{\tau}\cdot x_{\tau}=0$ but $x_{\sigma}$ is invertible. Since for any $\tau\in J'$, $\lambda_{\tau}$ is not zero, we have that for all $c \in K$, $\sigma(c) = \tau(c)$, i.e. $\sigma = \tau$. Hence $\sigma$ is in $J' \subseteq J$ after all; contradiction. If $K/F$ is finite dimensional and Galois, then $\dim_{F}K$ is equal to the cardinality of $\gal(K/F)$, then by the linear independence of $\{x_{\sigma}|\sigma\in\gal(K/F)\}$, we conclude that it is indeed a $K$-basis for $A$.
nodes.statement_short: Linear dependence over $K$ and the conjugation relations force two distinct automorphisms to agree. Galois case: count dimensions.

nodes.name: Maximal independent subset
nodes.statement: Suppose $\{x_{\sigma}\}$ is linearly dependent. Let $J \subseteq \gal(K/F)$ be such that $\{x_{\sigma}|\sigma\in J\}$ is a maximally linearly independent subset.
nodes.statement_short: Assume dependence; take a maximal independent subset $J$.

nodes.name: Express x_sigma
nodes.statement: Then $J \ne \gal(K/F)$, let $\sigma \in\gal(K/F)$ be an arbitrary automorphism that is not in $J$. Since $\{x_{\tau}|\tau\in J\}$ is maximally linearly independent, $x_\sigma \in \left\langle x_{\tau}|\tau\in J\right\rangle$. Hence, by~\cref{con:good-rep-mod} we have \[ x_\sigma = \sum_{\tau\in J'}\lambda_{\tau}\cdot x_{\tau} = \sum_{\tau\in J'}\iota_{A}\left(\lambda_{\tau}\right)x_{\tau}, \] for some non-zero $\lambda_{\tau}\in K$ and $J' \subseteq J$.
nodes.statement_short: Write $x_\sigma$ as a combination of $x_\tau$, $\tau\in J'$.

nodes.name: Two expansions
nodes.statement: For each $c \in K$, we have the following equality \[ \begin{aligned} \iota_{A}\left(\sigma \cdot c\right) x_{\sigma} &= x_{\sigma} \iota_{A}(c) &\text{by~\cref{def:conj-factor}}\\ &= \sum_{\tau\in J'}\lambda_{\tau}\cdot x_{\tau}\iota_{A}(c) & \\ &= \sum_{\tau\in J'}\lambda_{\tau}\cdot \iota_{A}\left(\tau\cdot c\right)x_{\tau} &\text{by~\cref{def:conj-factor} again}\\ &=\sum_{\tau\in J'}\iota_{A}\left(\lambda_{\tau}\tau(c)\right)x_{\tau};\\ \iota_{A}\left(\sigma\cdot c\right)x_{\sigma} &= \sum_{\tau\in J'}\iota_{A}\left(\lambda_{\tau}\right) x_{\tau}\iota_{A}(c)\\ &= \sum_{\tau\in J'}\iota_{A}\left(\sigma(c)\lambda_{\tau}\right)x_{\tau}. \end{aligned} \]
nodes.statement_short: Expand $\iota_A(\sigma c)x_\sigma$ in two ways.

nodes.name: sigma equals tau
nodes.statement: Since $\{x_{\tau}|\tau\in J'\}$ is linearly independent, we have that for each $\tau \in J'$, $\lambda_{\tau}\tau(c) = \sigma(c)\lambda_{\tau} = \lambda_{\tau}\sigma(c)$. Note that $J'$ is not empty, for otherwise $x_{\sigma}=\sum_{\tau\in\emptyset}\lambda_{\tau}\cdot x_{\tau}=0$ but $x_{\sigma}$ is invertible. Since for any $\tau\in J'$, $\lambda_{\tau}$ is not zero, we have that for all $c \in K$, $\sigma(c) = \tau(c)$, i.e. $\sigma = \tau$. Hence $\sigma$ is in $J' \subseteq J$ after all; contradiction.
nodes.statement_short: Coefficients force $\sigma=\tau\in J$, a contradiction.

nodes.name: Basis in the Galois case
nodes.statement: If $K/F$ is finite dimensional and Galois, then $\dim_{F}K$ is equal to the cardinality of $\gal(K/F)$, then by the linear independence of $\{x_{\sigma}|\sigma\in\gal(K/F)\}$, we conclude that it is indeed a $K$-basis for $A$.
nodes.statement_short: Count: $|\mathrm{Gal}|=\dim_K A$.

nodes.name: the Second Group Cohomology
nodes.statement: Let $G$ be a group and $M$ an abelian group (written multiplicatively) with a $G$-action. A function $f : G \times G \to M$ is a {\em 2-cocycle\/} if for all $g,h,j\in G$, \[ f(gh, j)f(g, h) = \left(g\cdot f(h, j)\right) f(g, hj). \] We denote the subgroup of 2-cocycles as $\mathcal{Z}^{2}(G, M)$. A function $f : G\times G \to M$ is a {\em 2-coboundary\/} if there exists an $x : G \to M$ such that for all $g, h \in G$ \[ \frac{g\cdot x(h)}{x(gh)} x(g) = f(g, h). \] We denote the subgroup of 2-coboundaries as $\mathcal{B}^{2}(G, M)$. The second group cohomology $\hh^{2}\left(G, M\right)$ is defined to be the quotient group of 2-cocycles modulo 2-coboundaries $^{\mathcal{Z}^{2}(G, M)}/_{\mathcal{B}^{2}(G, M)}$. If $s, t \in \mathcal{Z}^{2}(G, M)$, we say $s$ and $t$ are cohomologous if their equivalence class $[s], [t] \in \HH^{2}(G, M)$ are the same; in another word $st^{-1}\in\mathcal{B}^{2}(G, M)$.
nodes.statement_short: $H^2(G,M)$ = 2-cocycles modulo 2-coboundaries (multiplicative notation).
nodes.label: def:second-group-coh

nodes.name: Values of a 2-cocycle at the identity
nodes.statement: If $f \in \mathcal{B}^{2}(G, M)$ is a 2-cocycle and $x\in G$, we have \[ \begin{aligned} f(1, x) &= f(1, 1) \\ f(x, 1) &= x\cdot f(1, 1). \end{aligned} \]
nodes.label: lem:2-cocycle-one-one

nodes.name: Proof of Values of a 2-cocycle at the identity
nodes.statement: Indeed: \[ \begin{aligned} f(1\cdot 1, x)f(1, 1) &= (1\cdot f(1,x))f(1, 1\cdot x) \\ f(1, x)f(1, 1) &= f(1, x) f(1,x) \\ f(1, x) &= f(1,1) \end{aligned} \] and \[ \begin{aligned} f(x\cdot 1, 1)f(x, 1) &= (x\cdot f(1, 1))f(x, 1\cdot 1)\\ f(x, 1)f(x, 1) &= (x\cdot f(1, 1))f(x, 1)\\ f(x, 1) &= x \cdot f(1, 1). \end{aligned} \]
nodes.statement_short: Specialize the cocycle identity at identity elements.

nodes.name: Standing assumption: A is a good representation of X
nodes.statement: In the following sections of this chapter, we assume that $X \in\br(F)$ and $A$ is a good representation of $X$.

nodes.name: Notation rho, sigma, tau for Galois elements
nodes.statement: We use $\rho, \sigma, \tau$ to denote elements of $\gal(K/F)$.

nodes.name: Twisting Conjugation Factors
nodes.statement: If $x$ and $y$ are two conjugation factors of $\sigma$, then there exists a unique $c \in K$ such that $x = y\iota_{A}(c)$.
assumptions: $x$ and $y$ are two conjugation factors of $\sigma$
conclusions: there exists a unique $c \in K$ such that $x = y\iota_{A}(c)$
nodes.label: lem:twist-spec1

nodes.name: Proof of Twisting Conjugation Factors
nodes.statement: The uniqueness is clear: suppose $x = y\iota_{A}(c)=y\iota_{A}(c')$, then $c = c'$ because $x, y$ are units and $\iota_{A}$ is injective. We first observe that $y^{-1}x\in C_{A}(\iota(A))$: for any $z \in K$, $y^{-1}x\iota_{A}(z)=y^{-1}\iota_{A}(\sigma(z))x=\iota_{A}(z)y^{-1}x$ (by~\cref{rem:conj-factor-alternative-eq}). By~\cref{lem:centralizer-range-good-rep}, $y^{-1}x\in \iota(A)$, that is for some $z \in K$, we have that $y^{-1}x = \iota_{A}(z)$ and the claim is proved.
nodes.statement_short: Uniqueness by injectivity; existence since $y^{-1}x$ centralizes $\iota_A(K)$, which is self-centralizing.

nodes.name: Uniqueness and centralizing
nodes.statement: The uniqueness is clear: suppose $x = y\iota_{A}(c)=y\iota_{A}(c')$, then $c = c'$ because $x, y$ are units and $\iota_{A}$ is injective. We first observe that $y^{-1}x\in C_{A}(\iota(A))$: for any $z \in K$, $y^{-1}x\iota_{A}(z)=y^{-1}\iota_{A}(\sigma(z))x=\iota_{A}(z)y^{-1}x$ (by~\cref{rem:conj-factor-alternative-eq}).
nodes.statement_short: Uniqueness by injectivity; $y^{-1}x$ centralizes $\iota_A(K)$.

nodes.name: Self-centralizing
nodes.statement: By~\cref{lem:centralizer-range-good-rep}, $y^{-1}x\in \iota(A)$, that is for some $z \in K$, we have that $y^{-1}x = \iota_{A}(z)$ and the claim is proved.
nodes.statement_short: So $y^{-1}x\in\iota_A(K)$.

nodes.name: Twist notation
nodes.statement: We denote such $c$ by $\twist^{\sigma}(x, y)$ or $\twist^{\sigma}_{x, y}$, when $\sigma$ is clear from context, we often omit the superscript. With this notation, $x = y\iota_{A}(\twist_{x,y})$.

nodes.name: Twist of x with itself is 1
nodes.statement: $\twist(x, x)$ is equal to $1$ by uniqueness.

nodes.name: Twist is a unit and antisymmetric
nodes.statement: In fact, $\twist(x, y)$ is in $K^{\star}$ and $\twist(x, y)^{-1}=\twist(y, x)$.

nodes.name: Twist on the left
nodes.statement: If $x$ and $y$ are conjugation factors for $\sigma$, $x=\iota_{A}(\sigma(\twist_{x, y}))y$.
nodes.label: lem:twist-spec2

nodes.name: Proof of Twist on the left
nodes.statement: \[ \begin{aligned} x &= x \iota_{A}\left(\twist_{x,y}\right) x^{-1} x \iota_{A}(\twist_{y,x}) \\ &= \iota_{A}\left(\sigma\cdot\twist_{x,y}\right)x\iota_{A}\left( \twist_{y,x}\right)\\ &=\iota_{A}\left(\sigma\cdot \twist_{x,y}\right)y \end{aligned}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Direct computation with the conjugation relation.

nodes.name: Comparing Conjugation Factors
nodes.statement: Let $x$ be a conjugation factor for $\sigma$, $y$ for $\tau$ and $z$ for $\sigma\tau$. Since $xy$ is a also a conjugation factor, we define the comparison coefficient to be $\comp^{\sigma, \tau}_{x,y,z}:=\sigma\left(\tau\left(\twist_{xy, z}\right)\right)$. We often omit superscript when the context is clear. Note that $\comp_{x,y,z}$ is a unit in $K$ with inverse $\sigma\left(\tau\left(\twist_{z, xy}\right)\right)$. By~\cref{lem:twist-spec1} and~\cref{lem:twist-spec2}, we have the following useful equalities \[ \begin{aligned} xy &= \iota_{A}\left(\comp_{x,y,z}\right)z \\ \iota_{A}\left(\comp_{x,y,z}^{-1}\right)xy &= z \\ \iota_{A}\left(\comp_{x,y,z}\right) &= xyz^{-1}\\ \iota_{A}\left(\comp_{x,y,z}^{-1}\right) &= zy^{-1}x^{-1}\\ \dots &=\dots \end{aligned}. \]
nodes.statement_short: The comparison coefficient $\comp_{x,y,z}\in K^*$ with $xy=\iota_A(\comp_{x,y,z})z$ for factors of $\sigma,\tau,\sigma\tau$.

nodes.name: Cocycle identity for comparison coefficients
nodes.statement: Let $x : \gal(K/F) \to A^{\star}$ be a conjugation sequence. We have \[ \comp_{x_{\rho}, x_{\sigma}, x_{\rho\sigma}}\,\comp_{x_{\rho\sigma},x_{\tau},x_{\rho\sigma\tau}} = \rho\left(\comp_{x_{\sigma},x_{\tau},x_{\sigma\tau}}\right)\,\comp_{x_{\rho}, x_{\sigma\tau}, x_{\rho\sigma\tau}}. \]
nodes.label: lem:compare-conj-factor-spec

nodes.name: Proof of Cocycle identity for comparison coefficients
nodes.statement: It is sufficient to make the following calculations: \begin{align} x_{\rho}\,x_{\sigma}x_{\tau} &= \iota_{A}\left(\comp_{x_{\rho},x_{\sigma},x_{\rho\sigma}}\right) \, \iota_{A}\left(\comp_{x_{\rho\sigma}, x_{\tau}, x_{\rho\sigma\tau}}\right)\, x_{\rho\sigma\tau} \\ x_{\rho}\left(x_{\sigma}x_{\tau}\right) &= \iota_{A}\left(\rho\cdot\comp_{x_{\sigma},x_{\tau},x_{\sigma\tau}}\right)\,\iota_{A}\left(\comp_{x_{\rho},x_{\sigma\tau},x_{\rho\sigma\tau}}\right) x_{\rho\sigma\tau} \end{align} Then since $x_{\rho\sigma\tau}$ is invertible and $\iota_{A}$ is injective, we proved the desired result. \Cref{eq:1} is because: by the first equality in~\cref{con:compare-conj-factors} (twice) \[ x_{\rho}x_{\sigma}x_{\tau}=\iota_{A}\left(\comp_{x_{\rho},x_{\sigma}, x_{\rho\sigma}}\right)x_{\rho\sigma}x_{\tau}=\iota_{A}\left(\comp_{x_{\rho},x_{\sigma},x_{\rho\sigma}}\right)\iota_{A}\left(\comp_{x_{\rho\sigma},x_{\tau},x_{\rho\sigma\tau}}\right)x_{\rho\sigma\tau}. \] \Cref{eq:2} is because: by~\cref{def:conj-factor}, we have \[\iota_{A}\left(\rho\cdot\comp_{x_{\sigma},x_{\tau},x_{\sigma\tau}}\right)x_{\rho}=x_{\rho}\iota_{A}\left(\comp_{x_{\sigma},x_{\tau},x_{\sigma\tau}}\right),\] therefore by~\cref{con:br-base-change} \[ \begin{aligned} x_{\rho}\left(x_{\sigma}x_{\tau}\right) &= x_{\rho}\iota_{A}\left(\comp_{x_{\sigma},x_{\tau},x_{\sigma\tau}}\right)x_{\sigma\tau} \\ &= \iota_{A}\left(\rho\cdot \comp_{x_{\sigma},x_{\tau},x_{\sigma\tau}}\right)x_{\rho}x_{\sigma\tau}\\ &= \iota_{A}\left(\rho\cdot\comp_{x_{\sigma},x_{\tau},x_{\sigma\tau}}\right)\,\iota_{A}\left(\comp_{x_{\rho},x_{\sigma\tau},x_{\rho\sigma\tau}}\right)x_{\rho\sigma\tau} \end{aligned}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Expand $x_\rho x_\sigma x_\tau$ in two ways and compare coefficients.

nodes.name: Two expansions
nodes.statement: It is sufficient to make the following calculations: \begin{align} x_{\rho}\,x_{\sigma}x_{\tau} &= \iota_{A}\left(\comp_{x_{\rho},x_{\sigma},x_{\rho\sigma}}\right) \, \iota_{A}\left(\comp_{x_{\rho\sigma}, x_{\tau}, x_{\rho\sigma\tau}}\right)\, x_{\rho\sigma\tau} \\ x_{\rho}\left(x_{\sigma}x_{\tau}\right) &= \iota_{A}\left(\rho\cdot\comp_{x_{\sigma},x_{\tau},x_{\sigma\tau}}\right)\,\iota_{A}\left(\comp_{x_{\rho},x_{\sigma\tau},x_{\rho\sigma\tau}}\right) x_{\rho\sigma\tau} \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Expand $x_\rho x_\sigma x_\tau$ in two ways.

nodes.name: Expansion of x_rho x_sigma x_tau (left grouping)
nodes.statement: x_{\rho}\,x_{\sigma}x_{\tau} &= \iota_{A}\left(\comp_{x_{\rho},x_{\sigma},x_{\rho\sigma}}\right) \, \iota_{A}\left(\comp_{x_{\rho\sigma}, x_{\tau}, x_{\rho\sigma\tau}}\right)\, x_{\rho\sigma\tau}
nodes.label: eq:1

nodes.name: Expansion of x_rho x_sigma x_tau (right grouping)
nodes.statement: x_{\rho}\left(x_{\sigma}x_{\tau}\right) &= \iota_{A}\left(\rho\cdot\comp_{x_{\sigma},x_{\tau},x_{\sigma\tau}}\right)\,\iota_{A}\left(\comp_{x_{\rho},x_{\sigma\tau},x_{\rho\sigma\tau}}\right) x_{\rho\sigma\tau}
nodes.label: eq:2

nodes.name: Compare
nodes.statement: Then since $x_{\rho\sigma\tau}$ is invertible and $\iota_{A}$ is injective, we proved the desired result.
nodes.statement_short: Cancel and use injectivity of $\iota_A$.

nodes.name: First expansion
nodes.statement: \Cref{eq:1} is because: by the first equality in~\cref{con:compare-conj-factors} (twice) \[ x_{\rho}x_{\sigma}x_{\tau}=\iota_{A}\left(\comp_{x_{\rho},x_{\sigma}, x_{\rho\sigma}}\right)x_{\rho\sigma}x_{\tau}=\iota_{A}\left(\comp_{x_{\rho},x_{\sigma},x_{\rho\sigma}}\right)\iota_{A}\left(\comp_{x_{\rho\sigma},x_{\tau},x_{\rho\sigma\tau}}\right)x_{\rho\sigma\tau}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Apply the comparison equality twice.

nodes.name: Second expansion
nodes.statement: \Cref{eq:2} is because: by~\cref{def:conj-factor}, we have \[\iota_{A}\left(\rho\cdot\comp_{x_{\sigma},x_{\tau},x_{\sigma\tau}}\right)x_{\rho}=x_{\rho}\iota_{A}\left(\comp_{x_{\sigma},x_{\tau},x_{\sigma\tau}}\right),\] therefore by~\cref{con:br-base-change} \[ \begin{aligned} x_{\rho}\left(x_{\sigma}x_{\tau}\right) &= x_{\rho}\iota_{A}\left(\comp_{x_{\sigma},x_{\tau},x_{\sigma\tau}}\right)x_{\sigma\tau} \\ &= \iota_{A}\left(\rho\cdot \comp_{x_{\sigma},x_{\tau},x_{\sigma\tau}}\right)x_{\rho}x_{\sigma\tau}\\ &= \iota_{A}\left(\rho\cdot\comp_{x_{\sigma},x_{\tau},x_{\sigma\tau}}\right)\,\iota_{A}\left(\comp_{x_{\rho},x_{\sigma\tau},x_{\rho\sigma\tau}}\right)x_{\rho\sigma\tau} \end{aligned}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Use the conjugation relation.

nodes.name: from good representation to 2-cocycle
nodes.statement: Let $x$ be an $A$-conjugation sequence. We associate with $x$ a function $\mathcal{B}^{2}(x) : \gal(K/F)\times\gal(K/F)\to K^{\star}$ defined by \[ (\sigma,\tau)\mapsto \comp_{x_{\sigma},x_{\tau},x_{\sigma\tau}}. \] We will write $\mathcal{B}^{2}(x)$ as $\mathcal{B}^{2}_{A, x}$, $\mathcal{B}^{2}_{A}(x)$ or $\mathcal{B}^{2}_{x}$ as well.
nodes.statement_short: A conjugation sequence $x$ gives $\mathcal{B}^2_x(\sigma,\tau)=\comp_{x_\sigma,x_\tau,x_{\sigma\tau}}$.

nodes.name: B^2_x is a 2-cocycle
nodes.statement: For any $A$-conjugation sequence $x$, $\mathcal{B}^{2}_{x} \in \mathcal{B}^{2}\left(\gal(K/F), K^{\star}\right)$, that is $\mathcal{B}_{x}$ is indeed a 2-cocycle.

nodes.name: Proof of B^2_x is a 2-cocycle
nodes.statement: We need to prove \[ \mathcal{B}_{x}(\rho\sigma, \tau)\, \mathcal{B}_{x}(\rho,\sigma) = \rho\left(\mathcal{B}_{x}(\sigma, \tau)\right)\, \mathcal{B}_{x}(\rho, \sigma\tau). \] But this is exactly~\cref{lem:compare-conj-factor-spec}.
nodes.statement_short: Exactly the identity for comparison coefficients.

nodes.name: Second good representation B with conjugation sequence y
nodes.statement: Let us fix another good representation $B$ of $X \in \br(K/F)$ and a $B$-conjugation sequence $y$.

nodes.name: Isomorphism e and conjugating unit u between good representations
nodes.statement: By~\cref{lem:good-rep-iso}, $A$ and $B$ are isomorphic as $F$-algebras, we use $e_{A,B}$ to denote an arbitrary $F$-algebra isomorphism between $A$ and $B$. When there is no confusion, we write $e$ instead of $e_{A, B}$ Since $e \circ \iota_{A}$ and $\iota_{B}$ are two $F$-algebra homomorphism from $K$ to $B$, by~\cref{thm:skolem-noether}, there exists some $u \in B^{\star}$ such that for all $r \in K$, we have $\iota_{B}(r) = ue\left(\iota_{A}(r)\right)u^{-1}$ (or equivalently, $u^{-1}\iota_{B}(r)u = e\left(\iota_{A}(r)\right)$). When there is confusion, we write $u_{A, B}$ instead of $u$.
nodes.statement_short: An $F$-isomorphism $e:A\cong B$ and, by Skolem-Noether, a unit $u$ with $\iota_B=u\,e\iota_A\,u^{-1}$.

nodes.name: Transport of the conjugation relation to B
nodes.statement: For any $c \in K$, $\sigma\in\gal(K/F)$ and $A$-conjugation factor $x$ of $\sigma$, we have \[ \iota_{B}\left(\sigma\cdot c\right) = ue(x)u^{-1}\,\iota_{B}(c)\,ue\left(x^{-1}\right)u^{-1}. \]
nodes.label: lem:iso-conj-coeff-spec2

nodes.name: Proof of Transport of the conjugation relation to B
nodes.statement: From~\cref{def:conj-factor}, we have $e\left(\iota_{A}(\sigma \cdot c)\right) = e\left(x\iota_{A}(c)x^{-1}\right)$. Substituting it in~\cref{con:good-rep-iso-coeff}, we get \[ \begin{aligned} \iota_{B}(\sigma \cdot c) &= ue\left(x\iota_{A}(c)x^{-1}\right)u^{-1}\\ &= ue(x)e\left(\iota_{A}(c)\right)e\left(x^{-1}\right)u^{-1}\\ &= ue(x)u^{-1}\iota_{B}(c)ue\left(x^{-1}\right)u^{-1}. \end{aligned} \]
nodes.statement_short: Apply $e$ to the conjugation relation and substitute.

nodes.name: Push-forward of conjugation factors
nodes.statement: If $x$ is an $A$-conjugation factor for $\sigma$, we can obtain a $B$-conjugation factor for $\sigma$ by defining $B_{\star}x := ue(x)u^{-1}$ with inverse $ue\left(x^{-1}\right)u^{-1}$. We use~\cref{lem:iso-conj-coeff-spec2} to check that $B_{\star}x$ is indeed a conjugation factor for $\sigma$. If $y$ is a $B$-conjugation factor for $\sigma$, another useful constant is $v := \sigma\left(\twist_{y, B_{\star}x}\right)$. We have \[ \begin{aligned} y &= \iota_{B}\left(v\right)\, B_{\star}x \\ \iota_{B}\left(v\right) &= u e\left(\iota_{A}\left(v\right)\right)u^{-1}\\ v^{-1} &= \sigma\left(\twist_{B_{\star}x, y}\right) \end{aligned}. \] We also write $v_{x,y}$ or even $v^{A,B}_{x, y}$ when we stress the importance of good representation $A$ and $B$ and their conjugation factor $x$ and $y$.
nodes.statement_short: $B_*x=u e(x)u^{-1}$ is a $B$-conjugation factor; $v=\sigma(\twist_{y,B_*x})$ compares it with $y$.

nodes.name: Comparison of comparison coefficients
nodes.statement: Let $x$ be an $A$-conjugation sequence and $y$ a $B$-conjugation sequence. We have \[ \comp_{y_{\sigma}, y_{\tau}, y_{\sigma\tau}} v_{x_{\sigma\tau},y_{\sigma\tau}} = v_{x_{\sigma},y_{\sigma}} \sigma\left(v_{x_{\tau},y_{\tau}}\right) \comp_{x_{\sigma},x_{\tau},x_{\sigma\tau}}. \]
assumptions: $x$ be an $A$-conjugation sequence and $y$ a $B$-conjugation sequence
nodes.label: lem:compare-to-2-cocycle-aux

nodes.name: Proof of Comparison of comparison coefficients
nodes.statement: By~\cref{con:compare-conj-factors}, we have $y_{\sigma}y_{\tau} = \iota_{B}\left(\comp_{y_{\sigma},y_{\tau},y_{\sigma\tau}}\right)y_{\sigma\tau}$. By repeated application of~\cref{con:push-forward-conj-factor} and~\cref{con:good-rep-iso-coeff}, we have \[ \begin{aligned} y_{\sigma\tau}&= u\,e\left(\iota_{A}\left(v_{x_{\sigma\tau},y_{\sigma\tau}}\right)x_{\sigma\tau}\right)\,u^{-1}\\ y_{\sigma}y_{\tau} &= u\,e\left(\iota_{A}\left(v_{x_{\sigma},y_{\sigma}}\right)x_{\sigma}\iota_{A}\left(v_{x_{\tau},y_{\tau}}\right)x_{\tau}\right)\,u^{-1}\\ &= \iota_{B}\left(\comp_{y_{\sigma},y_{\tau},y_{\sigma\tau}}\right)y_{\sigma\tau}\\ &= \iota_{B}\left(\comp_{y_{\sigma},y_{\tau},y_{\sigma\tau}}\right)u\,e\left(\iota_{A}\left(v_{x_{\sigma\tau},y_{\sigma\tau}}\right)x_{\sigma\tau}\right)\,u^{-1}\\ &= u\,e\left(\iota_{A}\left(\comp_{y_{\sigma},y_{\tau},y_{\sigma\tau}}\right)\right)\,u^{-1}\,\,\,ue\left(\iota_{A}\left(v_{x_{\sigma\tau},y_{\sigma\tau}}\right)x_{\sigma\tau}\right)\,u^{-1}\\ &= ue\left(\iota_{A}\left(\comp_{y_{\sigma},y_{\tau},y_{\sigma\tau}}v_{x_{\sigma\tau},y_{\sigma\tau}}\right)x_{\sigma\tau}\right)u^{-1}. \end{aligned} \] Hence \[ \iota_{A}\left(v_{x_{\sigma},y_{\sigma}}\right)x_{\sigma}\iota_{A}\left(v_{x_{\tau},y_{\tau}}\right)x_{\tau} = \iota_{A}\left(\comp_{y_{\sigma},y_{\tau},y_{\sigma\tau}}v_{x_{\sigma\tau},y_{\sigma\tau}}\right)x_{\sigma\tau}. \] We also have by~\cref{def:conj-factor} \[ x_{\sigma} \iota_{A}\left(v_{x_{\tau},y_{\tau}}\right) x_{\tau} = \iota_{A}\left(\sigma\cdot v_{x_{\tau}y_{\tau}}\right) x_{\sigma}x_{\tau}. \] Hence \[ \begin{aligned} \iota_{A}\left(v_{x_{\sigma},y_{\sigma}}\right)x_{\sigma}\iota_{A}\left(v_{x_{\tau},y_{\tau}}\right)x_{\tau} &= \iota_{A}\left(v_{x_{\sigma},y_{\sigma}}\, \sigma\left(v_{x_{\tau},y_{\tau}}\right)\right) x_{\sigma}x_{\tau} \\ &= \iota_{A}\left(v_{x_{\sigma},y_{\sigma}}\sigma\left(v_{x_{\tau},y_{\tau}}\right)\comp_{x_{\sigma},x_{\tau},x_{\sigma\tau}}\right)x_{\sigma\tau}\\ &= \iota_{A}\left(\comp_{y_{\sigma},y_{\tau},y_{\sigma\tau}}v_{x_{\sigma\tau},y_{\sigma\tau}}\right)x_{\sigma\tau}. \end{aligned} \] Cancelling $x_{\sigma\tau}$ and by injectivity of $\iota_{A}$, the result is proved.
nodes.statement_short: Express $y_\sigma y_\tau$ in two ways through $u e(\cdot)u^{-1}$ and cancel.

nodes.name: Comparison for y
nodes.statement: By~\cref{con:compare-conj-factors}, we have $y_{\sigma}y_{\tau} = \iota_{B}\left(\comp_{y_{\sigma},y_{\tau},y_{\sigma\tau}}\right)y_{\sigma\tau}$.
nodes.statement_short: Write $y_\sigma y_\tau$ via its comparison coefficient.

nodes.name: Push forward
nodes.statement: By repeated application of~\cref{con:push-forward-conj-factor} and~\cref{con:good-rep-iso-coeff}, we have \[ \begin{aligned} y_{\sigma\tau}&= u\,e\left(\iota_{A}\left(v_{x_{\sigma\tau},y_{\sigma\tau}}\right)x_{\sigma\tau}\right)\,u^{-1}\\ y_{\sigma}y_{\tau} &= u\,e\left(\iota_{A}\left(v_{x_{\sigma},y_{\sigma}}\right)x_{\sigma}\iota_{A}\left(v_{x_{\tau},y_{\tau}}\right)x_{\tau}\right)\,u^{-1}\\ &= \iota_{B}\left(\comp_{y_{\sigma},y_{\tau},y_{\sigma\tau}}\right)y_{\sigma\tau}\\ &= \iota_{B}\left(\comp_{y_{\sigma},y_{\tau},y_{\sigma\tau}}\right)u\,e\left(\iota_{A}\left(v_{x_{\sigma\tau},y_{\sigma\tau}}\right)x_{\sigma\tau}\right)\,u^{-1}\\ &= u\,e\left(\iota_{A}\left(\comp_{y_{\sigma},y_{\tau},y_{\sigma\tau}}\right)\right)\,u^{-1}\,\,\,ue\left(\iota_{A}\left(v_{x_{\sigma\tau},y_{\sigma\tau}}\right)x_{\sigma\tau}\right)\,u^{-1}\\ &= ue\left(\iota_{A}\left(\comp_{y_{\sigma},y_{\tau},y_{\sigma\tau}}v_{x_{\sigma\tau},y_{\sigma\tau}}\right)x_{\sigma\tau}\right)u^{-1}. \end{aligned} \]
nodes.statement_short: Express $y$'s through $u e(\cdot) u^{-1}$.

nodes.name: Pull back to A
nodes.statement: Hence \[ \iota_{A}\left(v_{x_{\sigma},y_{\sigma}}\right)x_{\sigma}\iota_{A}\left(v_{x_{\tau},y_{\tau}}\right)x_{\tau} = \iota_{A}\left(\comp_{y_{\sigma},y_{\tau},y_{\sigma\tau}}v_{x_{\sigma\tau},y_{\sigma\tau}}\right)x_{\sigma\tau}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Equation in $A$.

nodes.name: Move coefficient
